title: 3 Books to read instead of doomscrolling every day
content: How often do you pick up your phone to check one notification and end up spending the next hour scrolling through Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts or endless social media updates? Doomscrolling has quietly become part of everyday life. What begins as a few minutes of entertainment can turn into hours of consuming content without much thought or purpose. While social media keeps us occupied, it can also leave us feeling distracted, mentally exhausted and dissatisfied. One way to break this habit is to replace mindless scrolling with something that adds value to your life. Reading is a great place to start. Even dedicating 15–20 minutes a day to a good book can help you develop new perspectives, improve your focus, and use your free time better. If you are looking for a reason to put your phone down, here are three books worth adding to your reading list. 3 Books to read instead of doomscrolling every day 1. Digital Minimalism by Cal Newport If you constantly find yourself checking your phone without a specific reason, Digital Minimalism is a good place to begin. In this book, Cal Newport introduces the idea of using technology intentionally rather than allowing it to dictate how you spend your time. He explains that digital minimalism is not about abandoning technology altogether. Instead, it involves identifying which digital tools genuinely add value to your life and reducing the ones that create unnecessary distractions. One of the book's key ideas is a 30-day digital declutter, which encourages readers to step away from optional digital activities and gradually reintroduce only those that serve a meaningful purpose. Why you should read it: This book can help you rethink your relationship with social media, set healthier boundaries with your phone and make more room for activities that genuinely matter. 2. Stolen Focus by Johann Hari Have you ever opened an app for a few minutes, only to realise that an entire hour has passed? Or found yourself switching between multiple tabs while struggling to finish a simple task? Stolen Focus explores the growing attention crisis and the factors that make it difficult for people to concentrate. Johann Hari investigates how technology, constant interruptions, information overload and other aspects of modern life affect our ability to pay attention. Rather than blaming individuals for having poor self-control, the author examines the wider systems and habits that contribute to distracted living. Why you should read it: If you want to understand why doomscrolling and constant notifications make it difficult to focus, this book offers an insightful look at the problem and how we can begin reclaiming our attention. 3. How to Break Up with Your Phone by Catherine Price If you have tried reducing your screen time but keep returning to the same scrolling habits, this book offers a practical starting point. How to Break Up with Your Phone explores how smartphones influence our attention , daily routines and relationships. Catherine Price encourages readers to examine their phone habits and understand what keeps them reaching for their devices. The book offers a 30-day plan designed to help readers develop a healthier relationship with their phones. Instead of asking you to give up technology completely, it focuses on making more conscious choices about when and why you use it. Why you should read it: This is a useful choice if you want practical steps to reduce unnecessary screen time, build better habits and spend more time enjoying life away from a screen. Also Read 5 lessons from 30 Something Millionaire by Mohit Chawla Final thoughts Doomscrolling can make us feel occupied without necessarily making our lives more meaningful. We consume hundreds of posts, watch countless videos and follow endless updates, yet often struggle to remember what we actually gained from all that screen time. These three books offer different ways to understand and address the problem. While Digital Minimalism helps you use technology more intentionally, Stolen Focus explores why our attention is constantly under pressure, and How to Break Up with Your Phone offers practical steps to change your habits. You do not have to stop using social media completely. Start by replacing just 15 minutes of scrolling with reading every day. Over time, that small change can help you build a more intentional and fulfilling routine.

title: Beyond the cloud: Why businesses are turning to on-device AI
content: AI tools have made it easier for businesses to analyze documents, generate content, and automate tasks. But how much do companies know about where the data they enter into these tools goes? At TechSparks 2026, Akash Saxenaa, CEO of Brilyant, discussed why businesses should consider moving routine AI workloads from the cloud to local devices. He argued that on-device AI can help organizations manage costs, protect data, and reduce their dependence on internet connectivity. The costs of taking AI to the cloud The economics of AI are changing. While the cost of individual tokens may be falling, Saxenaa pointed out that inference costs could rise as businesses deploy more AI agents and consume more tokens. Citing Gartner, he referred to predictions that inference costs could increase more than fivefold . Cost is only one concern. When employees use cloud-based AI tools, sensitive business information may leave the organization’s own environment. This raises questions about data privacy, intellectual property protection, and compliance with data protection requirements. Saxenaa cited India's Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act as another reason for businesses to review their AI infrastructure. “If you look at 83% of Indian enterprises, they have not yet begun comprehensive DPDP implementations, or they are not even aware. What is the cost? Rs 250 crore. Now, if you are a large company, 5,000 employees, that’s a budget line. But if you are an SMB, that's a company,” he said. For smaller businesses, in particular, the financial consequences of non-compliance could be significant. Saxenaa’s recommendation is to bring the model to the data rather than take the data to the model. Not every task requires a frontier model Saxenaa compared cloud-based AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude with on-device AI, where models run locally. Cloud-based tools can involve recurring input and output token costs, latency, and less direct control over where data is processed. On-device AI, by contrast, can operate without an internet connection and does not incur recurring token charges for local inference. “Almost 60-70% of your workload can move on to on-device. But the balance 30%, you will have to use large, complex, latest front-end AI models," Saxenaa said. He stressed that the two approaches are not mutually exclusive. Businesses can use larger cloud-based models for complex tasks while moving suitable everyday workloads to local devices. On-device AI: From the office to the factory floor Saxenaa outlined several areas where businesses could use on-device AI, including endpoint security, support operations, internal search, and finance. “There are these beautiful use cases out there for on-device: you look at endpoint security or support operations. All those things can be done on-device. You look at finance, local rack, internal search, finance, operations. Everything can be done on-device,” he said. For software development teams, keeping code on local devices can reduce the risk of intellectual property being exposed through cloud-based tools. In contact centers, on-device AI can support real-time call translation, note-taking, and product recommendations. These functions can operate locally, reducing dependence on network connectivity. Saxenaa also highlighted devices equipped with neural processing units (NPUs), which allow AI models to run locally. This can help reduce recurring cloud costs while supporting data governance and operational resilience. During his keynote, Saxenaa presented a case study involving Tech Paramount Solutions to show how on-device AI could be used in an industrial setting. The company’s TP Smart Sol platform combines visitor and vehicle management, asset management, energy monitoring, surveillance, and workforce management. With Brilyant's support, Tech Paramount Solutions explored using Apple's Mac mini as an edge-computing device to process video analytics locally, while keeping its platform connected to the cloud for alerts, dashboards, and remote access. The setup can process live AI video analytics from around 100 on-premise cameras. Tech Paramount Solutions' co-founder shared that deployment reduced annual security overhead by more than Rs 12 lakh, cut lifetime compute costs by over Rs 11 lakh per Mac mini compared with comparable GPU-based options, and increased factory machine uptime by more than 240 hours a month. Making on-device AI work at scale Moving AI workloads to local devices involves more than installing a model. Businesses also need to consider device management, security, governance, and the infrastructure required to support large-scale deployments. Saxenaa explained how Brilyant works with partners including Apple and Jamf to provide device provisioning, AI setup, and lifecycle management. Leasing and financing options can help businesses spread the upfront cost of devices over time. For organizations managing hundreds of laptops, Brilyant also offers containerized runtimes and governance measures designed to keep data within controlled environments. The larger challenge is deciding which AI workloads should run locally, which require cloud-based models, and how to manage data and devices across an organization. On-device AI will not eliminate the need for the cloud. However, as more capable models become available for local hardware, businesses have more options to balance cost, privacy, and performance. For Saxenaa, the shift is not about using AI everywhere in the same way, but deciding where workloads should run and where business data should remain.

title: Why storytelling can be a startup's strongest competitive moat
content: Technology, capital, and talent can help startups build and scale their businesses. But as competitors gain access to similar resources, founders also need to explain what makes their companies different. At TechSparks 2026, Shweta Rajpal Kohli, President and CEO of Startup Policy Forum, spoke about the role of storytelling in building a business. Leading a masterclass titled ‘Startups and Storytelling: Making Narrative Your Moat’, Kohli said founders often treat storytelling as something to consider after developing their products. However, before achieving product-market fit, their story is often what they are selling. “Every startup is a story no one believes in yet,” she said. The ‘why’ behind the business Kohli began by asking the audience why storytelling matters. Participants spoke about building trust, creating personal connections, and differentiating a business. She then used her own career to demonstrate what founders often leave out of their stories. After summarizing nearly 28 years of work in a few minutes, she asked the audience what was missing. It was the reason behind her decision to establish Startup Policy Forum. While she had explained how founders approached her to work with them, she had not mentioned the gap she had identified: India lacked an institution to represent the startup ecosystem’s policy concerns to the government. Kohli said a mission alone does not make a startup distinctive because competitors may have similar goals. Founders must also explain why them —what makes them suited to building the business—and why now —what makes the timing relevant. Their passion and the community supporting their work also help make the story harder to replicate, she said. Why details matter Kohli said people tend to remember stories more easily than statistics. Instead of simply presenting market-size figures, founders should explain how their products could change someone's life. She encouraged them to use techniques learned in school English classes, including anecdotes, sensory details, drama and emotion. Drawing on her own experiences, Kohli described how Startup Policy Forum's logo came about. An early backer had dismissed her initial designs as “tacky”. The eventual idea came to her while watching her son play with a Rubik's Cube. She also recalled how a chance meeting with a member at an airport became a social media post that gained traction. On another occasion, a session she attended at an awards evening reminded her of how the forum got its name and prompted a LinkedIn post. Her point was that founders need not wait for major milestones to find stories worth sharing. She advised them to document the early stages of their businesses, from the first garage office and notebooks to whiteboards and the arrival of their first employee. For founders who struggle to write, Kohli suggested talking through their experiences with a friend, recording the conversation using an AI voice tool and turning the transcript into a post. “You'll realize that you've actually said it well,” she said. Using AI without losing authenticity Kohli said AI has made storytelling easier, but it has also made it harder to stand out. Generic stories can now be produced in seconds, and readers can often recognize content that does not reflect a founder's own experience. She encouraged founders to use AI to improve their language, but not to generate facts or experiences. “You can write stories; you can't cook them,” she said. Referring to her own experience with the Rubik's Cube, Kohli said AI could help present the incident more clearly, but should not add details that never happened. She also stressed the importance of consistency. Founders may speak to investors, customers, the media, and government representatives, but the underlying story should remain the same. Changing it to suit different audiences can affect credibility. Knowing when to tell the story The masterclass also addressed how often founders should communicate and when their public presence could become a distraction. Kohli said storytelling should accompany meaningful business developments, such as a new feature, product launch, or milestone. However, founders must balance the time spent communicating with the time needed to build their businesses. She also cautioned that a founder’s public presence could become a liability if not managed carefully. While formats and audiences may change, Kohli said the facts behind a founder’s story must remain consistent. Storytelling can help startups attract attention, build trust, and connect with their audiences. But those stories need to be based on real experiences rather than manufactured narratives. Edited by Teja Lele

title: Neha Nagar wants to help people take control of their financial future through her debut book
content: Finance educator and content creator Neha Nagar recently launched her debut book Simple Money Serious Wealth: How to Turn Ordinary Income into Extraordinary Net Worth . Neha, who has been in the finance field for over a decade and in content creation for about seven years, decided to don the role of an author when she realised that, while people in India know more about money today than earlier, they aren’t necessarily good at managing it. “Almost everyone has watched a video on SIPs, insurance or tax -saving. They have information, but they don't have a structure. People start investing with excitement, but when markets fall or an unexpected expense comes up, they stop. Often, it's because they never had a plan behind that investment,” Neha tells YourStory. While a social media platform helps disseminate information, it has its structural limitations. A book, on the other hand, gives the author the space to explain an entire concept elaborately. “We wanted to help people build their own financial plan, choose products that actually suit their lives, and understand how to structure their money better. For me, social media can introduce people to money. But this book is about teaching them how to manage it,” says the New Delhi-based author. Her debut book Simple Money Serious Wealth was published on October 24. It sold over 3,000 copies in the first 24 hours, according to a post on the author's Instagram account. “At a bookstore in the city, we saw people in the 60–70 years age group picking up the book. Some were buying it for themselves, while others wanted it for their children and grandchildren. We also saw students, young professionals, working women, and parents,” she says. Also Read How Neha Nagar is demystifying personal finance through simple content Educating a nation of billions While embarking upon the book project, Neha thought that having explained finance through videos for seven years, writing a book would be a piece of cake. But she soon realised that was not the case. “A book has to work even when the author isn’t around. In my videos, if someone doesn't understand something, they can leave a comment and I can respond. But when someone is reading a book alone, every step has to be clear,” says Neha, who was recognised by Hurun India as India's most-followed female personal finance influencer in 2025. The creator-turned-author believes India is still far away from reaching financial literacy. There are many reasons for this, she says. One, our education system never teaches students how to manage salary , calculate insurance requirements, save taxes, or plan for retirement. The second reason is that money isn’t discussed openly in many Indian households. “So, one goes from never being made aware of finance to suddenly stumbling upon an information overload on social media. That transition makes it very hard for people to identify needful information from noise,” she elaborates. Also Read Beyond assets: Why 'family continuity' is the missing link in personal finance The ultimate reason is fear, says Neha. Many Indians still associate the stock market with gambling. Due to this notion, they do not make attempts to understand different investment options, and a lot of money remains in savings accounts without a clear purpose. “My goal with Simple Money Serious Wealth is to help people understand their own money, make informed decisions, and take control of their financial future. Because financial independence isn’t just about how much you earn; it’s about how confidently you can manage what you earn,” she says. Edited by Swetha Kannan

title: How Bout India built a travel company without selling packages
content: Himanshu Maru started Bout India in 2013 with a simple bet: that international travellers to India wanted something built around them, not a fixed itinerary sold off a brochure. Thirteen years later, that bet has become the foundation of a distinctive inbound travel business. Most travel companies begin by asking how many packages they can sell. Bout India took a different route. Founded in Jaipur in 2013 by Himanshu Maru, Managing Director; Bhupender Rana, Director, Operations; and Vinod Jhajharia, Director, Marketing, the company built its offering around a simple proposition: international travellers visiting India should not have to fit themselves into a pre-designed itinerary. Each journey is planned around the traveller’s interests, pace and practical requirements. The company’s model centers on 100% tailor-made trips, with no fixed group packages and a direct relationship between the traveller and the person responsible for planning the experience. Why tailor‑made mattered more than packages Planning a trip to India can be complex for a first-time international visitor. The country’s geographic scale, distinct cultural regions, transport options, and local logistics require decisions that go beyond booking flights and hotels. A traveller interested in Rajasthan may want heritage sites and local experiences, while someone visiting Ladakh may need planning around altitude, road conditions, and acclimatization. A wellness traveller heading to Kerala may prioritize retreat quality and time for rest. Maru’s founding insight was that travellers would value a company that removed this complexity while preserving the feeling that the journey belonged to them. Rather than selling a standard route, Bout India positioned itself as a planning partner. That approach is reflected in the company’s Destination Expert model. Each client is assigned a named expert who manages the relationship from the initial enquiry through the trip. Reviews published on the company’s website frequently mention individual team members by name. While testimonials are not independent audits of service quality, this pattern illustrates the personal accountability the company seeks to build into its operating model. Zero negative reviews and repeat travellers According to Bout India’s reported company information, its traction includes: 4.9/5-stars average rating across 970+ reviews on TripAdvisor and Google Maps A claimed zero-negative-review and 100% happy-customer record Travellers served from over 50 countries References to repeat customers who have booked second or third trips The distinction between company-reported claims and independently verified performance is important. Review platforms can change, ratings can fluctuate, and customer-satisfaction records should ideally be assessed through the underlying reviews. Nevertheless, the reported figures indicate the reputation Bout India has sought to build. For a services business, repeat and referral behavior can be especially valuable. A returning traveller is placing trust in the company’s ability to understand their preferences and deliver consistently. Keeping personal involvement at the core Bout India’s positioning continues to emphasize founder involvement. Company testimonials reference Maru personally checking in with clients, responding to concerns, and remaining involved in the travel experience. Its Destination Expert structure combines individual ownership with a broader team. The company has also expanded across categories, including heritage travel, luxury experiences, wellness and Ayurveda retreats in Kerala, high-altitude adventure travel in Ladakh and Spiti, wildlife safaris, spiritual circuits, honeymoon and family travel, and corporate/ MICE travel . Why bespoke journeys beat standardized tours Bout India’s model reflects a broader shift in the experience economy. As travellers gain access to online booking platforms and standardized packages, the value of a specialist may increasingly lie in interpretation, judgement, and reassurance. A booking platform can compare prices, but a specialist can help a traveller decide whether a route is realistic, whether a destination suits their interests, or how to balance sightseeing with rest. That is particularly relevant to inbound travel, where customers may be unfamiliar with local distances, seasonal conditions and operational realities. A tailor-made approach can address those concerns before they become problems. Personalized travel does require skilled staff, detailed communication, and careful execution. The company must, therefore, demonstrate that the additional service creates enough value to justify the model. Lessons in trust, service, and differentiation Bout India is not a technology startup in the traditional sense. Its core proposition is built around people, destination expertise, and service delivery. Yet its approach offers a lesson relevant to India’s wider services economy. In high-trust, high-consideration purchases such as international travel, radical personalization can be a durable differentiator. Customers may compare prices, but they also evaluate how confidently a company understands their needs and responds when plans change. For founders, the lesson is to identify which parts of the customer experience should remain personal as the business grows. Technology can improve communication and operations, but the underlying relationship still depends on judgement and accountability. Bout India’s journey illustrates one possible answer: build a system in which personal attention is not an exception, but a defining part of the product itself. (Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of YourStory.)

title: 5 lessons from Hospitality with a Heart by Amrita Tripathi
content: The stories that deserve to be heard are not always the ones that get told. Some remain hidden behind societal expectations, fear of judgement and the struggle to find acceptance. I recently attended the launch of Hospitality with a Heart, written by Amrita Tripathi, with an introduction by Keshav Suri, Executive Director of The LaLiT Suri Hospitality Group. Held on October 31, 2026, at the Crystal Ballroom of The LaLiT New Delhi, the event brought together the people behind the book and those who have been part of the organisation's inclusion journey. The book documents the personal journeys and lived experiences of queer team members at The LaLiT, exploring themes of identity, discrimination, resilience, acceptance and belonging. The evening began with a welcome address by Dr Jyotsna Suri, Chairperson and Managing Director of The LaLiT Suri Hospitality Group, followed by a keynote address by Saurabh Kirpal. A panel discussion moderated by journalist Faye D'Souza, featuring Amrita Tripathi, Rithik Hukku, Shaurya and Shruti, explored workplace inclusion, queer representation and the importance of empathy. The launch also featured the unveiling of the book by the Group's leadership and the people whose stories it captures, followed by drag performances by Hash Brownie and Hiten Noonwal. Beyond the celebrations, what stood out was the larger message of creating spaces where people are not merely included but genuinely accepted. 5 Important lessons readers can take away from Hospitality with a Heart 1. True inclusion begins with acceptance One of the central ideas explored in Hospitality with a Heart is that inclusion goes beyond simply allowing people to be part of an organisation. For individuals from marginalised communities, finding acceptance can be a difficult journey. Social expectations, discrimination, bullying and fear of judgement can make it challenging to express one's identity openly. The stories in the book highlight why acceptance matters. People should not have to hide parts of themselves to fit into a workplace or earn respect. True inclusion begins when individuals are welcomed for who they are, without being expected to change their identities to meet someone else's expectations. 2. Everyone deserves to feel safe and valued at work A workplace is more than a place where people earn a living. It is also where they spend a significant part of their lives, build relationships and develop their confidence. Through the experiences of queer employees at The LaLiT, the book highlights the importance of creating environments where people can work without constantly worrying about discrimination or judgement. It also reflects an important realisation in the organisation's inclusion journey: hiring people from marginalised communities is only the beginning. Organisations must also establish systems, policies and support structures that allow employees to feel protected and respected. A truly inclusive workplace is one where everyone has the opportunity to grow without compromising their sense of identity. 3. Empathy can change the way we see others People often form opinions about others without understanding the experiences they have lived through. Hospitality with a Heart encourages readers to look beyond assumptions and recognise the human stories behind individual identities. The experiences shared in the book include isolation, societal pressure, bullying and the struggle to find acceptance. These stories remind readers that everyone carries experiences that may not be immediately visible. Empathy begins when we make an effort to listen instead of judge. By understanding another person's journey, we can build stronger relationships and create communities where differences are respected rather than questioned. Also Read 5 Books you must add to your November 2026 reading list 4. Every individual story deserves to be heard Representation is important because it allows people to see their experiences acknowledged rather than overlooked. The book brings together the personal journeys of queer team members whose stories reflect different struggles, milestones and experiences. By documenting their voices, Amrita Tripathi creates space for conversations that are often missing from mainstream narratives. Sharing these experiences also challenges stereotypes and helps readers understand the realities faced by people from marginalised communities. The lesson is simple: listening to people and giving them the space to tell their stories can help build understanding. Every individual deserves to have their experiences recognised, respected and heard. 5. Belonging is built through everyday actions Perhaps the most meaningful lesson from Hospitality with a Heart is that belonging cannot be created through statements or policies alone. It is built through everyday actions. An inclusive environment requires consistent efforts from leadership , colleagues and the wider organisation. It means treating everyone with dignity, challenging discriminatory behaviour, listening to different perspectives and ensuring that people feel comfortable being themselves. The LaLiT's inclusion journey, as documented in the book, highlights the importance of moving beyond representation towards meaningful acceptance. Whether in a workplace, a community or personal relationships, making someone feel that they belong is an ongoing responsibility. Final thoughts Hospitality with a Heart by Amrita Tripathi is a reminder that behind every conversation about diversity and inclusion are real people with individual stories, struggles and aspirations. By documenting the lived experiences of queer employees at The LaLiT, the book explores what it means to move from representation to acceptance and from employment to genuine belonging. The October 31 launch brought these ideas into focus through conversations involving the author, the organisation's leadership, speakers and the people whose experiences form the heart of the book. Ultimately, the book leaves readers with an important thought: hospitality should not end with welcoming someone through the door. It should extend to making them feel respected, accepted and at home.

title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 10, 2026)
content: From Neha Nagar's debut book to tech leaders and startup founders that saw their careers derailed by personal scandals, YourStory brings you this and other latest developments across sectors. Featured stories Neha Nagar’s debut book aims to make personal finance accessible Finance educator and content creator Neha Nagar has launched her debut book, Simple Money Serious Wealth: How to Turn Ordinary Income into Extraordinary Net Worth , to help readers make informed financial decisions and manage their money better. Published on October 24, the book sold over 3,000 copies within its first 24 hours, according to a post on her Instagram account. Nagar, who has over a decade of experience in finance and seven years in content creation, says she decided to write the book after recognising that while people have access to financial information, many lack a structured approach to managing their money. Nagar believes financial literacy in India still faces challenges, including the absence of personal finance education in schools, reluctance to discuss money within households, and the overwhelming amount of information available on social media. Recognised by Hurun India as the country's most-followed female personal finance influencer in 2025, she wants the book to help readers build financial plans, understand investment options and make decisions suited to their needs. Her goal is to help people realise that financial independence is not just about how much they earn, but how confidently they manage their money. Read more Five tech and startup leaders whose personal controversies affected their careers From India to Silicon Valley, several prominent technology and startup leaders have faced career setbacks following controversies involving personal relationships or workplace conduct. YourStory looks at five such cases, including former Infosys executive Phaneesh Murthy, who was dismissed as iGate CEO in 2013 following an investigation into his relationship with a subordinate, and The Viral Fever (TVF) founder Arunabh Kumar, who stepped down as CEO in 2017 after sexual harassment allegations surfaced. Kumar denied the allegations and was acquitted by a Mumbai court in 2022. The list also includes former Intel CEO Brian Krzanich, who resigned in 2018 after the company found that his consensual relationship with an employee violated its non-fraternisation policy; former Google executive Andy Rubin, whose exit from the company came under scrutiny following reports of a sexual misconduct complaint and a $90 million exit package; and former HP CEO Mark Hurd, who resigned in 2010 after an investigation found violations of the company's business conduct standards. The report examines how the circumstances and outcomes differed across these cases. Read more Other news IIT Madras, Gauhati University researchers develop new method to identify monsoon onset at local levels Researchers at the Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IIT Madras) and Gauhati University have developed a new method to identify when the monsoon arrives at individual locations, distinguishing sustained monsoon rainfall from short-lived local showers. The climate-network approach tracks how clusters of local rainfall onsets across India connect and evolve into a larger, interconnected monsoon system. The findings were published in the Journal of Climate , a peer-reviewed journal of the American Meteorological Society. The researchers treated geographical locations as nodes in a climate network, with links representing spatial connections between locations experiencing local rainfall onset. By tracking the growth and movement of these clusters, the study offers an objective method to identify when local rainfall patterns become part of a larger, sustained monsoon system, rather than treating every spell of rain as the monsoon's onset. The study was co-authored by Yogenraj Patil, Gaurav Chopra, Shruti Tandon and Professor R I Sujith from IIT Madras, and Professor B N Goswami of Gauhati University. Paras Semiconductors partners with US-based BroadPak Paras Semiconductors, a subsidiary of Paras Defence and Space Technologies, has entered into a strategic technology partnership with US-based BroadPak Corporation to strengthen India's advanced semiconductor packaging capabilities. The collaboration will combine Paras Semiconductors' manufacturing ambitions in optoelectronics, photonics and co-packaged optics with BroadPak's expertise in advanced semiconductor packaging, heterogeneous integration and chiplet-based architectures. The partnership aims to establish an advanced heterogeneous integration and 3D packaging facility in India under the Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test (OSAT) model. The proposed facility will focus on 2.5D and 3D packaging, chiplet integration, hybrid bonding, wafer-level and panel-level fan-out packaging, co-packaged optics, and advanced semiconductor testing and qualification. BroadPak, headquartered in San Jose, California, brings experience in packaging design, manufacturing and system integration, with capabilities spanning architecture, simulation, assembly, testing and production. IIT Bhubaneswar study identifies silver iodide surface as potential host for stable electron spin Researchers at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Bhubaneswar have identified a specific surface of cubic zinc-blende silver iodide (AgI) as a promising candidate for hosting persistent spin texture (PST), a quantum phenomenon that could have applications in next-generation electronic devices. The study, led by Dr Manish Kumar Mohanta, Ramanujan Faculty in the Department of Physics at IIT Bhubaneswar, has been published in Physical Review B , a journal of the American Physical Society. Persistent spin texture refers to the stable, unidirectional alignment of electron spins in certain nonmagnetic semiconductors. Since electrons possess an intrinsic property called spin, alongside their electric charge, this phenomenon could enable information to be processed and stored using electron spin. The researchers note that persistent spin texture can suppress unwanted spin relaxation, allowing spin information to persist longer. This makes materials exhibiting the phenomenon promising candidates for spintronic devices, which use electron spin alongside electrical charge to process and store information. title: 5 tech and startup leaders whose personal scandals shook their careers
content: They built successful businesses, shaped industries and became some of the most influential names in technology. But for some, it was controversy over their personal lives, rather than competition or business failure, that disrupted their careers. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is the latest tech leader to face such scrutiny. His admission of an extramarital affair has come amid allegations of foreign intelligence activity, an independent board investigation and a shareholder lawsuit. Huang continues to lead Nvidia with the backing of its board, and the intelligence-related allegations remain contested. On November 9, Nvidia and Huang were named in a proposed shareholder class-action lawsuit alleging that they misled investors by failing to disclose his reported relationship with a businesswoman suspected by US authorities of working for Chinese intelligence, Reuters reported. The lawsuit followed Nvidia's November 8 announcement of an investigation into reports that Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. Nvidia has said it has no reason to believe company secrets or US national security have been compromised. China has rejected the espionage allegations. Huang's controversy brings to mind five other cases involving prominent tech and startup executives in India and abroad, although the allegations and outcomes differ. Phaneesh Murthy: The Indian IT executive dismissed by iGate In May 2013, Phaneesh Murthy was dismissed as president and CEO of US-listed IT services company iGate following an investigation into his relationship with a subordinate employee. Murthy had earlier helped build Infosys' international business before leaving the company in 2002 following a sexual harassment lawsuit, which was subsequently settled out of court. He later founded Quintant Services, acquired by iGate, and went on to oversee iGate's expansion, including its $1.2 billion acquisition of Patni Computer Systems in 2011. In a statement on May 20, 2013, iGate said an investigation by outside legal counsel had found that Murthy failed to disclose a relationship with a subordinate, violating company policy and his employment contract. The company said its investigation had not uncovered a violation of its sexual harassment policy at that stage. Murthy acknowledged the relationship but disputed the company's account of the disclosure and denied the harassment allegations. Following his dismissal, iGate shares fell approximately 13%, Reuters reported. Murthy later founded IT advisory firm Primentor, where he has served as CEO. In June 2025, enterprise AI company Covasant announced his appointment as a strategic advisor to help expand its global business. Arunabh Kumar: The TVF founder who stepped down but was later acquitted In June 2017, Arunabh Kumar, founder of digital entertainment company The Viral Fever (TVF), stepped down as CEO after sexual harassment allegations surfaced against him. The allegations first appeared in an anonymous online account by a woman claiming to be a former TVF employee. Other women subsequently made similar allegations. Kumar denied wrongdoing. TVF's then Chief Operating Officer Dhawal Gusain took over as CEO, while Kumar continued as a mentor to the content team. In September 2022, a Mumbai magistrate's court acquitted Kumar in a sexual harassment case registered against him in 2017. According to PTI, the court found that the prosecution had failed to establish its case beyond reasonable doubt, citing inconsistencies in the evidence and an unexplained delay in filing the complaint. The court also observed that the complaint could have arisen from a grudge or business rivalry. Kumar remains associated with TVF. In January 2026, the company announced a leadership restructuring under which he would focus on mentoring producers and showrunners while remaining involved in select creative projects. Brian Krzanich: The Intel CEO who resigned over a consensual relationship Brian Krzanich resigned as Intel CEO in June 2018 after the chipmaker discovered that he had previously been involved in a consensual relationship with an employee. Krzanich had spent more than three decades at Intel, joining as an engineer in 1982 before becoming CEO in 2013. Intel said an investigation by internal and external counsel confirmed that the relationship violated its non-fraternisation policy, which applied to all managers. The board accepted his resignation and appointed Chief Financial Officer Robert Swan as interim CEO. Intel described the relationship as consensual and did not publicly establish that it was extramarital. The company did not announce any finding of sexual harassment. Krzanich returned to a top executive position in October 2024, when he became president and CEO of Cerence, a Nasdaq-listed company developing AI-powered technology for the automotive industry. He continues to lead the company. Andy Rubin: The Android creator and Google's $90M controversy Andy Rubin, widely credited with creating Android, left Google in 2014 after helping establish the mobile operating system as a global platform. His departure was initially presented as amicable. However, a 2018 New York Times investigation reported that Google had investigated a sexual misconduct complaint involving Rubin and a female employee with whom he had been having an extramarital relationship. The newspaper reported that Google had found the employee's allegation credible and that Rubin had received a $90 million exit package. Rubin denied the sexual misconduct allegations and disputed reports that he had been forced to leave Google. The revelations prompted protests involving thousands of Google employees in 2018 over the company's handling of sexual misconduct complaints and accountability for senior executives. After leaving Google, Rubin founded technology investment firm Playground Global and smartphone company Essential Products, which shut down in 2020. In November 2025, The Information reported that he had launched Genki Robotics, a Tokyo-based startup working on humanoid robots. Rubin confirmed his involvement in the venture but declined to share further details. Mark Hurd: The HP CEO who resigned following a conduct investigation Mark Hurd resigned as chairman and CEO of Hewlett-Packard in August 2010 following an investigation prompted by a sexual harassment complaint from a former company contractor. HP said the investigation found no violation of its sexual harassment policy but identified breaches of its business conduct standards. Contemporaneous reports said the investigation had uncovered inaccurate expense reports involving Hurd's interactions with the contractor, who subsequently stated that they had not had a sexual relationship. Hurd's departure was therefore linked to findings concerning business conduct, not a substantiated sexual harassment allegation or a confirmed extramarital affair. He subsequently joined Oracle, becoming its co-CEO in 2014. Hurd died on October 18, 2019, aged 62, after taking medical leave the previous month. What the reported cases don't tell us These five cases attracted significant media attention. But there is no reliable public count of how many workplace relationship disputes or misconduct complaints involving senior executives are handled internally or never formally reported. Aon's 2024 Voice of Women study, which surveyed nearly 24,000 professional women across more than 560 Indian companies, found that 6% had experienced sexual harassment at least once. Fewer than half of those affected formally reported the incident to their employer. The survey did not specifically examine misconduct involving CEOs or senior executives, and cannot establish how many such cases remain undisclosed. The circumstances of the five executives differ. Some resigned after company investigations identified policy violations. Others stepped down amid allegations they denied, while Kumar was subsequently acquitted. In Huang's case, Nvidia's investigation is ongoing and the intelligence-related allegations remain contested. He continues to lead the company with the board's support. Feature image: Nihar Apte

title: With Jensen Huang under fire, Nvidia looks at sucession plans
content: The controversy surrounding Nvidia founder & CEO Jensen Huang has raised questions about the future leadership and succession planning at the company. At $4 trillion, the chipmaker is second only to Apple in terms of valuation. A report in the The Wall Street Journal says that Huang runs a very flat leadership structure with about 60 direct reportees and there is no visible second rung of leadership or any potential successors in the company. This has become an important question for Nvidia as Huang will come under increased scrutiny for his improper relationship with a Chinese national Alice Huang, who is allegedly a spy for the Chinese government. This relationship supposedly enabled China to get access to the high-end processors of Nvidia. Also, reports quoting United States President Donald Trump said that the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is looking into the relationship between the Nvidia CEO and the Chinese national. Trump has defended Huang as a very "honorable" man. In addition, the US Congress will also come into the picture seeking information on the kind of relationship and whether any sensitive technology has been passed onto China bypassing regulation. However, reports also quoting an Nvidia spokesperson said, Jensen Huang is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption. The Board of Nvidia has already stated that it would be investigating the entire matter. The leadership question comes into picture as there is the angle of national security with regard to the CEO’s relationship with the Chinese citizen and this brings the government into the picture. This is not a leadership crisis which a corporate typically faces where the issues are generally around business challenges, shareholder dissatisfaction, and physical health of the CEO. Jensen Huang has built a larger-than-life picture not just for Nvidia but also for the AI world. He is seen as an influential individual determining the contours of any new policy with regard to the AI industry. Along with this, he is also well networked with the various heads of States across the globe. Though, it must be noted that both his children, Madison Huang and Spencer Huang work at Nvidia. Additionally, his son-in-law Nico Caprez also works with the company. At this point of time, it is difficult to gauge the future direction of Nvidia as there are several elements in play. The improper relationship is one aspect, the bigger repercussion is whether technology was illegally acquired by a foreign country. Although at the same time, some industry watchers see it as a proxy fight between the United States and China to gain the upper hand in the world of AI. China is seen as being close to matching the technology prowess of the United States and potentially overtaking it.

title: National Startup Awards 6.0 opens applications; winners to receive Rs 25 lakh prize in 20 categories
content: The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) has opened applications for the sixth edition of the National Startup Awards, offering a prize of Rs 25 lakh in each category to recognise innovative, scalable and impactful startups across the country. These awards recognise startups demonstrating outstanding performance in innovation, scalability, sustainability and socio-economic impact, according to DPIIT. The award exercise is organised under the Startup India initiative of the commerce and industry ministry. It seeks to identify and recognise entrepreneurial ventures making significant contributions across 20 sectoral categories, spanning areas from agriculture to space technology. The awards also include special categories for women-led startups, North-East Startup Excellence, student innovators, and aspiring entrepreneurs. This exercise will provide national-level visibility and recognition to selected startups, while also facilitating access to industry stakeholders and potential investors. Further, the DPIIT-recognised startups are eligible to apply for these awards under the 20 sectoral categories and the specified special categories. Over 2.6 lakh units are recognised as startups by the department. Students aged 10 and above can also submit applications for the award, provided their proposed solutions align with the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047 and 'Shakti Ki Sapta Dhara'. On August 15, Prime Minister Narendra Modi laid out a seven-point reform framework, 'Sapta Dhara', aimed at accelerating India's journey towards becoming a developed nation by 2047, with a focus on manufacturing, agro-food production and food processing, technology and innovation, logistics, defence, green and blue economy, and soft power. Interested applicants can submit their applications through the Startup India portal at https://www.startupindia.gov.in/content/sih/en/nsa2026.html.

title: Arka Fincap raises Rs 525 Cr from The Rise Funds of TPG
content: Arka Fincap Limited, a Kirloskar Group-promoted non-banking financial company (NBFC) recently raised an initial investment of Rs 525 crore from The Rise Funds, the global impact investing arm of TPG. A statement said this agreement could also lead to an additional Rs 275 crore through a subsequent tranche, subject to the achievement of specified business milestones aligned with Arka’s growth strategy and requisite regulatory approvals. The investment from TPG will provide growth capital for Arka to expand its geographical reach and accelerate investments in technology and risk management capabilities. Founded in 2018, Arka is a diversified retail lending institution with an assets under management (AUM) of over Rs 8,000 crore and a presence across ten states through 146 branches. On the funds raised, Gauri Kirloskar, Vice Chairperson and Managing Director, Kirloskar Oil Engines Limited, said “As a Group, we have always placed great value on enduring partnerships and the institution-building ethos of creating businesses that stand the test of time. We seek partners who share this philosophy, and we see a strong alignment with TPG’s approach.” Arka offers a diversified portfolio of financing solutions spanning pre-owned vehicle financing, secured business loans, loan against property and wholesale lending. The company serves entrepreneurs, MSMEs, vehicle operators and corporate clients through a combination of specialised lending businesses and a growing distribution network. Samrat Gupta, Managing Director, Arka Fincap Limited, said, “Crossing Rs 1,000 crore in secured retail assets is a defining milestone in our ambition to build a formidable, future-ready financial enterprise, serving entrepreneurial aspirations of our country.” Simit Batra, BU Partner, TPG, said, “Many of India’s MSMEs and vehicle operators remain underserved by formal financial services, and Arka has built a disciplined, secured retail lending platform to serve these customers, with the potential to reach even more customers at scale.” Founded in 2016 by TPG in partnership with Bono and Jeff Skoll, The Rise Funds invest behind impact entrepreneurs and growth-stage, high-potential companies.

title: Nvidia probes whether foreign intelligence targeted Jensen Huang
content: Dear Readers, Nvidia’s board has opened an independent investigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The move follows a New York Times report alleging that a business executive with whom Huang had a close relationship passed information to Beijing. The company shares slid sharply on Monday following this news. Nvidia said its board had no reason to believe company secrets or US national security had been compromised. In other news, Sashikumar Sreedharan, the former MD for India at Google Cloud, has joined AI company Sarvam as President and Chief Business Officer. He will also be on the company’s board. Sreedharan will run Sarvam’s business across enterprises and government and expand its work with digital-native companies, developers and partners. Meanwhile, the India subsidiary of travel booking platform MakeMyTrip has received Sebi’s approval to launch an initial public offering (IPO). The proposed IPO is expected to comprise a sale of equity shares in MMT India by its parent MakeMyTrip and its wholly-owned subsidiary, ibibo Group Holdings (Singapore) Pte Ltd. Lastly, 2026 is on track to be one of the four warmest years on record, according to the World Meteorological Organization. In today’s newsletter, we will talk about How Bariflo uses AI to help factories treat wastewater How these Mothers of Courage are fighting to keep girls in school Here’s your trivia for today: What was Henry Ford’s original design for a car called? (Scroll down for the answer) In-focus How Bariflo uses AI to help factories treat wastewater Bariflo Cybernetics wants factories to get more use out of their wastewater treatment plants. The Odisha-based startup combines sensors, AI software, and automation to adjust treatment processes, aiming to reduce the energy and chemicals needed to clean water for reuse. It recently secured Rs 2 crore in milestone-linked funding from energy innovation platform MC² Plus, an initiative led by the Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas, and is preparing for a pilot with Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL), according to founder and CEO Mrityunjay Sahu. The funding comes as Bariflo moves from developing and testing its technology towards commercial deployments. That means persuading industrial customers to invest in upgrades that promise lower operating costs. Key takeaways Founded in 2018, Bariflo initially focused on monitoring and cleaning municipal waterbodies. It subsequently explored aquaculture, including shrimp and fish farming, before concentrating on industrial wastewater treatment and reuse. It is now engaged in making existing treatment infrastructure smarter and more efficient. Bariflo’s proprietary IoT sensors monitor wastewater parameters such as pH, total dissolved solids, and flow. Its AI models use the readings to determine chemical dosage and treatment processes at different stages. This automates some decisions that operators would otherwise make manually and helps plants respond as the characteristics of incoming wastewater change. The company has conducted pilots with Indian Oil Corporation’s R&D centre in Faridabad. Its planned BPCL pilot will test treatment efficiency, energy consumption, and chemical use in an industrial setting. Founder Sahu hopes successful validation will pave the way for a commercial work order. Social impact How these Mothers of Courage are fighting to keep girls in school Mothers of Courage , a documentary on girls’ education in Bihar, recently won the 2026 UN SDG Action Award in the Creativity category. It captures how women in rural Bihar are challenging social norms to keep girls in school. Directed by Vandana R Jaikumar and produced by Butterfly Effect Media, the documentary was chosen from more than 7,000 applications from 190 countries and territories. Key takeaways In rural Bihar, mothers are at the centre of a quiet revolution. They are negotiating with their families so their daughters can keep studying. Others are standing up for daughters-in-law who want to return to school. This quiet, stubborn conviction and resilience is the subject of the documentary. Mothers of Courage is part of Shikshagraha, a national movement to strengthen public education championed by Infosys Co-founder and former CEO S D Shibulal, and supported by Bengaluru-based non-profits ShikshaLokam and Mantra4Change. Urmila Kumari, State Head for Shikshagraha in Bihar, is the living embodiment of the movement. She has spent nearly three decades working for the rights and education of girls and young women. She says the UN recognition belongs to “thousands of women and adolescent girls whose courage and determination have driven the fight for girls' education and rights.” News & updates New GCC: SplashBI, a Georgia (US)-headquartered enterprise data intelligence platform, has opened its global capability centre in Hyderabad. The company plans to invest over $100 million over five to seven years in infrastructure, technology and talent to scale the Hyderabad centre and strengthen its global product engineering and delivery capabilities.
