title: From conversations to action: How Cogover is addressing commitment leakage in Indian enterprises
content: At 11 am, a borrower tells a collections agent they will make a payment on Friday. The conversation is recorded, the agent moves to the next call, and the account may be handled by someone else days later. When Friday arrives, does the team know what was promised, who owns the follow-up, and whether payment was received? This is the problem Cogover calls ‘commitment leakage’: customer commitments that lose context, ownership, or follow-through as work moves between people and disconnected systems. For Indian enterprises managing large volumes of calls, approvals and customer requests, the cost is not simply missed tasks. It is repeated conversations, delayed resolutions, and limited visibility into whether work actually gets done. The gap between a conversation and an outcome Most enterprises already have tools to store customer records, manage calls, and track tasks. The difficulty arises when employees must manually connect them. In lending, a promise-to-pay may be recorded without a clear next action. In brokerage, a customer seeking help with KYC can wait while teams coordinate. In real estate, a promised site visit may never become a confirmed appointment. Managers can see call volumes but may struggle to identify unresolved commitments. Employees piece together notes and messages, while customers repeat information they have already shared. Cogover is addressing that operational gap with an Agentic Enterprise Platform that brings CRM, built-in calling, workflows, and AI agents into one environment. Its central proposition is straightforward: a customer interaction should lead to a visible, accountable next step. What makes the approach agentic? An AI summary can save time, but it does not by itself assign an owner, approve an exception, or ensure a follow-up happens. In Cogover, AI agents are designed to participate in defined business processes. They can help extract information from a conversation, propose a record update or prepare a task. Permissions and workflow rules determine what can proceed automatically and what requires human review. Because calling is built into the same platform, an employee can dial from a customer record and access the relevant history, disposition, and subsequent work without moving between separate tools. A supervisor reviewing an exception can trace a task back to its originating interaction. The goal is not to replace employee judgment. It is to make the context, responsibility, and next action available to the right person at the right time. A promise-to-pay, followed through Consider a collections workflow. An agent calls a borrower from the account record. AI helps identify the proposed amount, payment date and intent. The employee checks those details before confirming the commitment. The workflow then assigns a follow-up with an owner and deadline. If the borrower requests an arrangement beyond the agent’s authority, the request moves to an approver with the conversation context attached. If a relevant payment-status integration is available, that update can guide the next action. When a deadline passes, the unresolved item becomes visible to the responsible supervisor instead of disappearing into personal notes. Crucially, the process distinguishes what the customer promised , what the employee must do, and whether the business outcome occurred . A completed follow-up is not the same as a received payment. Both need to be measurable. The same design can support brokerage KYC resolution, real-estate site-visit coordination and service escalations, each with its own ownership, approval and exception rules. Building around real enterprise processes Enterprise workflows rarely match a rigid template. An approval may depend on transaction value, customer type, or branch. A service exception might involve sales, operations, and finance. Cogover combines AI-assisted application creation with low-code configuration so teams can shape fields, stages, permissions, and escalation paths around those realities. They can review an initial working application and refine it against actual cases rather than relying solely on a static specification. That flexibility matters in enterprises where formal systems coexist with conversations, messaging and cross-functional decisions. To operate reliably, those informal handoffs must become explicit business rules. Why NetApp Excellerator matters Cogover’s selection for NetApp Excellerator creates an opportunity to connect this application-led approach with a broader enterprise data perspective. One customer request may depend on a recording, CRM history, an approval policy and a transaction update. For AI to assist responsibly, it needs relevant data and controlled access. For the organization to trust the process, actions need ownership and traceability. NetApp brings an enterprise data infrastructure perspective; Cogover brings the customer interactions and operational workflows where data is translated into decisions and actions. Participation in the program provides a setting to explore that connection further. Measure actions, not just activity For businesses evaluating agentic AI, Cogover suggests starting with a specific workflow rather than a broad automation target. Can managers identify every commitment made yesterday and its owner? Can approvers access the original context? How many follow-ups are overdue? How often must customers call again for an update? A focused pilot can measure ownership coverage, approval turnaround, missed deadlines, repeated data entry, and customer follow-up rates. Teams should also monitor errors and human corrections, not merely processing speed. For simple, low-volume work, shared task tracking may be sufficient. As customer interactions, handoffs, and approvals multiply, a connected system becomes more valuable. Cogover’s argument is that enterprise AI delivers practical value when it moves beyond generating information to helping people complete work with clear permissions, accountability, and evidence of outcomes.

title: IIFL Finance to raise Rs 6,414 Cr led by Blackstone
content: IIFL Finance has approved a Rs 6,414 crore ($686 million) primary capital raise, with Blackstone leading the round. The board cleared the preferential issue at a meeting on Tuesday. The deal is one of the largest primary private equity infusions in a listed Indian non-banking finance company, according to IIFL. Funds managed by Blackstone Private Equity will invest Rs 5,000 crore ($535 million) in compulsorily convertible preference shares, which will convert into equity at Rs 602 a share, in line with the regulatory price, within 18 months of allotment. The company said this would give Blackstone a stake of about 16 % on a fully diluted basis. The promoters, Nirmal Jain and R. Venkataraman, will invest Rs 1,264 crore (135 million) through a preferential allotment of warrants, and will continue as co-promoters. Anchorage Capital is also participating, with a Rs 150 crore (16 million) primary equity investment. The company and its promoters have signed definitive agreements with both investors. IIFL Finance said the entire sum will go in as primary capital. On a pro forma basis for September 2026, which would lift its capital adequacy ratio from roughly 17% to roughly 30%. The company said the money would support growth in its secured lending businesses, particularly gold finance, and could, over time, improve its credit ratings and lower its borrowing costs. Nirmal Jain, founder and managing director of IIFL Finance, said: “We are delighted to welcome Blackstone as a partner in IIFL Finance. Their investment is a strong endorsement of the franchise our team has built, and of the opportunity to bring formal, secured credit to millions of underserved households and small businesses across India. Venkat and I are investing Rs 1,264 crores alongside Blackstone, which reflects our own conviction in the Company’s next phase of growth. “This partnership is about more than capital. Blackstone brings deep experience in building market-leading businesses in India, strong governance discipline, and a global perspective. The investment strengthens our balance sheet and gives us the headroom to scale our franchises, invest further in technology, and deepen our co-lending partnerships with banks, while staying disciplined on risk and capital.” IIFL Finance also expects to draw on Blackstone’s global network and operational expertise, including in technology, data and artificial intelligence. Blackstone representatives are proposed to join the board, which the company said would strengthen governance while preserving its entrepreneurial culture. Mukesh Mehta, chief investment officer for India private equity and senior managing director at Blackstone, said: “We are pleased to invest in IIFL Finance, a leading retail lending platform in India with a strong franchise and commitment to serving underserved customers. Building great businesses has been central to our approach over more than two decades of investing in India, and we look forward to partnering with Nirmal, Venkat and the management team to support IIFL Finance’s continued growth.” The transaction remains subject to customary regulatory and shareholder approvals. Trilegal advised IIFL Finance, while Khaitan & Co advised Blackstone. IIFL Finance offers gold, business, home and microfinance loans, among other products, through 5,091 branches across urban and rural India. Blackstone, which says it manages nearly $1.4 trillion in assets, has been investing in India for 20 years."

title: Anthropic targets upto $1.4T valuation with $70 to $78 IPO price range
content: AI company Anthropic has set $70 to $78 as the price band for its initial public offering (IPO) which potentially values the company in the range of $1.26 trillion to $1.41 trillion. The company will be offering 825 million shares. According to the filings, leading technology companies such as Google, Nvidia, Microsoft, AMD, Broadcom will be purchasing $26 billion worth of shares in Anthropic through a private placement. Reports suggest that the company could raise in excess of $100 billion. The report also said Anthropic will be pricing the shares of its IPO on November 18 and trade on November 19. The shares will be traded on Nasdaq stock exchange. Anthropic, which has raised a total of $130 billion in funding, was last valued at $965 billion. The AI company's valuation comes at a time when investors are questioning the valuation of AI companies. Anthropic, which was founded by Dario Amodei and others in 2021, was earlier seeking a valuation of $2 trillion. In comparison, the company reported revenue of $1.16 billion and losses of $12.96 billion in the first half of 2025. Anthropic’s growth has been remarkable, with revenue rising from just $41 million in 2023 to $4.5 billion in 2025. In its IPO filing, Anthropic said, “We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history. If managed well, it could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, greatly increase economic growth rates, bring cures for major diseases within reach and solve problems that have resisted generations of human efforts.” “Anthropic aims to realise these while navigating and preventing the risks that come with a technological revolution this fast and this powerful.” Anthropic believes the diffusion of AI through the global economy represents one of the largest opportunities in history to improve how humans live and work, and it is just beginning. It further noted that the world has only begun to use the capabilities of today’s frontier models, and the gap between what Claude can do and how broadly it is used represents one of our largest growth opportunities, alongside continued advances at the frontier.

title: OpenAI unveils a 'Control Room' safety feature that shuts down AI agents from going rogue in 35 seconds
content: OpenAI has introduced Control Room, a feature that halts any artificial intelligence (AI) output that raises safety or security concerns within 35 seconds, the company said in a blog post. On the need for Control Room, the blog post said, “As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential issues, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed. To solve this, we built Control Room.” Control Room will be a central system to track model workloads across the research infrastructure of OpenAI. OpenAI said Control Room will connect every research inference workload, including agentic sampling for model training and evaluation, data processing, and more. It will work together with its misalignment monitoring systems The Control Room will be integrating a few systems: the workload, the inference engine and the centralised control room service. The workload is the job being run, such as a reinforcement learning experiment, an evaluation, a high-volume sampling or data processing job. The inference engine is the key of any AI model. The Control Room service tracks jobs and controls whether they are allowed to continue generating model output. The blog post noted that engines check with the Control Room service before fulfilling a request. If a job has been stopped, the service denies the request, preventing further output. OpenAI said it runs continuous checks to detect unauthorised or modified inference engine implementations that may bypass Control Room. “We additionally run continual agentic and programmatic sweeps to check that users are not accidentally or maliciously launching rogue engine implementations with Control Room unimplemented or disabled,” it noted. OpenAI said it will continue to strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside its investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches.

title: SplashBI opens GCC in Hyderabad, to invest over $100M
content: SplashBI, a Georgia (US)-headquartered enterprise data intelligence platform, has opened its global capability centre (GCC) in Hyderabad. The company plans to invest over $100 million over the next five to seven years in infrastructure, technology and talent to scale the Hyderabad centre and strengthen its global product engineering and delivery capabilities, a release said. The 20,000-square-foot facility, with capacity for 275 professionals, was inaugurated by Telangana IT Minister D Sridhar Babu. SplashBI has had a presence in Hyderabad since 2014. The new facility brings its teams in the city together under one roof, designed to support collaboration and growth, the release said. The centre will support the development of SplashBI’s data intelligence platform and global customer delivery, helping enterprises connect business data, establish shared business context and use that data for decisions, AI, analytics and reporting, it said. Platform engineering, AI development, domain analytics and customer delivery teams will work closely together at the Global Capability Center, the release said. They will work on data connectivity and business modelling, develop SplashAI capabilities and support customer implementations. “Enterprises need a practical way to turn the data they already have into decisions they can trust. That requires understanding how their business works, connecting information across functions and giving people useful ways to explore it,” said Naveen Miglani, CEO and Co-Founder of SplashBI. “Our Hyderabad centre strengthens the engineering and customer expertise behind that work, as we help customers advance their data foundations and adopt AI with the right business context,” he added. Kiran Reddy Pasham, President and Co-Founder of SplashBI, said, “Our teams in Hyderabad will build the platform capabilities and domain content that help customers connect their data, make sense of it and use it in their everyday work.”

title: MakeMyTrip's India arm gets Sebi nod to float IPO
content: Nasdaq-listed travel booking platform MakeMyTrip's India subsidiary has received Sebi's approval to launch an initial public offering (IPO), according to an update available on the markets regulator's website. MakeMyTrip (India) Ltd (MMT India) had filed draft papers with Sebi in July through the confidential route. After examining the draft documents, the regulator issued its final observations on November 6. Sebi's observations mark an important step in the IPO process, allowing the company to proceed with preparations for its public issues, subject to applicable regulatory requirements. The proposed IPO is expected to comprise a sale of equity shares in MMT India by its parent MakeMyTrip and its wholly-owned subsidiary, ibibo Group Holdings (Singapore) Pte Ltd, the Gurugram-headquartered company said in a regulatory filing with Nasdaq. Following the completion of the proposed IPO, MMT India will continue to remain a subsidiary of MakeMyTrip, with its financial results continuing to be consolidated with those of the parent company, it had said. "MakeMyTrip expects the proposed initial public offering and listing of MMT India to enhance its brand visibility and support MMT India's ability to incentivise and promote talent in a competitive technology recruitment landscape," the filing stated. The net proceeds received by MakeMyTrip and ibibo Group Holdings from the sale of shares in MMT India are expected to strengthen the parent's cash position. The proceeds will be utilised for long-term growth, strategic inorganic initiatives and repurchases of different classes of securities, including convertible securities, by MakeMyTrip, the filing stated. MakeMyTrip swung back into profit for the three months ending September, 2026 boosted by increased booking across all categories. The company reported a net profit of $1.8 million for the second quarter of FY27 as compared to loss of $5.7 million in the similar period a year ago. The revenue for the second quarter touched $235.2 million which was a 11.2% increase when compared to the similar period of last fiscal.

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admits affair amid Chinese spying allegations; board launches probe
content: Nvidia has launched an independent investigation into reports that its founder and CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese intelligence operation, following his admission of an extramarital affair with a business executive whom US intelligence officials reportedly suspect of passing information to Beijing. The development has raised questions about corporate security and the potential exposure of sensitive information at the world's most valuable company, whose advanced chips are central to the global artificial intelligence race. In a letter to employees obtained by multiple news organisations, Huang, 63, acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and apologised to his family and colleagues. He said he took full responsibility for his actions. "Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life," Huang wrote. "My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility." Nvidia's board announced on Sunday that it would examine reports suggesting Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The investigation will be overseen by a committee of independent directors, assisted by external legal counsel. The board said it had no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia's confidential information had been compromised. However, it said the inquiry would review all available information. Huang has agreed to cooperate with the investigation and will continue serving as CEO. "Today's news will not slow Nvidia," company spokesperson John Rizzo said in a statement, adding that Huang remained committed to leading the company without interruption. Who is Alice Huang? The investigation follows a report by The New York Times in October that US intelligence agencies had identified a close relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and business executive who allegedly supplied information to Beijing. The two are not related. Alice Huang, a former television reporter in China, subsequently became a senior executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, a major purchaser of Nvidia's AI chips. According to The New York Times , Megaspeed purchased more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years. US authorities have also scrutinised Megaspeed over suspicions that it helped China obtain advanced AI processors subject to American export restrictions. The allegations involving Alice Huang have not been established by Nvidia's investigation, and the company has not reported evidence that its confidential information was compromised. US lawmakers seek answers The controversy has drawn attention from senior lawmakers in Washington, with three Republican congressional committee chairs seeking a closed-door briefing from Huang. In a letter dated November 4, House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, House Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar and House Intelligence Committee Chairman Eric Crawford asked Huang to provide a briefing on November 18, according to Reuters. The lawmakers raised concerns about whether the alleged intelligence operation could have exposed sensitive American technology or information to China. Nvidia previously said Huang interacts with thousands of customer executives annually and that its cloud customers in Asia receive ordinary business information rather than sensitive trade secrets or information connected to US national security. The company also said it acts on information received from US authorities about parties or organisations of concern. Trump backs Huang US President Donald Trump defended Huang on Sunday, praising his leadership and indicating that the controversy would not necessarily affect their working relationship. Speaking to reporters before returning to the White House, Trump said Huang had done an exceptional job and indicated he remained open to taking the Nvidia chief on an upcoming trip to Asia. Huang serves on the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, declined to comment on the allegations, citing the nature of the matter and Nvidia's internal investigation. Why the investigation matters The controversy comes at a sensitive time for Nvidia, which has become one of the most influential companies in the global AI industry. Its graphics processing units power the infrastructure used to develop and deploy advanced AI models. The company's dominance has also placed it at the centre of US-China technology tensions, particularly as Washington restricts exports of advanced chips to China. The investigation presents Nvidia with questions extending beyond Huang's personal conduct, including the adequacy of corporate safeguards and whether intelligence concerns warrant changes to how senior executives engage with customers and business partners. For now, Nvidia's board has expressed confidence in Huang's continued leadership. Whether the investigation identifies any security lapses, and whether those findings lead to further corporate action, remains to be seen.

title: Startup ecosystem sees sharp rise VC inflow; Building a hemp ecosystem in Uttarakhand
content: Happy Diwali, Financial services firm Angel One has climbed to the position of India’s second-largest stockbroker by active client count, according to the latest National Stock Exchange (NSE) data. By the end of October, the brokerage reported 69.98 lakh active investors, commanding a 14.97% share of the exchange's total 4.67 crore active client base. Meanwhile, benchmark indices Sensex and Nifty edged lower during Sunday’s special Muhurat trading session as profit-taking halted a seven-day rally, snapping an eight-year Diwali winning streak. The BSE Sensex dipped 28.62 points, or 0.04%, to settle at 80,999.40, with 16 of its constituents ending higher and 14 lower. During the special session on Diwali, it hit a high of 81,442.11, surging 414.09 points, or 0.51%, PTI reported. In the world of technology, a new cybercrime ‘ gold rush ’ is emerging as more and more people use the internet. Per a BBC Future article, around two billion people are expected to come online for the first time by 2030, but this digital leap comes with serious risks. Rather than entering a simple web, these newcomers are stepping straight into sophisticated cybercrime traps powered by AI, automated scams, and localised fraud. As CrowdStrike’s Zeki Turedi notes, while the internet unlocks life-changing opportunities, today's digital landscape is far more complex and dangerous for first-time users than the one earlier generations navigated. In today’s newsletter, we will talk about Startup ecosystem sees sharp rise VC inflow Building a hemp ecosystem in Uttarakhand Here’s your trivia for today: What iconic consumer luggage company was founded in 1971 by Dilip Piramal, named after a Roman goddess of victory? (Scroll down for answer) Venture capital Startup ecosystem sees sharp rise VC inflow November began on a positive note for the Indian startup ecosystem with venture capital inflow seeing a sharp rise. In total, the amount was $263 million across 23 deals against $115 million raised a week ago. This week marked two notable milestones for the Indian startup ecosystem. Total weekly funding comfortably crossed the $200 million mark—rebounding after a four-week slump below that threshold. Simultaneously, jewellery brand GIVA snapped the ecosystem’s month-long megadeal drought with a $100 million round. Key takeaways: Industry watchers expect that a post-US midterm slowdown in AI funding could work in favor of Indian startups. Consumer AI startup EloElo Group raised $80 million from Hornbill Capital, NBCUniversal, MIT Investment Co, Play Ventures, Kalaari Capital, Waterbridge Ventures and Griffin Gaming Partners. Peppermint Robotics raised Rs 100 crore (~$10.5 million) from pi Ventures, Crane Venture Partners and Asiana Fund. Social impact Building a hemp ecosystem in Uttarakhand While pursuing a master’s in Social Entrepreneurship at the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, Pavitra Joshi decided to return to the mountains, determined to tackle regional challenges through enterprise. What began as a classroom project soon evolved into KumaonKhand, a social enterprise building a hemp-based ecosystem in Uttarakhand. In 2021, Joshi turned the initiative into a full-time venture alongside his mother, Sangeeta, and Anuj Sharma, founder and CEO of impact incubator Alsisar Impact. Key takeaways: KumaonKhand’s product range is largely focused on hemp seed and hemp fibre. From hemp seed, they process hemp seed oil, which is in high demand in the skincare and pharmaceutical industries. The company uses hemp in its own skincare range: lip balms, face creams, moisturisers, and handmade, sulphate-free soaps. It also makes hemp protein powder that has 44 grams of protein per 100 grams, making it one of the best sources of vegan protein. Built using hemp-based materials, KumaonKhand’s factory incorporates hemp plaster and leftover hemp stalks as construction material. The material, known as hempcrete, is also being developed into a pre-mix plaster combining hemp and lime. title: Google Cloud India MD Shashikumar Sreedharan joins Sarvam as President and CBO
content: Sarvam, one of the leading artificial intelligence (AI) startups in India, has announced the appointment of Sashikumar Sreedharan as President and Chief Business Officer. Sreeedharan was previously Managing Director - India of Google Cloud. A blog post by Sarvam said Sreedharan will also be joining as a board member of the company. His responsibilities include leading the business of Sarvam across enterprises and government, and expanding its work with digital native companies, developers and partners. He will also be responsible for marketing, finance, forward deployed engineering, service delivery, and commercial operations. “India should be a maker of the intelligence the world runs on. For me, joining Sarvam is a commitment to that opportunity. I look forward to working with the team and our customers to build products that become part of how industries and governments operate,” said Sreedharan. Sreeedharan has more than three decades of experience building and leading technology businesses. Previously, he led Microsoft India’s enterprise business as the managing director for over five years. Sarvam said the new appointment comes at a time when the startup is growing in scale and scope. It noted that over 100 enterprises and government institutions are building with Sarvam’s full-stack offering. “The next phase of Sarvam is about advancing our research, developing products loved by people around the world, and building a company that can operate at a much greater scale. Every enterprise should own its AI,” the blog post said. Sarvam became a unicorn startup after raising $234 million in the first close of its Series B funding round in June 2026. This round valued the company at $1.5 billion and saw participation from investors such as HCLTech, Bessemer Venture Partners, Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners.

title: Workflow, AI, health: test your business creativity with Edition 257 of our weekly quiz!
content: Lateral Sparks, the weekly quiz from YourStory, tests your domain knowledge, business acumen, and lateral thinking skills (see the previous edition here ). In this 257th edition of the quiz, we present issues tackled by real-life entrepreneurs in their startup journeys. What would you do if you were in their shoes? At the end of the quiz, you will find out what the entrepreneurs and innovators themselves actually did. Would you do things differently? Check out YourStory’s Book Review section as well, with takeaways from over 355 titles on creativity and entrepreneurship, and our weekend PhotoSparks section on creativity in the arts. Also Read Breaking barriers in 2025: Women’s progress at work and what the road ahead demands Q1: Healthcare The healthcare system is generally built to treat illness, not to find it early. Where are the entrepreneurial opportunities in preventive care at scale? Q2: Elder care Senior citizens today are unwilling to let age define how they live, and are looking for more quality of lifestyle. Where is the business opportunity here? Also Read Year in Review: Top 10 celebrity-backed ventures of 2025 Q3: Recycling Efficient recycling of components in used objects can be complex in terms of determining what is inside, how much material can be recovered, and what it will cost to process. How can efficiency be improved here? Q4: Social insights Social media is a key discovery and evaluation channel for consumers, but brands don’t leverage these insights well. What can be done to deepen and apply business signals here? Q5: Construction Cost overruns, project delays, and disconnected processes remain major challenges in the construction industry. How can technology help here? Answers! Congratulations on having come this far! But there’s more to come – answers to these five questions (below), as well as links to articles with more details on the entrepreneurs’ solutions. Happy reading, happy learning – and happy creating! A1: Healthcare Founded by Shashank ND, Arpit Garg, and Anshul Khandelwal, healthtech startup Cent is building a vertically integrated preventive health platform. It combines customised hardware, AI-driven radiology, and bioinformatics. It has reportedly completed 10,000 preventive whole-body scans in three cities since launch, and is targeting 10 million scans by 2035. Read more here about its disease detection capabilities, and its recent fundraise from Blume Ventures and South Park Commons. A2: Elder care Founded by Sharad Gadsing, Cradle Of Life focuses on offering seniors four fundamental human aspirations: freedom, purpose, health, and happiness. It enables seniors to learn, contribute and pursue what matters personally. In terms of design, the residential facilities include a central balcony that extends to every room, layouts with more usable area, and safety through age-friendly furniture. Read more here about its other offerings in healthcare, emergency response, wellness, and community engagement. Also Read Year in review: startups that raised big from VCs in 2025 A3: Recycling Attero is an e-waste and battery recycling company that uses AI to speed up decisions across thousands of appliances, suppliers and locations. It processes 200,000 metric tonnes of e-waste and 10,000 metric tonnes of lithium-ion batteries annually, according to Ayush Agarwal, Head of Product. Its pricing engine combines material intelligence with market intelligence to calculate what the material should cost in a particular market. Read more here about its AI-powered compliance engine that checks documents, reconciles information across records, and flags exceptions. A4: Social insights “Brands today are drowning in signals and starved of action,” explains J Venkat, Co-founder of Live2.ai. It monitors conversations across Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, X, and review websites. It integrates trend analysis, influencer-content audits, campaign publishing, and performance measurement for ecommerce. Read more here about how it serves more than 200 brands across the US, Europe and Southeast Asia. Also Read How IIT Madras Incubation Cell is powering India’s next-gen deeptech startups A5: Construction Founded by Saurav Bhaik and Ankit Sinha, ﻿Tagbin has developed an AI-powered product that integrates architectural drawings, mechanical systems, and project costing. The integrated workflow can be controlled through natural-language prompts. The platform generates building models, incorporates applicable regulations, and creates construction schedules. Read more here about how it also takes soil-bearing strength and the water table into account while generating foundations and excavation plans. title: Angel One becomes India's second-largest broker by active clients
content: Financial Services firm Angel One has become the country's second-largest stockbroker in terms of active clients, with 69.98 lakh investors on the National Stock Exchange at the end of October, according to the exchange's latest data. With an active client base of 69.98 lakh, the brokerage now accounts for 14.97% of 4.67 crore active clients across all brokers on the exchange. The firm added 2.43 lakh net active clients on NSE in October alone. Its overall client base reached 4.06 crore at the end of October, up 17.4% year-on-year. The company crossed the 4-crore mark during the month after adding nearly 15 lakh clients in the July-September quarter. Trading activity also picked up in October, with average daily orders rising 19.6% month-on-month to 69.7 lakh. Gross client additions stood at 6.6 lakh, the highest in nine months. In terms of the number one position, Groww retained its spot with 1.37 crore active clients for the month of October. It also added the highest number of clients at 3.04 lakh during the month and also Groww’s market share was 29.43%. Bengaluru headquartered Zerodha slipped to third position with overall 67.59 lakh active clients for the month of October which was down by 32,435 from 67.91 lakh in September. This resulted in Zerodha’s market share slipping to 14.46%. The growth in client numbers of Angel One came alongside an improvement in financial performance. Angel One's consolidated revenue from operations rose 18.7% year-on-year to Rs 1,427 crore, and net profit grew 58.2% to Rs 335 crore. Its wealth management assets under management stood at Rs 16,000 crore at the end of the quarter, up 19.1 per cent sequentially.

title: Artist Bhagya Ajaikumar explains how good curation balances individual expression and collective vision
content: Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,030 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival , telecom expo , millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival. The Venkatappa and Swasti art galleries in Bengaluru recently hosted the group exhibition titled Bhoomi (see our coverage of earlier exhibitions at Venkatappa gallery here ). It was curated by Bhagya Ajaikumar and Pradeep Kumar DM, with works by around 40 artists. The Swasti gallery was launched in Bengaluru in 2007 to promote art and raise funds for the HCG Foundation as support for cancer patients. Since 2018, Swasti has also conducted art therapy events for cancer patients and their family members. Dedicated art space in a hospital setting gives a positive energy to patients and their family members. With that goal in mind, Swasti has been actively involved in organising art shows, camps and workshops, with artists coming from across the country and abroad. “I am currently planning and working on several exciting projects, both as an artist and a curator. This includes a solo presentation titled THANDAV, featuring my art creations inspired by classical Indian dance,” Ajaikumar tells YourStory. The exhibition will be presented at the RASA cultural festival at Prestige Auditorium in Bengaluru, January 8-10. 2027. She is also curating the upcoming third International KALA Symposium in Mysuru. Also Read Year in Review: The great Indian consumer reset powered by protein, pickleball and micro-dramas “With the vision of art as a catalyst for healing and development, the symposium is conceived as a creative platform connecting fine art, healthcare philanthropy, and grassroots community development. It will be hosted at Bharath Cancer Hospital,” she adds. Her gallery is also planning an art activity with paediatric oncology patients to celebrate Children's Day this month. “Another ongoing initiative is the installation of artworks in consultation rooms across our hospitals,” Ajaikumar says. As trends in Indian contemporary art, she points to the revival of traditional Indian art forms through contemporary interpretations. “Styles such as Madhubani, Gond, Pichwai and Mysore are being explored through acrylics on canvas, square compositions, minimalistic presentations, and unconventional materials,” she observes. “With increasing competition and the pressure to produce work within shorter periods, many traditional processes are gradually disappearing. Traditional knowledge and techniques should also be respected,” she affirms. Another exciting development is the transformation of traditional Indian crafts into large-scale contemporary installations. “Some traditional art forms are moving beyond small-format works on paper to large canvases, murals and public installations,” she says. Indian contemporary art is also responding to changes in social, political and environmental realities. “Many artists are exploring themes of identity, migration, displacement, urbanisation, globalisation, and ecology. They encourage viewers to question and reflect on the world around them,” Ajaikumar observes. Also Read Year in Review: Top 10 celebrity-backed ventures of 2025 “I believe this shift is important because art should not merely be decorative. It can communicate ideas, challenge perceptions and create awareness about issues that affect society,” she affirms. Collectors are increasingly interested in theme-based series rather than isolated, standalone artworks. “Conceptual works, installations, environmentally conscious practices, and works addressing social and women's issues are receiving greater attention,” she adds. As for tech trends, AI offers digital artists exciting tools and possibilities for experimentation. “However, use of AI also raises important questions about originality, authorship, authenticity and the value of the human hand and imagination in art,” she cautions. “Another development I find particularly encouraging is the increasing presence of art in public spaces, especially airports. Major airports in cities such as Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru are providing opportunities to showcase large-scale artworks and installations,” she observes (see our photo essay on art and design at Bengaluru’s airport here ). With their large spaces, airports can bring art closer to people who may not necessarily visit galleries or museums. “These installations often combine art, architecture, unconventional materials, and multimedia practices. They can transform otherwise functional spaces into engaging cultural environments,” she adds. The exhibitor lineup in her Bhoomi exhibition includes Meenakshi Chinna Rathod, Meghana Gante Ravish, Nagappa Pradhani, Nikhil R Sharma, Nirmala Kumari CS, Premkumar K, Ranganath Amrad, Revanasiddayya SH, Renuka Markande, SG Vasudev, and Santosh Pattar. Also Read Year in review: What 2025’s data tells us about women in India Akshay Bhat is an emerging contemporary artist from Karnataka whose practice reflects an interest in expressive visual language and contemporary aesthetics. Alka Chavda is a contemporary visual artist whose practice centres on painting and mixed media. Renuka Markande is an accomplished artist, educator and researcher whose creative practice bridges academic inquiry and contemporary visual expression. Bhagya Ajaikumar explores expressive painting and the emotional possibilities of colour and form. Hanumanta T frequently draws inspiration from local traditions, landscapes and everyday human interactions, transforming familiar imagery into evocative narratives. Ishwarayya OM explores themes of identity, environment and human resilience. Manushya explores universal themes of humanity, coexistence and personal identity through painting and interdisciplinary practice. Marishamachar draws inspiration from regional narratives and lived experience, and creates works that resonate with both cultural specificity and universal human concerns. As a curator of such a diverse exhibition, Ajaikumar particularly likes placing emerging artists alongside established professionals. “This allows them to learn from one another and gain greater exposure,” she explains. “I believe that an exhibition should offer more than a collection of individual artworks. It should create a meaningful visual and intellectual experience for the viewer,” she says. Also Read Year in review: startups that raised big from VCs in 2025 This can be particularly challenging when working with a specific theme. “The curator must establish a meaningful connection between the exhibition's concept and the individual artist's interpretation. There should be a common thread connecting their contributions,” she describes. “Curators also encourage emerging artists and help them develop their ideas. A carefully curated exhibition can challenge younger artists to think beyond their usual boundaries, experiment with new approaches and raise the quality of their work,” Ajaikumar signs off. Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world? (All photographs taken by Madanmohan Rao on location at Venkatappa Art Gallery.)

title: Vast, varied, vivid: How this art festival celebrates pan-India creativity
content: Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,030 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival , telecom expo , millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival. The Namma Art Bengaluru national festival was held at Karnataka Chitrakala Parishath (KCP) for the second time this year (see our coverage of earlier exhibitions at this popular cultural hub here ). KCP’s flagship event is the annual Chitra Santhe , regarded as India’s largest street fair for art. India’s artistic landscape is as vast and varied as the country itself. It spans intricate visual languages of Madhubani, Warli, Gond and Pattachitra; sculptural traditions of Channapatna, Dhokra and Thanjavur; miniature painting and textile traditions, and much more. The worlds of contemporary painting, photography, installation, and new media add new perspectives and vocabularies for art lovers. The beauty of this artistic panorama truly emerges when these creative forms are showcased together. “Art has always served as a powerful medium of expression that transcends boundaries, connects communities, and reflects the spirit of society,” explains Shashidhara Rao, General Secretary, KCP. A pan-India exhibition that brings traditional and contemporary art into one shared space can create a powerful visual and cultural conversation. Instead of presenting India’s art traditions as isolated regional categories, such an exhibition reveals the connections between them. Also Read 2026 Outlook: AI, robotics, biotech, unicorns and the road ahead As seen in this photo essay, there are recurring ideas of nature, spirituality, community, identity, mythology, and everyday life. The differences are equally important: they demonstrate the extraordinary plurality of Indian experience and the many ways in which communities have interpreted and expressed their worlds. Bringing traditional and contemporary practices together also allows the exhibition to move beyond the idea of heritage as something belonging only to the past. Traditional art forms are living practices, continually evolving through artists, artisans and new generations. Contemporary artists, meanwhile, frequently draw upon inherited visual languages and stories while questioning, reinterpreting and transforming them for the present. Placing these works side by side makes this continuity visible. “In an increasingly dynamic world, the role of art in preserving heritage, encouraging dialogue, and inspiring fresh perspectives has become more significant than ever,” KCP’s Rao adds. The Namma Art festival is thus more than a showcase of beautiful objects, as shown in this photo essay. It serves as a map of India’s cultural imagination — one in which a folk painting from one region can resonate with a contemporary installation from another, and where regional identities can coexist within a larger national story. The experience of seeing many art forms together is also deeply democratic. It invites audiences to discover unfamiliar traditions and appreciate the knowledge embedded in craft. It creates opportunities for dialogue between artists, craftspeople, designers, collectors, students, and the wider public. Also Read Year in review: startups that raised big from VCs in 2025 “Our festival represents a wide spectrum of artistic approaches, mediums and regional sensibilities. Their works collectively reflect the dynamism of contemporary practice in India,” says KCP president BL Shankar. Such a national exhibition celebrates an idea that is central to India itself: unity does not require uniformity. Its strength lies in the coexistence of many languages, histories, materials, communities and ways of seeing. By bringing traditional and contemporary art together, the exhibition can offer audiences not simply a view of Indian art, but an experience of India — diverse, layered, evolving, and connected. Featured artists at the KCP festival include Vivek Vadkar, AG Nellagi, Ashok Mansur, Sunil Barman, Dhiraj Balchandra Patil, and Sudha Sridhar. Vivek Vadkar is a contemporary Indian artist renowned for his powerful and emotive oil paintings of horses in motion. His popular Seven Horses compositions draw on traditions where running horses symbolise success, victory and positive energy. AG Nellagi is known particularly for his expressive paintings of bulls. His work draws deeply on his personal experience as a farmer and on the cultural symbolism associated with the bull, which represents strength, determination, fertility, and confidence. He has received awards and recognition from the Karnataka Lalit Kala Academy and other cultural institutions. Also Read How IIT Madras Incubation Cell is powering India’s next-gen deeptech startups Ashok Mansur is a visual artist and photographer with an interest in art, history and cultural imagery. A farmer by profession, he is also known for his beautiful landscapes along with people portraits. Sunil Barman is a self-taught artist whose paintings focus on the quiet beauty of village life in Bengal. He works primarily with fine pen-and-ink drawing layered over delicate watercolour washes. His paintings evoke nostalgia for rural life where people and nature coexist in an unhurried rhythm. “This edition has proudly presented 150 invited artists from across India. They showcase the diverse ideas, mediums and voices that reflect the spirit of traditional and contemporary art today,” festival convener SA Vimalanathan signs off. Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world? AG Nellagi Ashok Mansur Dhiraj Balchandra Patil S M Lohar Sudha Sridhar Sunil Barman Vivek Vadkar (All photographs taken by Madanmohan Rao on location at Karnataka Chitrakala Parishath.)

title: VibeCode30 2026: The 30 AI-built products to watch from India
content: The next generation of technology builders may not all be software engineers. They could be students, product managers, marketing professionals, small business owners or simply individuals who understand a problem well enough to solve it. With AI-powered coding tools lowering the technical and financial barriers to software development, more people are turning ideas into working products without conventional development teams or large budgets. Recognising this shift, YourStory launched VibeCode30, a new initiative presented by Hostinger, at the 17th edition of TechSparks 2026 in Bengaluru. The inaugural cohort celebrates 30 AI-native products built to solve real-world problems, from simplifying house hunting and improving financial literacy to supporting healthcare professionals and making everyday business operations more efficient. Unlike traditional startup showcases, Vibecode30 focuses on products and their builders, whether they work independently or in small teams, with or without formal coding experience. The inaugural edition received 207 applications from across the country, including smaller centres such as Ajmer, Silvassa, Sugauli, and Thoothukudi. The final 30 products represent 19 industries and 11 cities, reflecting the range of problems that AI-native builders are addressing. Importantly, every selected product had moved beyond the prototype stage and was accessible to real users. The cohort demonstrates that while AI can accelerate software development, understanding the problem, validating the output, and improving the product remain essential. It also shows how smaller, highly specific problems can now become viable opportunities for innovation. Meet the VibeCode30 2026 cohort: AjmerAstro Built by Himanshu Dadhich in Ajmer, AjmerAstro is an AI-powered astrology platform offering personalised Vedic and KP astrology guidance in English and Hindi, with a system that remembers previous conversations. AlgoTrips Delhi-based Tushar Garg built AlgoTrips , an AI travel planner that creates day-by-day itineraries with live pricing for flights, hotels, activities, and transfers, allowing users to plan and book trips. Arena Developed by Bengaluru-based Prathik Arunkumar and Arun Kumar, Arena helps schools manage house competitions through live leaderboards, digital scoring, and real-time updates. Beet.Health Built by Vatsl Goswami and Shivanshi Shukla, Beet.Health helps nutrition clinics manage appointments, payments, and meal plans while enabling clients to track their progress through a mobile app and WhatsApp assistant. Bengaluru.rent Created by Bengaluru-based Harshit Anand, Bengaluru.rent is a free platform where tenants anonymously share rental prices and connect directly with property owners and prospective flatmates without brokers. Benki.tech Developed by Sonam Rao, Avinash Narsimah, and Kumaraswamy BV in Bengaluru, Benki.tech uses a simulated panel of customers to help businesses pressure test business ideas, marketing messages, and product offerings. Bloom UPSC Built by Bengaluru-based former banker Guru Sasidhar Pattem, Bloom UPSC provides civil services aspirants with study materials, practice questions, answer evaluation, and video lessons in English and Telugu. Boolean Beyond Coimbatore-based Boolean Beyond developed BeyondSave, a WhatsApp-based platform that enables local jewellery businesses to manage customer savings schemes, payments, and balances. ElderNest Bengaluru-based Shubham Jain created ElderNest to help families discover and compare senior care homes across India, with information on services, pricing and admission support. Gold Investment Monitor Created by Surendhran Sivalingam in Coimbatore, Gold Investment Monitor analyses 24 market signals and combines them into a single verdic to help Indian households assess whether to buy gold or wait. Holt Built by Bhubaneswar-based Debashis Nayak, Holt is an open-source memory tool for AI coding assistants that runs locally on a developer’s machine, helping them retain project context across sessions. IndianCoffeeBeans.com Hyderabad-based Abhishek Thrilok built IndianCoffeeBeans.com , a searchable directory tracking more than 90 Indian specialty coffee roasters and 1,200+ coffees. Indiccore Developed by Sahil Gulati and his team in Gurugram, Indiccore helps civil services aspirants analyse mock-test performance, identify weaknesses, and improve examination strategies. Madhav.live Built by Ashish Singh Shekhawat in Bengaluru, Madhav.live lets users talk to Krishna about everyday problems and receive guidance rooted in the Bhagavad Gita, in the language they are most comfortable with. MagicSlides.app Created by Bengaluru-based Sanskar Tiwari, MagicSlides instantly converts topics, documents, web links, and YouTube videos into presentations, supporting more than 100 languages. Mira Developed by Shagun Verma and Abhaya Trivedi in Mumbai, Mira is an AI voice assistant that helps short-term rental hosts handle guest enquiries and check property availability, giving small hosts the kind of front desk usually only hotels can afford. NextDoor.Company Built by Sankalp Sinha in Bengaluru, NextDoor.Company helps jobseekers discover startups hiring nearby through a map-based platform with company and employment information. Nomira Created by Bengaluru-based Prernaa Agarwal, Nomira is a women-first travel platform combining safety information, offline maps, travel communities, and group trips. Orbit Research Developed by Silvassa-based student Aditya Singh, Orbit Research combines academic research tools into a single platform for discovering papers, checking references, preparing manuscripts, and creating presentations. Penfight Built by Amarjeet Sarma and his Bengaluru-based team, Penfight recreates the popular school desk pen-flicking game as an online multiplayer experience. Pretend AI Pune-based Kareena Rogers developed Pretend AI , an iPhone app that allows users to rehearse conversations with custom AI personas through realistic text exchanges. RayAI Created by Reshma Budhia and Swetha Sree Kannan at Chennai-based agency Toss The Coin, RayAI helps marketing teams create campaigns, content and design assets using shared brand knowledge and workflows. Soma Built by Gurugram-based Saurav Singhal, Soma brings together health reports, wearable data, nutrition, and fitness information to provide personalised health insights. TofuBofu Hyderabad-based Arnav Neil developed TofuBofu to help B2B companies measure and improve how often AI recommends them, as buyers increasingly turn to AI for product research and decision making. Vitfinity Created by Bengaluru-based Pranay Reddy and his team, Vitfinity teaches financial literacy to school children through interactive simulations and a 180-lesson curriculum. Voqalize Built by Sripathi Krishnan and his Bengaluru-based team, Voqalize enables enterprises to integrate multilingual conversational voice AI into software applications. Whitefield Womania Developed by Rakshita Dwivedi and Abhishek Dwivedi in Bengaluru, Whitefield Womania is a digital directory connecting residents with women-led local businesses. Youdemy Created by Bengaluru-based Rohit Ranjan Singh, Youdemy organises free YouTube lectures into structured courses with learning streaks, points, and leaderboards. Zespan Built by Udupi-based Abhishek N, Zespan monitors AI agents operating in enterprise environments, identifies incorrect decisions and helps prevent recurring errors. Zoku Developed by Bengaluru-based Priyanshu Dangi, Zoku is a voice-first development application that allows software developers to manage multiple AI coding agents simultaneously. title: Mamaearth parent’s profit surges 87%; Goyal defends Temple amid backlash
content: Dear Readers, AI is finding cyber flaws swiftly. But are enterprises quick enough to fix them? Nikesh Arora, Chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks, raises this crucial point. He notes in a LinkedIn post that most organisations, especially the smaller ones, do not have the capacity to patch flaws at the speed needed. Arora advocates virtual patching as an interim measure and calls for a shared vulnerability clearing house and faster development of protective signatures. As AI agents become capable of handling everyday tasks, here’s a smart ring that promises to bring AI agents to our fingertips. At a private launch in Bengaluru, Aina unveiled an AI-powered ring that combines a colour display, voice commands, and gesture-based controls. The startup wants its device to become an everyday interface between users and AI agents. But can it offer enough utility to justify its Rs 47,000 price tag? In other news, the government has cleared 12 proposals worth over Rs 7,500 crore under the Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme. This round of approvals adds to the momentum behind the scheme, which aims to build a domestic ecosystem for components and reduce India’s dependence on imports. Meanwhile, MakeMyTrip has acquired a majority stake in Bengaluru-based Quick Ride, a tech-led shared mobility platform. Quick Ride connects people travelling along similar routes, enabling affordable ride pooling for everyday commute. Lastly, here’s a bit of weekend motivation. Built despite opposition, legal challenges, and questions over cost, Bihar Museum has marched into the global top 10, ahead of the Met and Louvre. For YourStory’s founder Shradha Sharma, the museum not only brings the region’s history to life, but is also a reminder of what ambition and perseverance can accomplish. According to Honasa Consumer, the second quarter revenue growth is the highest it has recorded since its public listing in November 2023. Key takeaways The company’s net profit in Q2FY27 was Rs 73.24 crore, compared with Rs 39.22 crore in the year-ago period. Revenue was Rs 731.18 crore, compared with Rs 538.06 crore a year ago. However, sequentially, profit fell from Rs 90.44 crore in the first quarter. Revenue in the first quarter was Rs 755.94 crore. For the six months of the fiscal year, the company reported a revenue of Rs 1,487.13 crore, a YoY growth of 31%. The net profit for the period was Rs 163.69 crore, a YoY rise of 103%. <Top Funding Deals of the Week> Startup: GIVA Amount: $100M Round: Undisclosed Startup: EloElo Group Amount: $80M Round: Series C Startup: Clinics On Cloud Amount: $12.5M Round: Series A Wearables Goyal defends Temple amid backlash Deepinder Goyal wearing Teample Deepinder Goyal has posted a series of updates and clarifications on X amid backlash from some Indian doctors who criticised his brain-monitoring wearable Temple. Describing Temple as “an ambitious project”, Goyal gave a detailed explanation on what the team is building. “The team is delusional enough to think we can build this. And we will,” he wrote on Friday. Earlier, on Thursday, he posted, “We stand by our science and our methods. Each of our claims is easily verifiable by individuals and institutions alike, and you will see a lot of independent studies come up on their own when the device becomes available to use.” Key takeaways: “First and foremost, a business lesson: if Temple were a scam, and any of what we said weren’t true, people would know it in just a few days of using Temple,” Goyal wrote on Thursday. He also highlighted that $30 million was invested in building the device, including $20 million of his personal money. Calling Temple his purpose, he said it’s not about the money. “I have enough of it to last for generations. My incentives are fully aligned with getting the science right.
