title: VeloDB’s Nitin Waghulde on why AI agents break down after the demo
content: AI agents tend to look good in a pilot. The scope is narrow, the data is controlled, and the questions are predictable. Production is different, and that gap is where many projects stall. Gartner predicts that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027, due to escalating costs, unclear business value, or inadequate risk controls. For Nitin Waghulde, Regional Director, APAC at VeloDB, a large part of the problem sits below the model, in the data layer. In a keynote titled ‘AI agents at scale: Surviving beyond the demo’, Nitin explained how AI agents use data differently from people, what they need to work reliably at scale, and how companies are redesigning their data infrastructure to support them. Nitin started his session with an example. In a traditional system, a business manager who wanted last year’s sales figure would run a ready-made report and get the number in one lookup. Ask an AI agent why sales dropped over the last three quarters, and the work changes. The agent pulls order records from the ERP and CRM systems, scans support tickets and chats to check whether major customers have escalated problems, and reads sales team reports on territory dynamics. If its reasoning is incomplete, it goes back for more. “What used to be completed in one simple lookup or one simple query, now you’re taking hundreds of lookups for the same thing,” he said. AI is now a customer of your data In the past, people and reports were the main consumers of business data, and systems were built around fixed reports with clear boundaries. Now, Nitin said, AI has become a new customer of that data, and it behaves very differently. Agents run around the clock, ask many questions at once, and work in an iterative loop: ask, think, search, and retry until they can answer. Their questions are also unscripted. That puts a heavy, unpredictable load on the data layer. The challenge grows because business data lives in several places at once: transactional records, chat memory, documents, dashboards and pre-built reports, and vector stores for meaning-based search. An agent has to search all of them and combine the results before it can answer. Each extra trip to the data adds cost. If the data is stale, the answer is wrong. Nitin compared it to driving with an inaccurate traffic map. And when data comes from many sources, it becomes harder to know where an answer came from, which creates a trust problem. He likened it to sending someone to five filing cabinets to collect pieces of paper. By the time the person returns from the fifth cabinet, the information from the first may already be out of date. What production agents need Nitin outlined four requirements for agents to move from pilot to production. Access to every data type: Agents need numbers from structured records, text from documents, and meaning from unstructured sources. Scale: A single query may now need to scan petabytes of data, not the few terabytes that systems were once designed for. Also, the platform should support concurrency at scale to support iterative querying for data-hungry agents Freshness: Agents can only act correctly on current information. If an agent processing a refund cannot see the latest transaction record, it has to wait. Every change, including updates and deletions, needs to be visible to the agent immediately, without waiting for a nightly batch job. A record of every interaction: Every AI interaction leaves a trail. These logs are growing faster than business data itself, and they feed back into decision-making. VeloDB’s answer is a single engine that handles all of these needs. The company was founded in 2023 by the original creators of Apache Doris, an open-source real-time analytics database that became a top-level Apache Software Foundation project in June 2022. According to VeloDB, Apache Doris has more than 14,000 GitHub stars and 700 contributors, and is used by over 5,000 enterprises worldwide. To cut down the back-and-forth trips that slow agents down, VeloDB supports hybrid queries. A single query can combine SQL, vector search, and text search, running deterministic and probabilistic searches in parallel. The result is one unified source of truth instead of scattered data. What it looks like at scale Nitin shared two examples of companies running this architecture in production. The first was one of the largest crypto exchanges, with more than 120 million users, which he did not name. The exchange makes transaction data available to AI agents that retail investors can query, for example to see what positions large traders are taking on an asset. He said its agents handle about 33,000 conversations with a tail latency of around 3 milliseconds, running round the clock. The second was MiniMax, a Chinese AI company that listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in January 2026 and says it serves 212 million users in more than 200 countries. MiniMax rebuilt its logging system on Apache Doris after moving away from Grafana Loki, because logs had become a valuable source of intelligence worth keeping and querying. Nitin said MiniMax ingests data at 10 Gbps and can query about 10 petabytes in under two seconds, at 70% lower cost. VeloDB has separately reported that the Doris-based system now supports logs across all of MiniMax’s business lines at petabyte scale with over 99.9% availability. The same challenges apply to early-stage startups building agents, Nitin added. VeloDB works with fintech startups that face the same scaling problems as MiniMax or the crypto exchange, just at an earlier stage. His closing point was that agents will always ask hundreds of questions, so the infrastructure has to make each one cheap, fast, and current. For Nitin, scaling AI agents is less about finding a better model and more about giving agents real-time, trustworthy data from a single source. Companies that get the data layer right, he argued, can make decisions faster, reduce costs, and move their agents from pilot to production with confidence.

title: If it works in India, it can work anywhere: TDK Ventures’ Nicolas Sauvage on building deeptech for the world
content: For years, India’s best scientists left for the US. Now they are staying, and more of them are choosing startups over corporate labs. For Nicolas Sauvage, Founder and President of TDK Ventures, those two shifts are the biggest changes in Indian deeptech over the past five to 10 years. “The best talent starts to go into the startups in deeptech, and they try things that they would not have tried 10 years or even five years ago,” Sauvage said in a fireside chat with Shivani Muthanna, Senior Director – Strategic Content & Video at YourStory, at TechSparks 2026 . TDK Ventures is the corporate venture capital arm of Japanese electronics company TDK Corporation. Set up in Silicon Valley in 2019, it opened its Bengaluru innovation hub in 2023, its first office outside the US. India is its second largest market by number of investments, Sauvage said. The ecosystem he is betting on is growing. India is home to more than 4,200 deeptech startups, which raised $2.3 billion in 2025, up 37% from the year before, according to a Nasscom–Zinnov report. During the session titled ‘Global by design: What Indian deeptech needs to become globally iconic’, he laid out what Indian founders need to get right to build companies that compete globally, from picking a first customer and the right investors to planning for scale before it becomes expensive to do so. Where India has the right to win Speaking on investing in SpaceTech, Sauvage named the US, China, and India as the three countries where he would consider investing as a VC. Space is one area where he believes India has a clear advantage, built on decades of institutional investment through the Indian Space Research Organisation. The government’s space promotion agency, IN-SPACe, projects that India’s space economy will grow from $8.4 billion to $44 billion by 2033 , raising its share of the global market from 2% to 8%. TDK Ventures co-led a $20.5 million Series A in Bengaluru-based spacetech startup Ethereal Exploration Guild (The Guild), which is developing a fully reusable medium-lift launch vehicle. Sauvage also pointed to a shift in AI. The conversation, he said, has moved from tokens and compute to electrons and gigawatts, which means everything involved in delivering power to chips now matters. TDK Ventures invested in C2i Semiconductors, a Bengaluru startup founded in 2024 by former Texas Instruments engineers that builds power management technology for AI data centres. Germany’s Infineon Technologies announced the acquisition of C2i in August 2026 and completed it in October, about two years after the startup was founded. Beyond individual sectors, Sauvage credited a cultural trait: jugaad , or resourcefulness under constraint. “Think about the entrepreneurship journey. It means going from an idea with massive constraints and creating something that’s valuable and does a job. That sounds like jugaad to me,” he said. That resourcefulness shows up in the numbers, he added. Capital efficiency among Indian portfolio companies is world class. “I’m from Europe, but don’t talk about Europe when we think about capital efficiency,” he said. Let the first market shape the product When asked what founders building from India for the world should think about first, Sauvage pointed to Exponent Energy. Founded in 2020 by former Ather Energy executives Arun Vinayak and Sanjay Byalal, the company offers 15-minute fast charging. In June 2026, TDK Ventures co-led a Rs 200 crore ($21.1 million) round in Exponent, taking the company’s total funding since 2020 to $65.7 million. Exponent’s long-term goal was megawatt-scale fast charging for intercity buses. It could not start there. Instead, it began by supplying battery management systems (BMS) to three-wheeler makers, a fragmented market with more than 70 manufacturers at the time. “There was no way a German startup would convince BMW to take their solution. No way a US startup would convince General Motors to take their BMS solution,” Sauvage said. India’s fragmented market let Exponent deploy across many manufacturers in Bengaluru and beyond, giving it a base to build from . Founders need superpowers, and so do their investors Sauvage described founders as superheroes. Each needs a superpower: something they know or can do that no one else can. That is what draws investors in. But, like any superhero film, there are many battles before the end, and founders need allies. “You want to make sure that the investors you pick as an entrepreneur bring the right superpower at the right time,” he said. Corporate VCs can bring a go-to-market channel, an early anchor customer, a hard-to-access supplier, or help reducing scientific risk, depending on who they are. He urged founders to choose investors based on what they add that the cap table does not already have. For TDK Ventures, that means drawing on TDK’s work in energy, sensing, passive components, and power supplies. Sauvage said electric motorcycle maker Ultraviolette now gets components typically reserved for TDK’s largest customers, while TDK is working with The Guild on future component requirements and roadmaps. Alongside seeking venture-capital financial returns, he said, TDK Ventures looks for ways TDK’s capabilities, or “superpowers”, can accelerate and de-risk a founder’s journey towards building a globally significant company. First principles over trade-offs Sauvage traced several portfolio wins back to first-principles thinking. TDK Ventures invested in AI chip company Groq in 2020. During an interview with founder Jonathan Ross before investing, Sauvage noticed that every answer, from setting company values to hiring, firing, and designing the compiler, came back to first principles. That approach produced a chip architecture designed around the compiler, which allowed for fully predictable, low-latency inference. Sauvage said he was convinced inference was the future before the ChatGPT moment, when he estimated the market for inference alone at more than $60 billion. In December 2025, NVIDIA signed a non-exclusive licensing deal for Groq’s technology, reportedly worth about $20 billion, and hired Ross and several members of his team. He applied the same lens to engineering decisions that look like trade-offs. Ultraviolette, he said, uses first-principles engineering to pursue improvements in performance, weight and cost together. The company now sells its bikes in Germany, France, Switzerland, the UK, and other European markets, bringing its products into markets served by established manufacturers such as BMW. Ultraviolette recently raised $85 million in a round led by Yali Capital and TDK Ventures. Patience and impatience at the same time Deeptech founders, Sauvage said, need both. “Overnight success takes 10 years,” he said, noting that Groq took 10 years and SpaceX took 17. At the same time, founders need urgency and a sense of contribution to society. Before investing, he looks for four things: a founder with a superpower, a category-defining product, a large enough market, and evidence the company can win one customer and then the next while staying capital-efficient. Markets worth $1 billion to $2 billion can be too small for the venture returns TDK Ventures seeks, he said, because the firm looks for each investment to have the potential to return the entire fund. He cited SPAN, a Silicon Valley company led by Indian-origin founder Arch Rao. SPAN began by redesigning the home electrical panel, a product largely unchanged for a century. As AI infrastructure demand surged, SPAN extended its power-management technology into distributed compute through partnerships, which Sauvage said changed the company’s trajectory. Longer cycles also explain why India needs more corporate investors now, he argued. Using a roughly four-year journey to success in SaaS and fintech as an illustration, Sauvage described an ecosystem that can recycle entrepreneurial experience about 2.5 times a decade, as founders and employees carry what they have learned into new companies. A ten-year deeptech journey allows only one such cycle over the same period. Networks of repeat founders and alumni-founded businesses, like those associated with PayPal and SpaceX, therefore take longer to develop. Corporate investors can help bridge that gap with technical expertise, suppliers and customer relationships. “I want global companies, corporates, and their corporate VCs to know this is the time to invest in India for deeptech,” he said. Build for scale before it gets expensive Sauvage emphasised thinking about scale and international expansion early, because shortcuts taken to win the first market in India can become expensive to reverse later. When TDK Ventures met Ultraviolette, the team was already deliberate about Europe while focused on winning in India first, with customers riding its bikes as far as the Himalayas. His advice to founders: find what is specific to India that a global customer would trust. India’s wide temperature range, for example, could favour energy storage that performs across extremes, such as sodium-ion or thermal batteries. “Try to think about what makes you being in India a proof point that because you’re successful in India, you will win everywhere,” he said. For Sauvage, India’s deeptech opportunity rests on more than talent. The founders most likely to build iconic companies are those who treat India as a starting point rather than a boundary, pick investors who fill specific gaps, and design for international markets before shortcuts become costly to undo. It is a long game that demands patience and impatience at once, and in his view, the moment for global capital to back it in India has arrived.

title: How Satin Group’s Sankalp plans to empower India’s next wave of founders
content: India’s startup ecosystem is witnessing a growing wave of innovation in climate action and sustainability. From students developing affordable technology solutions for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) to early-stage entrepreneurs tackling circular economy challenges, the ideas are promising. But turning a climate-focused idea into a scalable business requires more than passion. Founders need access to capital, industry networks and structured mentorship to translate their vision into viable enterprises. Recognising these gaps, Satin Group, based in Gurugram, Haryana, launched Sankalp this September. It is a platform designed to nurture sustainability-focused ideas from students and early-stage entrepreneurs. In an exclusive interaction with YourStory, Pramod Marar, CEO of Satin FinServ Limited, discussed the thinking behind the initiative, the importance of non-financial support alongside funding, and the role financial institutions can play in scaling climate innovation. Sankalp operates through two distinct tracks: student-led business ideas and early-stage startups. The student track encourages college students to develop technology-driven solutions to climate and environmental challenges. The startup track focuses on young businesses working in areas such as clean mobility, circular economy, waste management, and sustainable supply chains. Sankalp winners stand a chance to win Rs 32 lakh, with Rs 10 lakh for students and Rs 22 lakh for startups. Applications for the first cohort closed on October 4. Sankalp says the response has been encouraging, with more than 17,000 registrations and over 1,000 teams taking part. Student innovators, it adds, showed a notable interest in technology-led solutions for climate challenges. “We were pleasantly surprised to see a strong focus among students on creating technology-led solutions in the climate space,” Marar said. The genesis of Sankalp Marar brings more than two decades of experience across banking, microfinance, and sustainability-focused entrepreneurship. Having started his own venture early in his career, he experienced firsthand the challenges faced by entrepreneurs seeking initial funding, particularly those from salaried or service-sector families without access to financial backing. “Startup wasn’t a cool term at that time; it wasn’t even a term that existed. I come from a middle-class service background family. There was a lot of moral support, but there was no financial support. That’s when I realised how difficult it was to access early-stage capital,” Marar recalled. While founders may have the passion and business acumen to develop an idea, scaling it requires a broader support system. Capital is only one part of the equation; access to expertise, networks and institutional support can be equally important. “Most startup founders are very passionate about their ideas and have the acumen to scale them. But scaling requires a lot of elements beyond capital. That’s why we started Sankalp — to help build the ecosystem around sustainability and climate innovation,” Marar said. Satin Group, which was founded in 1990, comprises three non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) focused on microfinance , housing finance, and corporate and SME lending. Its broader ecosystem also includes Satin Growth Alternatives, a debt fund, and Satin Technologies, its technology arm. This combination of financial and technological capabilities provides the group with multiple avenues to support emerging sustainability-focused businesses. University incubators play an important role in nurturing early-stage ideas, but Sankalp aims to go further by helping entrepreneurs bridge the gap between developing a concept and preparing it for the market. “I wouldn’t call it a scaled-down version because we actually try to go beyond the conventional model of incubation. We want to understand whether we can support founders through experienced mentorship, both at an individual level and through institutions, as well as through debt and equity,” Marar said. With applications closed, Sankalp has moved from a wide pool of ideas to a tighter evaluation. KPMG is the programme’s assessment partner. It is independently evaluating every application against a predefined framework, helping with shortlisting and identifying the most promising ventures. Satin says this keeps the selection objective and based only on merit. Thirty teams have made it to the virtual jury round, where they will present to a panel of practitioners, venture capital (VC) fund managers and lenders. The shortlisted ventures cover climate tech, circular economy, clean energy, sustainable cities, waste management, water management and sustainable agriculture. According to Satin, what stood out was not just the range of ideas but the depth applicants showed in their chosen areas. Judges will look at the strength of the idea, innovation, feasibility, scalability and potential for meaningful impact. Based on the jury’s assessments, select finalists will go on to the in-person Grand Finale, where they will present before a jury and industry leaders for final evaluation and recognition. The jury rounds are also meant to open doors beyond the prize money. Both the virtual round and the Grand Finale will have representatives from VC funds, incubation centres and institutional investors, who can evaluate the ideas and explore funding possibilities. Satin has also signed formal arrangements with certain incubation centres to offer institutional mentoring to the selected founders. In addition, Satin Growth Alternatives, the group’s Category II alternative investment fund (AIF), will look at the ideas from an investment angle. Satin is careful about what this means for funding. At this stage, it says, Sankalp is not an announced debt-and-equity programme. Any financing would be considered case by case, depending on the business model, stage of development, funding needs and suitability, with the aim of finding viable opportunities and exploring ways to support their growth. For Satin, the programme fits in its wider ambition to help build a more sustainable and climate-resilient economy. Financing remains central to its business, the company says, but Sankalp gives it a chance to engage with emerging innovators and understand how climate-focused business models are evolving, along with the opportunities and challenges in the space. It also helps Satin spot solutions that may, over time, match its own financing capabilities. The group has already been building towards this. Satin Finserv set up its Sustainable & Emerging Businesses (SEB) vertical in August 2025 to offer financing to sustainability-oriented and emerging enterprises, with a streamlined process and dedicated relationship support. In the last 12 months, it has disbursed loans of roughly Rs 400 crore to businesses focused on sustainability, either as users or providers of sustainability-focused solutions. Sankalp complements that effort, Satin says, by helping it discover promising entrepreneurs and innovations. Why Sankalp matters for India’s green transition India’s transition towards a low-carbon economy will require more than technological breakthroughs. It will also depend on whether promising innovations can secure funding, find customers, and scale sustainably. Financial institutions, established businesses, and entrepreneurs all have a role to play in building this ecosystem. Sankalp seeks to bring these stakeholders together, combining access to finance with mentorship and industry connections. Its approach reflects the idea that supporting climate innovation should extend beyond funding a promising idea or awarding a one-time prize. “Rather than just waiting for institutions to put their money on the table, can financial institutions come together to create a platform that helps founders go beyond simply raising capital?” Marar said. By seeking to connect entrepreneurs with financing, expertise, and potential commercial partners, Sankalp aims to create a longer-term support system for sustainability-focused businesses.""

title: When code is cheap, trust is not: Inside the AI-era engineering roundtable
content: AI has made writing code faster than ever, but the harder question for engineering leaders is what happens after the code is written. At a roundtable on operating engineering in the AI era, leaders from logistics, food tech, healthcare, telecom, fintech, ecommerce and higher education compared notes on scaling with AI without losing reliability, security or control. The shared view was that speed is no longer the hard part. Governing it is. The roundtable, moderated by Ipshita Basu , brought together Manjunath Nakshathri , Head of Engineering, Mojro; Shobhit Suman , CPO, HungerBox; Pavan Kumar A T , CTO, Digii (DigiiCampus); Pranjal Nadhani , Co-founder and CTO, Cautio; Kenil Paul , VP, Technology and Solutions, 6D Technologies; Rimjhim Agrawal , Co-founder and CTO, BrainSightAI; Dhruv Rastogi , Chief AI Officer, MediAssist; Chandrakesh Pandey , Senior Vice President of Technology, Niyo Solutions Inc.; Achal Sharma , CTO, TechnoSport; Sunil Kumar , Director Engineering, Meesho; and Anshul Sharma , Director Engineering, Scaler. The session was hosted by groundcover and Data Signals in partnership with YourStory , and was led on the host side by Paul Trebe , Head of Sales and Partnership, groundcover, and Satish Dange , Founder, Data Signals. Where the bottleneck has moved Participants agreed that AI has compressed build time, but the pressure has shifted downstream. When agents generate large volumes of code, the questions become who reviews it, who tests it and who monitors dozens of deployments a day. Several leaders said their teams now spend more time on design, context and governance than on writing components. Agents are only as effective as the context they receive, and few organizations yet have repository knowledge, documentation and templates in a form an agent can reliably use. Drawing the line on autonomy The room converged on a progressive approach. Reversible, read-only work, such as fetching data or generating reports, can go to agents with little friction. Irreversible actions, such as deleting data or running database updates, stay behind human review. Blast radius matters as much as reversibility. If a wrong call could affect end users or production systems, a person makes it. One of the participants described a ‘ four eyes’ model in which AI does the maker work of reading and analyzing, deterministic rules deliver clear yes or no outcomes, and a human signs off. Another speaker described risk scoring based on severity and occurrence, which focuses human review on medium and high criticality items. Others drew the line by specialization, letting engineers use agents freely in their own domain while production ownership stays with people who can debug at 2 AM. That scenario also surfaced in a hopeful form. Instead of waking an engineer, an agent can investigate an incident and hand over a report by morning, leaving the decision with a human. Trust, participants said, will build gradually, much as it did with online payments, and the line will keep moving. Accountability and the skills question Accountability drew firm agreement: it cannot be delegated to a model. Leaders remain answerable for what agents do. AI works as an intelligence multiplier, one participant noted, which means mistakes are amplified as quickly as good decisions. Skill erosion sparked livelier debate. Some saw a shift in skills, much as calculators changed arithmetic. Others, particularly in healthcare, worried about losing the expertise needed to judge AI output at all. One practical answer was to decide deliberately where AI drafts and where humans do. Data control as a design decision For telecom and healthcare leaders, data control is settled at design time. Models cannot simply run in a public cloud when regulators, tenancy separation, and residency rules apply, and one mistake can bring heavy penalties. Others stressed governance from the first stage, covering what data is ingested, what is used for training versus inference, and how it is masked or de-identified. Concerns about intellectual property and bias also led to a call to vet AI tools as rigorously as new hires. Observability for an agentic world Observability ran through every topic. Teams described tracing agent inputs, decisions, and handoffs so they can see why an agent acted as it did and correct it. One ecommerce team learned the cost of underinvesting: a ranking change left every dashboard green while business impact surfaced days later, and the root cause analysis took more than a week. It has since built a change ledger, lineage, a system graph, and a debugging agent that proposes ranked hypotheses. The observability view was that it can no longer sit apart from development. Paul Trebe put it plainly: “You can no longer decouple observability from development.” Agents need context-rich data to act well, he noted, and the agents themselves must be monitored, since AI traces can run to 500,000 lines that only other agents can realistically parse. What comes next No one claimed a finished playbook. Open questions remain on measuring agent reliability and return on investment, protecting data and IP, and keeping engineers sharp enough to challenge what AI produces. Still, the conversation pointed to a common direction. Give developers room to move fast, but build the guardrails first. Keep humans in charge of irreversible and high-impact calls, and widen automation as trust is earned. Several participants argued that standing still is not an option, since competitors will not wait. The real test of the AI era is less about how quickly teams can build and more about how confidently they can run what they have built.

title: How a Rs 500 Cr bet put Bihar Museum ahead of the Met and Louvre
content: Bihar Museum in Patna was recently ranked ahead of New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Louvre in Paris. The museum has secured the ninth place on The World's 100 Best Museums 2026, published by German travel guide Worth a Journey. The Met stands tenth and the Louvre 31st. It is the only Indian institution on the list and the highest-ranked museum in Asia. For a museum that opened barely a decade ago, it is a significant achievement. More so because there was a time when the project itself faced serious opposition, with questions raised about its cost, relevance and the way it was being executed. Reflecting on the recognition in a recent LinkedIn post, YourStory Founder and CEO Shradha Sharma recalled the roles played by two people in getting the museum built: Nitish Kumar, who championed the project as Bihar's Chief Minister, and 1992-batch IAS officer Chanchal Kumar, who was entrusted with its execution. When the state government proposed spending nearly Rs 500 crore on a world-class museum in Patna, the decision attracted criticism. Why should a state struggling with basic infrastructure invest so much in a museum? Who would visit it? Could the money have been better spent elsewhere? According to Sharma, even people within the political establishment questioned the proposal. Nitish Kumar, however, stood by the project, convinced that Bihar needed an institution worthy of its historical and cultural heritage. This Diwali, this one is for everyone who has ever been written off. A museum in Patna now ranks above the Met in New York and the Louvre in Paris. The Bihar Museum is 9th on the World’s 100 Best Museums list for 2026 put out by the German travel guide Worth a Journey. The Met is… pic.twitter.com/1sUAvkUqfh — Shradha Sharma (@SharmaShradha) November 6, 2026 Getting the museum built The challenges began with the land. According to Sharma, the proposed 13-acre site had seven government bungalows, some occupied by senior officials and a state minister. Getting the occupants to vacate required considerable administrative effort and legal intervention. She also recounted an incident in which men allegedly linked to local politicians entered the construction site demanding subcontracts, prompting police intervention. The museum was designed by Pritzker Prize-winning Japanese architect Fumihiko Maki in collaboration with Mumbai-based architectural firm Opolis, while Larsen & Toubro was selected to construct it. But appointing internationally recognised architects and an established construction company was only part of the challenge. Getting the project completed was another matter. The museum also faced judicial scrutiny. In June 2015, the Patna High Court, hearing a public interest litigation, criticised the expenditure of approximately Rs 500 crore and questioned the transparency of the contracting process. The court held that the project was not in the public interest but declined to halt construction because the building was nearing completion. Those findings remain an important part of the museum's history. Its international recognition does not erase the questions raised about public spending and governance, although the institution has since gained recognition well beyond Bihar. Sharma credits much of the execution to Chanchal Kumar, who held the dual responsibility of Secretary of Art and Culture and Secretary of the Building Construction Department. The arrangement meant that both the museum's cultural vision and its construction came under the same officer. Sharma said she recently read his account of how the museum came together and was struck by how little he spoke about his own contribution. Behind the finished building were years of navigating approvals, land disputes, administrative resistance and the many complications that accompany a large public project. In Sharma's telling, Nitish Kumar's political backing and Chanchal Kumar's persistence were crucial to seeing it through. A reminder of Bihar's strengths For Sharma, who grew up in Bihar, the recognition carries a more personal meaning. Few places in India can claim the kind of historical and intellectual inheritance that Bihar possesses. Bodh Gaya is where the Buddha attained enlightenment. Vaishali is closely associated with Mahavira. Ancient Pataliputra was the capital of the Mauryan Empire under Ashoka, while Patna is the birthplace of Guru Gobind Singh. Nalanda and Vikramshila were among the great centres of learning in ancient India. Yet Bihar's present-day image often has little to do with this extraordinary history. Its achievements are celebrated in textbooks, but the state has struggled to build contemporary institutions that attract the same admiration. Sharma drew on an episode from the Ramayana to explain what the museum means to her. Before Hanuman makes his leap across the ocean to Lanka, Jambavan reminds him of the strength he has forgotten. Bihar, she suggested, needed a similar reminder of what it is capable of achieving. The museum offers one. Its galleries house sculptures, coins, manuscripts and artefacts that bring the region's history to life, including the celebrated Didarganj Yakshi. And now, a German travel publication has placed it among the world's ten best museums, ahead of institutions with far longer histories and international reputations. The ranking is one publication's assessment, but it is nevertheless a significant moment for a museum that faced so many questions during its creation.

title: (Weekly funding roundup Oct 31-Nov 6) Sharp rise in capital inflow
content: November began on a positive note for the Indian startup ecosystem with venture capital funding seeing a sharp rise, after four weeks of tepid inflow of funds. The total funding for the first week of November was $263 million across 23 deals, compared to just $115 million in the previous week . This week saw two key breakthroughs. First, the total funding amount was well above $200 million. This is significant as the funds raised in the preceding four weeks were below $200 million. Second, after four weeks, the Indian startup ecosystem saw a $100-million transaction from jewellery brand GIVA. These developments provide a big boost to the startup ecosystem, which has been struggling to raise large amounts of capital. Additionally, a potential investor slump in AI companies in the aftermath of the US mid-term elections could benefit Indian startups. This is because much of the money is concentrated in the AI segment in the US. Now one can expect some sort of rebalancing in capital distribution with certain funds flowing into India. However, it is early days to comment on how the capital will flow into the country. Key transactions Jewellery brand GIVA raised $100 million led by Multiples Alternate Asset Management. Consumer AI startup EloElo Group raised $80 million from Hornbill Capital, NBCUniversal, MIT Investment Co, Play Ventures, Kalaari Capital, Waterbridge Ventures and Griffin Gaming Partners. Healthtech startup Clinics On Cloud raised $12.5 million from Model42. Peppermint Robotics raised Rs 100 crore (~$10.5 million) from pi Ventures, Crane Venture Partners and Asiana Fund. Speciality chemicals startup altM raised $10.3 million from Rainmatter by Zerodha, Mela Ventures, Omnivore, Theia Ventures, Aureolis Ventures and Spectrum Impact. Cleantech startup Two Point O Capital (TW.O) raised $10 million from Transition Venture Capital, Omnivore and angel investors. Wealthtech startup PowerUp Money raised $10 million from Flourish Ventures, Peak XV Partners, Accel, Blume Ventures, Kae Capital, 8i Ventures and DeVC. Spacetech startup Cosmoserve Space raised $6 million from Rebright Partners, Aranya Holdings, Naandi Ventures, AUM Ventures and Shakti VC.

title: Why operational excellence will define the next phase of India’s startup growth
content: Growth rarely announces itself. It arrives as a signed term sheet on a Friday evening, a large client wanting to go live in three weeks, or an investor doubling a commitment. But the win is rarely the hard part. The hard part is the Monday after. That Monday tells you whether you have built a company or simply had a good quarter. When operations become a competitive advantage In most startups, operations sit in the back seat. It is the team that asks for approvals, slows down contracts, and says “not yet” when sales say “yes”. Founders tolerate it the way one tolerates a seatbelt. I have never accepted that framing. Bain & Company’s long-running research on growth found that 85% of the barriers to profitable growth are internal, with revenue outgrowing talent at the top of the list. Companies rarely lose to the market. They lose to their own machinery, and that machinery is operations. Build it before you need it Early on, operations feel optional. A small team, a founder who knows everything, a spreadsheet that works. Why design controls for a business that fits in one room? Because by the time you feel the need, you are already late. Operations built in the middle of a growth spurt is built under pressure: rushed hires, patched processes, controls bolted on after something breaks. Worse, it takes bandwidth from growth itself. The team that should be closing the next client is busy repairing the last one. You slow down precisely when you meant to accelerate. Nobody lays the tracks after the train has left the station. This is not a case for bloat. It is a case for sequencing. Build the backbone one stage ahead of where you are, lean and proportionate, so the organisation absorbs growth instead of buckling under it. The companies that scale most smoothly are rarely the ones scrambling when growth arrives; the reporting, controls and people for the next stage are already in place. Investors notice the difference. In due diligence, a clean data room and a well-documented control environment often say more about a company's readiness than its growth curve does. Run on data, not opinions Operations is also where a company's data lives, or should. Every onboarding, approval, and report generates information. Most startups treat it as exhaust. The better ones treat it as instrumentation. When operations own clean, consistent data, leadership stops arguing about whose number is right and starts debating what to do about it. You see a bottleneck forming before a client complains. And automation and AI, which nearly every board is now asking about, only work on data you can trust. Automate a messy process and you simply get the mess faster. If your founders and your operations team are looking at different numbers, you do not have a data problem. You have an operations problem. Never pay for the same lesson twice The same discipline applies to mistakes. A mistake made once is a lesson; made twice, it is a choice. Every error in a growing firm should leave something behind, whether a changed control, a clearer owner, or a better checklist. The corollary matters as much. If the same method keeps producing the same disappointing result, the problem is rarely effort. It is the method. Operations should be the function that notices, asks why, and has the licence to change how the work gets done. Processes are not scripture. They are hypotheses, and good operators keep testing them. Bring operations in before growth is sold, not after For founders and boards redrawing their organisation charts this year, one test is telling. Do operations hear about a new product, market, or client after it is sold, or while it is being designed? If it is after, operations will always be firefighting, and firefighters rarely get to build anything. Put operations where growth is planned, not at the end of the line where growth is processed. Give it a seat in strategy reviews, a voice in pricing and launches, and a mandate to say "here is how", not just "not yet". Three questions are worth asking every quarter: ● If our business doubled next quarter, what would break first? ● Which decisions still need the founder, and should they? ● Would our records survive an investor's due diligence this week? Will your growth last, or was it just a good quarter? There is an old military line: amateurs talk strategy, professionals talk logistics. India's startup story so far has been told in the language of strategy: rounds, valuations, category creation. The next chapter will be about sustaining growth rather than merely achieving it, and it will be told in the language of execution and governance. Momentary growth is an event. Sustained growth is a capability. And capability, in the end, is what operations builds. (Sandesha Jaitapkar is the COO at Artha Group)

title: Govt clears 12 more proposals worth over Rs 7,500 Cr under electronics components scheme
content: The government has approved a new tranche of 12 applications, worth over Rs 7,500 crore, under the Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme, IT Secretary S Krishnan said on Friday. The latest round of approvals also covers projects related to materials and capital goods, widening the scheme's reach across the electronics supply chain. This round of approvals adds to the momentum behind the scheme, which aims to build a domestic ecosystem for components and reduce India's dependence on imports. The government is keen to strengthen upstream segments such as raw materials and manufacturing equipment, alongside component production. The government also launched the Semicon 2.0 web application portal under the ambitious Semicon India Programme.

title: Delhi HC upholds interim protection for BharatPe’s shareholder rights, dismisses Unity Bank’s appeal
content: A division bench of the Delhi High Court has dismissed an appeal by Unity Bank, upholding the interim protection granted to BharatPe's parent company RIPL (Resilient Innovations Private Limited) under the Shareholders’ Agreement and affirming the order of a single judge. The court has now, on two occasions, declined to let the bank and its promoter proceed on reserved matters without the prior written consent of RIPL, as the Shareholders’ Agreement (SHA) requires. Rejecting the bank’s explanation that it had sought RIPL’s consent on Reserved Matters through an “inadvertent error”, the bench called the plea an “argument of desperation and nothing more”. It noted that Unity had expressly sought RIPL’s consent in writing, which showed it knew of the contractual requirement. The bench reaffirmed that Unity cannot take decisions on Reserved Matters without the prior written consent of RIPL and Centrum, observing that Clause 8 of the SHA explicitly bars any action on such matters without it. It endorsed the single judge’s findings, describing the matter as “elementary”. The court also rejected Unity’s contention that the Reserve Bank of India had turned down the SHA. It observed that the RBI had never objected to the agreement, which had been submitted to it for approval, and held that the injunction does not obstruct any RBI directive and merely requires enforcement of Clause 8. Turning down the argument that the SHA cannot override the Articles of Association, the bench noted that Clause 8 opens with a non obstante clause, giving it precedence over the relevant provisions of the Articles. BharatPe welcomed the decision. A spokesperson said, “The Board must ensure that the Bank complies with the Court’s directions in letter and spirit. We expect the Board to exercise independent judgment, free from undue influence, and act in the interests of the Bank and all its stakeholders, including minority shareholders. Governance processes followed since the Bank’s inception must be respected and applied consistently. They cannot be set aside to favour one shareholder group at the expense of another. “We expect the Board to guide the Bank in honouring its contractual obligations and ensuring that its actions comply with the Court’s directions. We believe the Hon’ble Division Bench’s decision reinforces the importance of the agreed governance framework and the shareholder rights that formed the basis of the joint venture in 2021. Respect for these commitments is essential to maintaining trust between shareholders and protecting the institution’s long-term interests.” The ruling reinforces that Unity Bank is bound by the Reserved Matter provisions of the SHA and cannot dismiss its own written requests for shareholder consent as inadvertent errors to avoid its contractual obligations.

title: AI-powered cyberattacks put Indian fintechs on alert; Shiprocket turns profitable in Q2 FY27
content: Dear Reader, Investor appetite for India’s B2C ecommerce sector appears to be cooling. Funding fell 33% to $1.6 billion across 356 rounds between January and November 3, 2026, compared with $2.4 billion across 621 rounds in the year-ago period, according to Tracxn. Late-stage and seed-stage funding declined 51% and 50%, respectively, while early-stage investments remained relatively stable, growing 3%. While investors are becoming more cautious, the AI infrastructure boom is facing a different challenge: rising public concerns over its impact on local communities. OpenAI has pledged to pay the full electricity costs of data centres it owns and operates, while committing to greater transparency around construction plans and community consultations. Meanwhile, India's cybersecurity watchdog CERT-In has warned of AI-driven attacks targeting fintech firms and NBFCs, with hackers exploiting payment systems to siphon off funds. Cybersecurity concerns are also surfacing across global financial services. Binance has revoked all API keys linked to third-party trading platform SignalPlus following a potential security issue reported by the company. The exchange said its own systems and user funds remain safe, and advised affected users to review their trading positions before reconnecting. The risks extend beyond financial services. A cyberattack targeting refrigeration control systems at three sites operated by France's national blood service raised storage temperatures for plasma and other blood products. Monitoring systems detected the breach in time, allowing staff to move supplies before any products were compromised. Authorities are investigating the incident. In today’s newsletter: CERT-In flags AI-driven attacks on NBFCs, fintech firms Saraniya Periasamy’s journey at Agnikul Cosmos Shiprocket turns profitable in Q2 FY27 Here’s your trivia for today: What is a 'zero-day' vulnerability in cybersecurity? (Scroll down for the answer) Artificial Intelligence CERT-In flags AI-driven attacks on NBFCs, fintech firms Attack on NBFCs AI-powered cyberattacks targeting India’s financial services sector are escalating, prompting a fresh warning from CERT-In. The government cybersecurity agency has flagged a campaign called CRAFTY FALCON, which uses AI tools to target NBFCs, fintech companies and other financial institutions. The attacks have involved exploiting payment systems and stealing cryptocurrency assets. Key takeaways: CERT-In has identified an active campaign called CRAFTY FALCON, which uses machine intelligence and AI-assisted tools to target financial institutions. Attackers have exploited merchant settlement APIs to move funds and stolen wallet keys to siphon cryptocurrency assets. The campaign has affected NBFCs, digital lending platforms, payment aggregators, fintech firms and crypto exchanges, with CERT-In warning that the threat remains active. Inspiration Saraniya Periasamy’s journey at Agnikul Cosmos From joining a space-tech startup with no prior experience in the sector to leading the development of an orbital launch vehicle, Saraniya Periasamy’s journey has been anything but conventional. As Agnikul Cosmos’ fourth employee, she has played a key role in the company’s efforts to build indigenous rocket technology. Today, as Executive Vice President and Vehicle Director, she is helping steer the development of Agnibaan while encouraging more women to explore careers in space-tech. Breaking barriers: Saraniya joined Agnikul Cosmos eight years ago as a Systems Engineer and went on to lead the development of its Agnibaan SOrTeD suborbital mission, which successfully flew in May 2024. She is now leading the development of Agnibaan, the company's orbital launch vehicle, with plans to demonstrate booster recovery and reuse, alongside exploring ways to repurpose its upper stage. Having transitioned from civil engineering and ocean technology into space, Saraniya believes self-doubt is often a bigger barrier for women than a lack of opportunities. Ecommerce Shiprocket turns profitable in Q2 FY27 Shiprocket turned profitable in Q2 FY27, reporting a net profit of Rs 60 lakh against a loss of Rs 20.3 crore a year ago, while revenue grew 35% to Rs 673.6 crore. Its emerging business, led by Martech and omnichannel solutions, grew 61% during the quarter. The company also repaid Rs 242 crore in borrowings following its IPO, ending the first half debt-free. News & updates Ambulance pricing: Blinkit Ambulance will charge Rs 2,500 for non-emergency transfers, while emergency services will continue to remain free. Zomato founder Deepinder Goyal said the move aims to discourage routine hospital visits and transfers from using emergency ambulances, keeping them available for critical cases. Ronaldo retires: Cristiano Ronaldo will retire from Portugal's national team after the November international break, ending a 23-year international career. He leaves as men's international football's record goalscorer with 146 goals in 234 appearances, having led Portugal to the Euro 2016 title and two Nations League victories. What is a 'zero-day' vulnerability in cybersecurity? Answer: A security flaw that attackers can exploit before a fix is available We would love to hear from you!
