title: Northern Arc's diversified debt fund hits first close at over Rs 400 Cr
content: Northern Arc Investment Managers, the asset management arm of Northern Arc Capital, has announced the first close of its Northern Arc Diversified Debt Fund with commitments of more than Rs 400 crore from institutions, family offices, ultra-high-net-worth individuals (UHNIs) and high-net-worth individuals (HNIs). The fund is the firm's 15th private credit vehicle. It is a sector-agnostic Category II Alternative Investment Fund (AIF) focused on performing private credit, rated AA (SO) by CareEdge Ratings. It targets a corpus of Rs 1,500 crore, with a greenshoe option of Rs 500 crore that could take it to Rs 2,000 crore. The fund has a five-year tenure and targets a 16% XIRR. The announcement coincides with the maturity of the Northern Arc India Impact Fund, which channelled global capital into financial inclusion opportunities across India. Over its tenure, the fund supported 60 businesses across credit cycles, with gross deployment of over Rs 1,398 crore at the fund level, backed by UHNIs, family offices, and domestic and global institutional investors. Commenting on the announcements, Ashish Mehrotra, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Northern Arc Capital, said, "The first close of the Northern Arc Diversified Debt Fund reflects continued investor interest in private credit and its evolving role in sophisticated investment portfolios. The maturity of our Northern Arc India Impact Fund further demonstrates our experience in managing private credit investments across credit cycles. Together, these milestones reinforce our focus on disciplined credit selection, portfolio diversification and risk management.” He added, “Over the past decade, we have built a diversified private credit platform that has deployed over Rs. 16,500 crores across 15 AIFs and two PMS offerings and served more than 1,500 investors across institutional and wealth segments. As private credit becomes an increasingly strategic allocation for investors, we remain focused on connecting capital with businesses across sectors while creating opportunities for risk-adjusted returns." Since its inception in 2014, Northern Arc Investment Managers has launched 15 funds, of which seven have fully matured, delivering returns at a weighted average XIRR of over 14.5%, in line with targeted returns, without any extension or principal loss to investors, the company said. It has cumulatively distributed over Rs 10,000 crore of principal and coupon since inception. Separately, Northern Arc Capital reported a 41% year-on-year growth in consolidated profit after tax to Rs 129 crore in Q2 FY27, while net interest income rose 32% to Rs 425 crore. Lending assets under management grew 34% to Rs 19,003 crore, supported by a 64% rise in direct lending AUM to Rs 12,502 crore, which now accounts for 66% of the overall portfolio. Credit costs improved by 11 basis points to 2.66%."

title: MakeMyTrip enters shared mobility space with majority stake in Quick Ride
content: MakeMyTrip on Friday announced it has acquired a majority stake in 'Quick Ride', a technology-led shared mobility platform, for an undisclosed sum. The investment provides an opportunity for MakeMyTrip to establish its presence in the shared mobility/ride pooling segment, complementary to the group's existing ground transportation portfolio, the company stated. Bengaluru-headquartered Quick Ride is a technology-led, asset-light shared mobility platform that connects people travelling along similar routes, enabling affordable ride pooling for everyday commutes. The 'Quick Ride' brand and its ride pooling business underwent an internal restructuring and are now housed under a new entity, Co Ride Mobility Private Limited. MakeMyTrip has acquired the Quick Ride brand and its ride pooling business with a majority stake in this entity. Quick Ride's promoters will continue to lead the business. Its erstwhile EV taxi business will remain with the predecessor entity, iDisha Info Labs Private Limited, MakeMyTrip stated. Rajesh Magow, Co-Founder & Group Chief Executive Officer, MakeMyTrip, said, "As part of our expansion strategy, we have pursued selective strategic partnerships, investments and acquisitions that complement and strengthen our existing business and expand the breadth and depth of our offerings. Ride pooling gives us a presence in high-frequency daily commutes within cities, as well as intercity travel". Quick Ride will be housed under our ground transport business, and we will bring the learnings from building redBus in India and overseas markets to grow and scale the business, he added. KNM Rao, Founder and CEO, Quick Ride, said, "Becoming part of the MakeMyTrip group is an important milestone for our team and for the community of users who have placed their trust in us. We look forward to drawing on MakeMyTrip's reach and experience in travel to further scale the business". In recent years, MakeMyTrip has made acquisitions across travel segments, including Savaari in car rental services, Happay in corporate travel and expense management, Flamingo Transworld in regional group holiday packages and through strategic minority investment in Atlys in visa processing.

title: Deepinder Goyal hits back at doctors, defends wearable device Temple
content: Eternal founder Deepinder Goyal has posted a series of updates and clarifications on X amid backlash from some Indian doctors who criticised his brain-monitoring wearable Temple. Describing Temple as “an ambitious project”, Goyal gave a detailed explanation on what the team is building. “The team is delusional enough to think we can build this. And we will,” he wrote on Friday. He also later added that the first 10,000 orders will not have to pay a subscription to use Temple. Criticising the doctors, he said, "All my emotion last night was directed at a few influencer doctors, who are more influencers than doctors. They did not read our research in detail, and spread twisted facts to call something new a scam. They get views by piling on us." The open debate started on Thursday when Goyal took to X to defend the device. He said, “First and foremost, a business lesson: if Temple were a scam, and any of what we said weren't true, people would know it in just a few days of using Temple.” He also said the device features a 14-day no-question return policy. “If the product doesn't work, it fails out of the gate and the company dies before recovering a tenth of its R&D," he said. Goyal is currently Vice Chairman and Non-Executive Director of Eternal (parent company of Zomato). He is also the founder of healthtech wearable startup Temple and LAT Aerospace. In the post, Goyal highlighted that $30 million was invested in building the device, including $20 million of his personal money. Calling this his purpose, he said it's not about the money. “I have enough of it to last for generations. My incentives are fully aligned with getting the science right. I am not staking a reputation earned over 20 years on making a quick buck.” Goyal argued that most wearable companies start with internal studies. He referred to Whoop which shipped its fitness band in 2015 but the first published validation happened a few years later. He also added that Temple had a higher standard. "Pre-prints are a step prior to peer reviewed publications, and they are coming up." Reposing confidence in the product, he said, “We stand by our science and our methods. Each of our claims is easily verifiable by individuals and institutions alike, and you will see a lot of independent studies come up on their own when the device becomes available to use.” Moreover, he added that this device is a fitness tracker, and wellness device, not a medical device. “If at some point, we clinically validate any of our metrics, we will let you know.” Dear Concerned Indian Doctors, I see your rage against Temple on X. I have a few points to make: 1. First and foremost, a business lesson: if Temple were a scam, and any of what we said weren't true, people would know it in just a few days of using Temple. We have 14-day,… — Deepinder Goyal (@deepigoyal) November 5, 2026 However, some doctors were not convinced by Goyal’s response. Responding to Goyal's claim on showing scientific evidence, an X user, who goes by the handle TheLiverdoc, said the Apple Watch Series 11 and Fitbit Sense had shown clinical evidence before launch. Similarly, Samsung Galaxy Watch8 and Watch9 also passed FDA trials prior to release. "Meanwhile, the Oura Ring 4 and Whoop 4.0 launched as wellness trackers backed by peer-reviewed sleep studies." To the people disparaging the Indian medical community, please note that we, me included, are not against technological solutions towards improved preventative care. In fact, preventative care is is the heart of medical science. But, let us not confuse fradulently selling… pic.twitter.com/5riczT3cli — TheLiverDoc™ (@theliverdoc) November 6, 2026 On X, Dr Rishabh Jain responded saying Goyal shared financial and personal sacrifices but no scientific evidence. "Stop calling legitimate scientific scrutiny 'rage'. You have responded to questions about medical accuracy with investment figures, return policies, personal reputation, and promises of future studies. None of these constitutes scientific validation.” Criticising the return policy he said, "Subjective satisfaction cannot establish medical accuracy.” Dr Jain further said that doctors are not against innovation. However the evidence needs to show it. "If Temple delivers what it promises, doctors will be among its biggest supporters." He also said that science is not a popularity contest, and criticism is not “rage". Dr Jain also asked for data that can be reviewed by independent researchers. Dear Temple Team, Doctors are asking for scientific evidence, not your financial history, personal sacrifices, or business credentials. Stop calling legitimate scientific scrutiny “rage.” You have responded to questions about medical accuracy with investment figures, return… https://t.co/wh6N0zPypu — Dr Rishabh Jain (@DrRishabhOnco) November 5, 2026 Temple is a wearable device that tracks blood flow and oxygenation inside the brain. Goyal has not disclosed the price of the device. In May this year, Goyal announced that the first 100 devices were ready to ship to select founding users and was aimed at athletes, scientists, doctors, founders, creators, and others who could provide feedback on the device. Pre-orders for Temple officially opened in India earlier this month. In February this year, Temple raised $54 million in its first funding round from friends and family investors, at a valuation of about $190 million. The copy was updated with additional information and quotes.

title: AI’s ability to find cyber flaws outpacing firms’ capacity to fix them: Palo Alto Networks' Nikesh Arora
content: Nikesh Arora, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Palo Alto Networks, has raised concerns about the growing use of frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models to identify software vulnerabilities and link them into potential attack paths. While these capabilities can help strengthen cybersecurity, they could also give attackers faster ways to exploit weaknesses in enterprise systems. The bigger challenge, Arora notes in a LinkedIn post , is ensuring that organisations can verify, prioritise and fix vulnerabilities at the same pace at which AI can discover them. “Most organizations do not have capacity to patch at the speed needed, especially the smaller ones,” Arora wrote. Smaller businesses often lack security specialists, while larger ones must test fixes against existing applications. He also says models identify different weaknesses, so one model cannot provide complete coverage. Finding a flaw is only the start. Teams must confirm it, assess the risk, develop a fix, test for disruption and deploy it. False positives, or incorrect alerts, waste time, while untested patches can disrupt services. The scale is growing. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology said submissions to its National Vulnerability Database rose 263% between 2020 and 2025. It enriched nearly 42,000 records in 2025, but this was still insufficient. In April 2026, it adopted risk-based prioritisation, focusing on exploited flaws and critical software. AI developers are linking discovery with repair. Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, launched in April 2026 with Palo Alto Networks among its partners, gives selected organisations access to Claude Mythos Preview for defensive security. Anthropic said partners had identified more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity flaws by June and expanded the programme to around 150 additional organisations. On November 4, OpenAI reported that a controlled Linux-kernel pipeline generated candidate patches for 948 local privilege-escalation vulnerabilities, which allow a user to gain higher access rights. Human researchers reviewed the findings before reporting them to maintainers. In India, CERT-In’s November 4 advisory warned of an AI-assisted threat actor targeting non-bank lenders, fintech firms, payment providers and cryptocurrency platforms through machine intelligence and payment APIs. The agency has also issued 2026 guidance on AI-assisted vulnerability defence and AI security auditing. Arora advocates virtual patching as an interim measure. “The most obvious solution is virtual patching. This is a time tested technology that is currently available with cyber vendors for endpoints, WAF, cloud, network use cases.” WAF is a web application firewall, which filters website and application traffic. A virtual patch is a security rule that blocks a known method of exploiting a flaw without changing the affected software. It buys time while a permanent update is tested, but does not remove the weakness. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project cautions that it protects only the traffic the system inspects and attacks variations its rules recognise. Arora calls for a shared vulnerability clearing house and faster development of protective signatures, or detection rules. He also highlights operational technology, systems that monitor or control physical processes such as energy, water and transport. Patching them can be difficult because downtime may affect safety or essential services.

title: Mamaearth parent Honasa's Q2 net profit rises 87%
content: Honasa Consumer, the parent company of beauty & personal care brand Mamaearth, registered an 87% year-on-year (YoY) rise in net profit for the second quarter of the current fiscal, while revenue rose 36% driven by strong growth across categories. The company reported a net profit of Rs 73.24 crore in Q2FY27, compared with Rs 39.22 crore in the similar period of FY26. Revenue during the quarter was Rs 731.18 crore, compared with Rs 538.06 crore a year ago. According to Honasa Consumer, the second quarter revenue growth is the highest it has recorded since its public listing in November 2023. However, sequentially, profit fell from Rs 90.44 crore in the first quarter. Revenue in the first quarter was Rs 755.94 crore. Honasa also operates the brands Dermacare and Aqualogica. CEO Varun Alagh said, “At the brand level, each business is writing its own growth story. Mamaearth has sustained its high-teens growth, The Derma Co. continues to grow profitably. Our Younger Brands grew over 45% YoY, reflecting highlighting the potential of our emerging portfolio.” He added that each brand has a distinct consumer, proposition and opportunity and the goal is to build a sustainable business in each category. The omnichannel channel retailer noted that its offline business saw growth, with general trade expanding to over 3.2 lakh outlets and modern trade (large-format retail outlets) recording a 40% YoY growth in offtake. “As we enter the next phase of growth, we will continue to push the boundaries of innovation, deepen our presence in core categories, and make our products accessible to more consumers across channels,” said Ghazal Alagh, CIO & Co-founder, Honasa Consumer. For the six months of the fiscal year, the company reported a revenue of Rs 1,487.13 crore, a YoY growth of 31%. The net profit for the period was Rs 163.69 crore, a YoY rise of 103%.

title: India rebased its GDP. It still can’t see the Rs 34.5 lakh crore women do free
content: In February 2026, India moved its GDP base year to 2022-23. The National Accounts of India brought in new data sources and reassessed the size of the informal economy. The exercise carried a lesson that policy debates often forget: economic measurement is not fixed. When the statistical system decides an activity deserves to be captured better, the numbers change. The same quarter, the economy grew 7.8%, keeping India the fastest-growing major economy even through the first full quarter of steep US tariffs and disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. The headlines celebrated. But one kind of work counted for nothing in all that arithmetic: the unpaid domestic and care work that makes every other job possible. The invisible fifth of the economy GDP has a defined production boundary, and for good reason. A creche worker paid to look after a child is counted as economic activity. A mother or grandmother doing the same job for free is not. The value has not disappeared; only the payment has. What sits outside that boundary is large. India's Time Use Survey 2024 shows women aged 15 to 59 spend about 201 minutes a day more than men on unpaid household work. A deeper analysis of the unit-level data puts women's unpaid domestic and care work at 343 minutes a day, against 43 for men. Some 93% of women do this work, compared with 44% of men. A Ministry of Women and Child Development study values this work at up to Rs 34.5 lakh crore, roughly 15–17% of GDP at weighted average wages. Even the Ministry of Statistics' Time Use Survey report concedes that leaving out unpaid services means GDP "underestimates considerably the total income of a nation." The global answer is not to abandon GDP but to add a satellite account that measures activity beyond the production boundary. India already has the raw material: two national Time Use Surveys, an accepted valuation method, and a statistical system that has just shown it can rebuild its accounts. What is missing is the decision. From invisible labour to the second shift Visibility matters because governments allocate money through the numbers they measure. According to the UNDP , 44.5% of Indian women outside the labour force cite childcare and homemaking as the main reason. Female labour-force participation has climbed from 23.3% in 2017-18 to about 40% in 2025, by the Periodic Labour Force Survey's measure. Yet women's unpaid workload has barely moved in five years. A woman who takes a paid job while carrying the same load at home has not been freed to work. She has taken on a second shift. The real policy question is not how to persuade more women to work. It is what infrastructure would make paid work compatible with care. India's jobs ambition has a care problem The contradiction shows up in the government's own documents. The Economic Survey's employment chapter calls the care economy a promising source of jobs, and the Economic Survey 2025-26 targets a 55% female workforce. Yet under the Palna scheme , only 11,395 anganwadi-cum-creches had been approved against a target of 17,000 by March 2025. Fewer than 10% of anganwadi centres are in cities, where women's participation is lowest. The shortfall does not mean the scheme has failed. It means care infrastructure is still being built while the country sets big employment goals. If policymakers want a real rise in women's paid work, childcare must stop being a side programme and become labour-market policy . What other countries did differently By the ILO's harmonised estimates, India's female labour-force participation was 32% in 2025. The figure is lower than the PLFS number because the ILO uses a different, internationally comparable definition. Female labour-force participation, 2025 (ILO estimates) Country Participation rate China 59% Japan 56.5% Bangladesh 46.5% India 32% Source: International Labour Organization (ILO) Among women of prime working age, participation reaches 85% in Japan and 78% in the United States. These gaps are policy outcomes, not accidents. Japan raised fathers' take-up of parental leave from 17.1% to 30.1% in a single year by paying for it. Bangladesh , with a fraction of India's output, lifted net pre-primary enrolment from 19.7% in 2018 to 28.5% in 2023 as part of a deliberate push to get women into work. The United States learnt the opposite lesson: prime-age women hit record participation, then gains among mothers of young children stalled where affordable childcare ran out. No country has gone from developing to developed while leaving half its working-age women outside the paid economy. The road to Viksit Bharat has to take her along, or it will not arrive. Three ordinary acts of statecraft 1. Measure it. Complete and regularly publish a satellite account for unpaid care work, linked to the Time Use Survey. It should show the work's value, who does it, where it is concentrated and how it changes. The aim is not to inflate GDP but to give planners a second dashboard to act on. 2. Invest in it. The UNDP estimates that spending about 2% of GDP on care services could create more than 11 million jobs. As India urbanises, fertility falls and joint families thin out, who provides care is becoming an economic question, not just a household one. 3. Reclassify it. Care spending should be judged not only as welfare but by its effect on employment, labour supply and productivity. If a childcare centre lets twenty parents stay in work, its value cannot be measured only by the children it serves. Seeing what GDP cannot This argument is no longer confined to feminist economics. A working paper from the Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister this year calls for moving care "from private burden to social and economic infrastructure." The diagnosis is in, and the evidence backs it. The harder question is whether measurement, budgeting and delivery will follow. The 2026 rebasing showed that India's statistical system can question long-held assumptions. The same willingness should now extend to the work that sustains the economy from outside its markets. That means collecting real-time data, publishing a satellite account for unpaid care linked to the Time Use Survey, and treating care infrastructure as a measurable public investment. Every new creche, eldercare service and community care programme should be judged not only by the people it serves but by the paid work it makes possible. If India wants more women in its workforce, it must budget for the care that makes their work possible. India has shown it can re-measure its economy. Now it must build the care that lets more women take part in it.

title: Aina launches Rs 47,000 ring to bring AI agents to your fingertips
content: What if booking a cab, sending a message or managing a meeting required nothing more than a flick of your thumb? Bengaluru- and San Francisco-based startup Aina believes the next phase of artificial intelligence will be less about asking machines questions and more about letting them anticipate what people need. At a private launch event in Bengaluru, the startup unveiled an AI-powered smart ring that combines a colour display, voice commands and gesture-based controls. Priced at $499 (Rs 47,000), the device is available for pre-order at a limited early-bird price starting at $399 (Rs 37,700), with shipments expected to begin in January 2027. Unlike conventional smart rings, which largely focus on health and fitness tracking, Aina wants its device to become an everyday interface between users and AI agents. The premise is simple: AI agents are getting smarter, but using them still involves unlocking phones, navigating apps and approving individual actions. Aina wants to reduce that friction. Its proposition revolves around a question displayed during the launch presentation: What if AI didn't wait to be asked? An AI ring that anticipates your next move To simplify these interactions, Aina has built its ring around three features: Cues, Voice and Remote. Cues uses contextual information, including routines and connected applications, to anticipate what users might want to do next. For instance, if someone regularly books a cab around the same time each morning, the ring could suggest booking a ride without waiting for an explicit request. At the launch event, Aina demonstrated a ride-booking interaction that illustrated how everyday transactions could be completed through minimal gestures. The ring can be operated using a five-way joystick-like control, allowing users to approve or reject suggestions with their thumb without reaching for a smartphone. Aina says its context-aware intelligence can learn users' routines and anticipate relevant actions over the next 15 minutes, drawing on information from the iPhone, Mac and connected services. The company showcased integrations involving Uber, Apple Music, Spotify, phone calls, calendar meetings, smart home controls and email actions. The second interaction method, Voice, allows users to dictate notes, set reminders, send messages and issue commands. Aina also showcased use cases involving WhatsApp and Telegram, alongside Mac dictation through Wispr Flow. The third feature, Remote, turns the ring into a controller for connected devices. According to the company, users can manage music, phone calls, smart home appliances and meeting controls without picking up another device. What goes into the $499 ring? According to specifications presented at the Bengaluru launch, the ring weighs less than 13 grams and features a titanium body, full-colour display, haptic feedback and directional audio. The company claims up to 18 hours of battery life and plans to offer the device in four colours: Eclipse Black, Amber Gold, Mercury Silver and Slate Titanium, across seven sizes. Aina also highlighted a five-way control mechanism called the Shifter, which works alongside its gesture-based interface. The startup says the ring will come with an open developer platform, allowing third-party developers to build new interactions and integrations. It also showcased support for AI agent platforms including Muse, Grokbot and Instinct. The company currently supports iOS and Mac, with further integrations expected to be announced later. Whether its open platform translates into a substantial developer ecosystem will become clearer once the device reaches customers. From Ultrahuman to Aina Aina was founded by Apoorv Shankar, who previously served as vice-president of hardware at Bengaluru-based wearable technology company Ultrahuman. Shankar founded Aina in May 2025 as a human-computer interaction lab, focusing on how people could interact with intelligent software beyond conventional screens and keyboards. The startup raised $5.5 million in seed funding in July 2026 , as previously reported by YourStory. The round was led by Redstart Labs and 360 ONE Asset, with participation from MIXI Global Investments, Antler, Blume Founders Fund and angel investors including CRED founder Kunal Shah and Razorpay co-founders Harshil Mathur and Shashank Kumar. The funding was earmarked for commercialising its AI-first hardware interface and expanding its engineering and product teams. Aina says it spent around 15 months developing the technology and began testing the ring with a limited group of users in October 2026. Can a ring replace everyday smartphone interactions? Aina's launch comes as technology companies experiment with new ways of bringing AI into daily life. While smartphones remain the dominant interface for digital services, the rise of AI agents is prompting startups to rethink how people give instructions, approve actions and receive information. Aina's approach is to make that interface smaller and more contextual, with users retaining control over whether suggested actions are executed. However, at $499, the ring is a premium purchase, particularly when smartphones and smartwatches already perform many of the functions it promises. Its usefulness will depend on how accurately its AI anticipates user needs, how reliably it works with third-party services and whether the thumb-based controls become intuitive enough for daily use. Battery life, voice recognition and application support will also matter when the product moves beyond controlled demonstrations. For now, Aina's claims remain to be tested at scale, with commercial deliveries planned for January 2027.

title: Shiprocket turns profitable in Q2 FY27 with Rs 674 Cr revenue
content: Shiprocket, an ecommerce enablement platform for MSMEs, turned profitable in the second quarter of FY27, reporting a net profit of Rs 60 lakh for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, against a net loss of Rs 20.3 crore in the corresponding period last year. The company's revenue from operations increased 35% year-on-year (YoY) to Rs 673.6 crore during the quarter. Adjusted EBITDA stood at Rs 14.2 crore, compared with a loss in the year-ago period. Shiprocket's core business revenue grew 25% YoY to Rs 461.5 crore, while its emerging business revenue increased 61% to Rs 212.2 crore. The emerging business, which includes cross-border shipping, omnichannel fulfilment, hyperlocal delivery, marketing technology (Martech) and ecommerce enablement solutions, contributed 31% to overall revenue, compared with 26% a year ago. Within the emerging business, Martech revenue grew 102%, while the omnichannel business registered 79% growth during the quarter. Shiprocket attributed the growth in its omnichannel business to brands using its platform to replenish quick commerce dark stores. Its appointment-based delivery services allow brands to schedule deliveries and access real-time purchase order visibility from platforms such as Blinkit and Zepto. The company's contribution increased 43% YoY to Rs 130 crore, accounting for 19.3% of revenue. The core business generated adjusted EBITDA of Rs 59.1 crore, up 29% YoY, with its adjusted EBITDA margin improving to 12.8% from 12.4%. The emerging business narrowed its adjusted EBITDA margin loss to 21.2% from 31.5%, while its contribution margin improved to 15.4% from 10.1%. Shiprocket's trailing 12-month gross merchandise value (GMV) stood at Rs 37,398.7 crore, generated through 233 million unique transactions. The platform served more than 2.36 lakh active merchants during the period. The number of merchants using its emerging business products increased 75% to 62,025 on a trailing 12-month basis. During the quarter, 17,281 new merchants joined through emerging products, more than three times the 5,396 additions reported a year ago. “Indian commerce is splitting across more channels every year. A small brand today sells on its own website and on Instagram, replenishes quick commerce dark stores, and is starting to be found through AI search. For a large company, every new channel means a new team. For a small seller, it means friction. Shiprocket is building the infrastructure that removes this friction, so that any MSME in India can sell, ship and grow on the same footing as India’s biggest brands, every channel a switch away on one dashboard," said Saahil Goel, Managing Director and CEO of Shiprocket. "Growing 35% with positive Adjusted EBITDA and operating cash flow shows we can build it from our own operations. We are in the business of making other people a business, and our ambition is simple: to see the next generation of great Indian brands built on Shiprocket,” he added. “PAT turned positive this quarter on three drivers. First, scale in Core: transactions grew 31% and Adjusted EBITDA grew faster than revenue. Second, the Emerging engine kept firing: Martech and Omnichannel, our fastest-growing lines, more than doubled Emerging contribution on 61% revenue growth. Third, a stronger balance sheet: IPO proceeds retired all our borrowings, which cut finance costs, and the surplus now earns interest income," said Tanmay Kumar, CFO of Shiprocket. "We generated Rs 55.1 crore from operations in the first half, more than twice last year, and we are debt-free. Emerging now brings merchants onto the platform on its own, not only through cross-sell from Core. Around 17,300 merchants joined Shiprocket through our Emerging products this quarter, more than three times the number a year ago,” he said. Shiprocket also reported net cash from operating activities of Rs 55.1 crore in the first half of FY27, compared with Rs 23.8 crore in the corresponding period last year. Following the receipt of proceeds from its initial public offering (IPO) during the quarter, the company repaid its outstanding borrowings of Rs 242 crore, ending the first half debt-free. The company also introduced several AI-powered features during the quarter, including Aitlas, which helps brands track their visibility in AI search, personalised marketing journeys, enhanced checkout features and AI-powered shipping analytics. Its platform currently handles more than 14 billion API hits a month.

title: Spacetech startup Cosmoserve raises $6M in seed round
content: Cosmoserve Space, a Hyderabad-based spacetech startup, has raised $6 million in a seed round of funding from Rebright Partners of Japan, Aranya Holdings, and Naandi Ventures. The round also saw participation from existing investors AUM Ventures and Shakti VC. This funding round has seen Cosmoserve raising over $9 million. Cosmoserve also inaugurated Base 1 - a facility to design, build, test and operate systems for satellite servicing and space debris recovery. A statement said, this facility will have an orbital rendezvous and capture lab to simulate spacecraft capture operations, a space robotics innovation Lab to develop robotic capture systems; a clean room for satellite integration, a mission simulation and control Centre to manage upcoming missions. “In our first year we have flown our first payload on an Indian rocket, raised our seed round, and today we open a facility where we can design, build, test and fly our missions under one roof. Debris is becoming the limiting factor for every nation's space ambitions, including India's. Base 1 is where we build the capability to keep orbits usable, for Gaganyaan, the Bharatiya Antariksh Station and every satellite that follows,” said Chiranjeevi Phanindra, Founder & CEO of Cosmoserve Space. Beyond removing space debris, the company said the facility will support satellite servicing, including in-orbit repairs and refuelling. Cosmoserve currently sources close to 60% of its mission components locally. The company aims to develop more critical technologies in-house through Base 1 and strengthen domestic manufacturing capabilities. According to the spacetech startup, space debris is one of the biggest challenges facing the global space industry. Of the approximately 28,000 satellites in orbit, nearly 10,000 are dead or non-operational. Beyond these inactive satellites, Earth's orbit is crowded with an estimated 68,000 debris objects. Even fragments can pose serious risks to operational satellites, spacecraft and missions such as the International Space Station (ISS), given the high speeds at which they travel.

title: ForgeCode’s Tushar Mathur wants software development to run like a factory, not a project
content: Traditionally, scaling software development meant adding engineers, time, and resources. AI is changing that equation by making code cheaper and faster to write. But generating code faster does not necessarily mean delivering software faster. Code still needs to be reviewed, tested, and deployed, creating new bottlenecks for engineering teams. For engineering leaders, this raises a question: how can software delivery scale without a corresponding increase in headcount? ForgeCode is addressing this challenge by building what it calls an AI-native software factory. The platform uses AI agents to manage the software development lifecycle, from specifications and implementation to testing and deployment, with humans providing oversight. At TechSparks 2026, Founder and CEO Tushar Mathur demonstrated how the platform works and explained why the falling cost of writing code is making review, testing, and deployment more important to software delivery. The shift in bottlenecks While AI has increased individual productivity, those gains have not necessarily translated into faster software delivery across organizations. “The first thing that we are seeing is practically all code is autogenerated today,” Mathur said. Engineering teams can now generate thousands of lines of code quickly, but the processes that follow: code reviews, testing, security checks, and deployment are struggling to keep up. According to Mathur, the bottleneck has shifted from writing code to managing what happens after it is written. “Earlier, writing code was the main fundamental bottleneck. But today, the cost of writing code is so low that all these other aspects have become the bottlenecks,” he explained. As a result, teams risk producing more poorly reviewed, buggy or uncoordinated code because the systems needed to manage the increased output have not kept pace. The rise of the AI-native software factory To address this gap between individual productivity and organizational output, Mathur introduced ForgeCode’s approach to an AI-native software factory. The idea is to move away from a software development lifecycle that depends on people manually coordinating each stage. Instead, AI agents handle tasks such as triaging, planning, implementation, and verification. Humans step in when decisions, direction, or more detailed feedback are required. Unlike conventional automation, which links a series of predefined steps, the software factory uses continuous feedback loops. Inputs from CXOs, product managers, and production monitoring systems can feed directly into the development backlog. Agents then work around the clock to develop features, identify bugs, and improve performance, including when engineering teams are offline. The aim is to keep software development moving without requiring engineers to manage every individual task. Six tenets of a modern software factory Mathur outlined six principles that he believes are essential to building an effective AI-native software factory. Autonomous operation: The system should work continuously, with humans supervising performance rather than coordinating individual tasks. High scalability: Organizations should be able to scale engineering work quickly, whether they are developing a small feature or rewriting an entire application in a different programming language. Cost-effectiveness: The factory delivers multifold returns compared with manual development, measured through two key factors: the cost of building software and the speed at which it can be shipped. Measurability: The system should track deployment frequency, bug density, and costs, using this information to assess and improve its performance. Self-improvement: The factory should use data and feedback to refine its processes over time and avoid repeating earlier mistakes. Business-driven development: Features should be prioritized according to business objectives, such as customer retention or compliance, rather than solely by technical backlog requirements. Together, these principles are intended to make software development more autonomous while keeping it aligned with business priorities. Handling trade-offs and non-functional requirements During the audience Q&A, Mathur was asked how engineering teams should approach trade-offs and complex non-functional requirements such as scalability and database architecture. He said requirements that can be objectively verified, such as scale targets, can be delegated to the software factory. The system continuously tests outcomes and optimises whenever a check fails. Trade-offs, however, require human judgment. Questions such as how much risk or failure a business is willing to tolerate remain decisions for engineers and business leaders, who step in to guide the agent when needed. ForgeCode said this is possible because the platform operates on a self-improving feedback loop. Every task, decision, and correction contributes to a knowledge base that informs future work. Engineers remain closely involved in the early stages, but as the system learns a team's engineering practices and business context, it can operate with greater autonomy. The platform also learns which decisions are critical and require expert oversight, particularly those involving security, reliability, performance, and competing business priorities. In such cases, it pauses and seeks human input before proceeding. This growing ability to distinguish between routine execution and decisions that require expert judgment is central to how the product works. Steering the factory floor ForgeCode's AI-native software factory is designed to turn gains in individual coding productivity into faster software delivery across an organization. By using agents to manage coordination, code reviews, testing, and other development tasks, the platform aims to reduce the bottlenecks that can slow engineering teams. For Mathur, the shift is about changing the role of engineers. Rather than managing every stage of development, they would focus on defining requirements, making decisions, reviewing outcomes, and guiding the overall process. The goal is not simply to generate more code or build larger teams, but to develop software more efficiently through autonomous systems that operate continuously, with human oversight.

title: Beyond assets: Why 'family continuity' is the missing link in personal finance
content: In the digital era, financial information is increasingly accessible. Banking apps, investment platforms, and insurance portals make it easier to track assets and monitor investments. Yet, knowing what a family owns is not the same as knowing how to manage it. When the person responsible for the family's finances is unavailable, even temporarily, loved ones may struggle to locate accounts, understand liabilities, or determine what needs to be done next. At TechSparks 2026 in Bengaluru, Priyanka Arora, CMO of The Plan Beyond, spoke about this gap between accumulating wealth and preparing families to manage it. People spend years building assets for their loved ones, but often leave them without the information needed to access or manage those assets. The scale of the problem extends beyond individual households. According to a figure shared by the Finance Minister in October 2025, Rs 1.84 lakh crore in financial assets remain unclaimed in India. These assets point to a gap between wealth and the intended beneficiaries. The issue is not simply whether financial records exist. It is whether the right people know where to find them, understand what they mean, and what to do with them. From data to context Arora explained the problem to the audience using a simple exercise. She asked how many people knew where their parents kept their financial documents, which mutual funds they held, and how many bank accounts they had. Some participants raised their hands, but few appeared to know the details of their parents' investments. She then asked the audience to imagine a family whose primary breadwinner takes a 30-day digital detox. Could the rest of the family manage the household finances during that period? Would they know where the assets were held, which loans needed to be repaid, or when the next equated monthly installment (EMI) was due? The questions pointed to a gap in how families manage their finances. One person may know where the money is invested, which insurance policies are active, and what loans are outstanding. Other family members may know these assets exist without knowing how to access or manage them. “Data tells us what exists,” she said. But knowing that an investment or bank account exists is only the first step. Families also need to understand the purpose of an asset, the liabilities attached to it, and the decisions involved in managing it. An investment, for instance, may be linked to a loan or mortgage. Knowing that the asset exists does not explain the obligations that come with it. Without this information, family members may have to piece together financial details when they need to make decisions about the household's finances. Defining family continuity Arora joined The Plan Beyond after meeting its founder, Kulwinder Rastogi, and hearing the story behind the problem he wanted to solve. The company is building what it calls "family continuity" to address the gap between the assets people create for their families and their families' ability to understand and manage them. The concept goes beyond storing financial records. It brings together information about investments, insurance policies, identity documents, education funds, loans, and other obligations. It can also include personal messages and instructions intended for important milestones, such as a grandchild going to college or reaching another stage in life. The premise is that preparing a family should not be limited to planning for death or a medical emergency. It should also involve helping family members understand their finances and make informed decisions while the person managing them is still around to provide guidance. For Arora, continuity means putting the family at the center of financial planning. Instead of leaving information across different applications, documents, and individual accounts, the aim is to bring it together so families can understand what they have and how to act on it. Building for trust and security The Plan Beyond is developing a platform to bring this information together. Given the nature of financial and personal records, privacy, access, and data security are central to its development. Arora said the company is in its incubation phase, working on the product and its security architecture. It aims to meet global standards for security and privacy, alongside compliance with India's Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) framework and applicable legal requirements. The company is working toward an architecture in which even The Plan Beyond’s team will not be able to access users' stored data. This approach is intended to address concerns about placing financial records and personal information on a single platform. The broader question extends beyond technology. Families may spend decades building wealth, but its intended purpose can be undermined if the people it is meant to support cannot locate the assets, understand their obligations, or act on the plans made for them. By focusing on family continuity, The Plan Beyond is looking to address the gap between wealth creation and wealth transition. The objective is not just to help people keep track of what they own, but to ensure that their families have the information and context to carry those plans forward. The company is currently in incubation and plans to launch in December 2026. Those interested in exploring the platform can visit The Plan Beyond's website and join its waitlist ahead of the launch.

title: EloElo Group raises $80M in Series C led by Hornbill Capital and NBCUniversal
content: EloElo Group, a consumer AI and entertainment company that operates micro-drama platform Story TV, has raised $80 million in a Series C round of funding led by Hornbill Capital and NBCUniversal. This funding round also saw participation from MIT Investment Co. and existing investors Play Ventures, Kalaari Capital, Waterbridge Ventures, Griffin Gaming Partners and others. The funding was done at a valuation of $500 million, which is almost a 5X jump from its previous fundraise in April 2025, sources indicated. The new round brings EloElo Group’s total capital raised to $130 million to date. Bengaluru-headquartered EloElo Group was founded in 2020 by former Flipkart executive Saurabh Pandey and it will use this latest fund raise to fund original content across local languages, launch its micro dramas internationally, and continue investments in Dolphin AI, its proprietary agentic platform. In an interaction with YourStory , EloElo Group Founder & CEO Saurabh Pandey said, “This funding will expand on our vision and usher in a new era of sorts of mobile entertainment. This entertainment in the form of storytelling has never been solved for the mobile phone.” Story TV has over 5,000 micro dramas in six languages, a new drama launched every three hours and 95 minutes of time spent per user every day. The group also runs Master (micro learning), Dolphin AI (its agentic AI creative suite) and Voxy AI (an AI companion agent). Also Read Eloelo's Saurabh Pandey bets that Dolphin AI can break the gatekeepers of Indian storytelling Across its apps, EloElo Group has over 40 million monthly active users. “Story TV shows us what India wants to watch, and Dolphin AI gives us the economics to make it, which is how we have scaled with solid unit economics. Consumer AI will change how content is created, distributed and consumed, and we intend to lead that shift from India,” Pandey remarked. According to the founder, EloElo Group's key strength has been its ownership across all three layers of mobile entertainment: creating content, distributing content and imbibing AI into the whole process. This fundraise also gives EloElo Group the ability to go deeper into various languages through a combination of live action shows, hybrid shows with AI, and pure AI shows. These will be original content. On the investment, Manoj Thakur, Founder and Managing Partner of Hornbill Capital said, “EloElo Group combines strong creative capabilities with the ability to scale content through technology, which is something we deeply believe in. The team’s execution, financial discipline, and AI capabilities position it well for its next phase of growth.” Micro dramas are among the fastest-growing formats in global entertainment. According to Omdia, the industry will generate $14 billion globally by the end of 2026. In India, Redseer estimates that 40 million people paid for a microdrama at least once in FY26, and Lumikai’s State of India Interactive Media Report projects the market will reach $4.5 billion by 2030.

title: Stockal investors allege unauthorised sale of US stocks worth millions
content: Nearly 30 Indian investors who trade US shares through Stockal Securities have reported unauthorised access to their accounts, alleging that their blue-chip holdings, worth millions of dollars in total, were sold off without their consent and replaced with shares in a little-known company that subsequently lost almost 60% of its value. According to the complaints, the proceeds from the forced sales were used to buy shares in Zhibao Technology Inc., which trades under the ticker ZBAO. One affected investor, a senior official, saw stocks worth $335,768 sold and converted into 300,000 ZBAO shares at $1.05 apiece. The share price subsequently fell to $0.42, putting his losses at around Rs 4.26 crore. The pattern has alarmed investors, who point out that coordinated buying across multiple accounts could inflate the price of a thinly traded stock, a tactic associated with so-called pump-and-dump schemes. However, the complaints do not establish who, if anyone, profited from the trades. Stockal has said that the intruders used valid login credentials to access 26 accounts, attributing the breaches to phishing attacks that allegedly compromised customers' login details through deception. DriveWealth, the US brokerage partner that holds the accounts, has disputed this explanation and instead pointed to security weaknesses at Stockal. The affected investors have lodged complaints with the Securities and Exchange Board of India, the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and Bengaluru police. The disagreement between the two companies over the cause of the breaches has left investors uncertain about who is responsible for their losses. The case also highlights risks for Indians investing in overseas markets through intermediary platforms. When a trade is made through an Indian app but settled by a US brokerage, questions can arise over the extent of investor protection, the division of responsibilities between the companies involved, and which regulator has jurisdiction to address grievances.

title: Why best consumer brands are built on everyday habits, not one-time marketing campaign
content: Acquiring a customer may take a marketing campaign, but retaining one requires a product that becomes indispensable. At YourStory's Techsparks 2026, Sangeeth Krishna, founder, BRÜK and Nikhil Khurana, co founder of Qubo explained why design, reliability and an obsession with consumer behaviour are key to building lasting brands. A security camera that lets parents check on their children, or an air purifier that quietly becomes part of a household routine. These products may serve very different needs, but they have one thing in common: their success depends on becoming part of consumers' everyday lives. For consumer brands , getting customers to try a product is only the first hurdle. The bigger challenge is getting them to return, particularly in a market where choices are abundant, competing products are easily accessible and new brands are constantly emerging. For Nikhil Khurana, Co-founder of smart devices maker Qubo , the transition from a product being used regularly to becoming a habit is not necessarily reflected in usage metrics alone. "Real product-market fit happens once you've hit those hygiene usage metrics. If you speak to consumers, are they using superlatives? Are they saying things like, 'I can't live without this now'? That is when you realise you have probably hit product-market fit," he said. The absence of a product, he believes, is often the best indicator of whether it has become a habit. "A habit is not defined by usage metrics. A habit is defined by how much anxiety it causes you in its absence," said Khurana, drawing a parallel with quick-commerce and food-delivery platforms that consumers increasingly depend on. Designing for everyday use Krishna of BRÜK saw that the opportunity in the drinkware market came from observing an emerging consumer trend. He noticed people matching their tumblers with their clothes and bags, much like they did with other lifestyle accessories. He also saw a gap in the Indian market for premium drinkware with better finishing and build quality. The idea was to create a product that combined functionality with aesthetics, offering consumers an alternative in a category dominated by established players. BRÜK’s product development focused on everyday convenience, particularly for people working in offices. "These are the small things we were very clear about. It has to be convenient for people to hold, carry and use," he said. The broader principle is that a product must solve a real consumer problem before a brand can expect it to become a daily-use item. Qubo's experience in the home-security category offers another example. Khurana said consumers are generally reluctant to experiment with security products because the consequences of a failure could be significant. "All you need to do is a good job. Provide a reliable service that consumers can depend on," he said. For Qubo, consistent performance and reliability are central to building trust, particularly in categories where consumers are unlikely to switch brands easily once that trust has been established. Why retention cannot be a marketing function With customer acquisition becoming increasingly expensive, brands often look at features, incentives and performance marketing to drive repeat usage. But Khurana believes retention should primarily be a consequence of the product's usefulness. "Marketing can only help you with acquisition, make users try for the first time. The product is responsible for making users come back and use it every day," he said. He cautioned against relying excessively on incentives such as streaks, points and cashback to bring customers back to a platform. Instead, brands should work backwards from consumer needs and build products that naturally encourage repeat usage. Beyond the first purchase For brands selling durable products such as tumblers, repeat purchases present a different challenge. Unlike consumables, customers are unlikely to replace their drinkware every few weeks or months. Besides expanding its product range, BRÜK is also exploring adjacent product categories such as lunchboxes and protein shakers, building on its understanding of consumers' everyday routines. Adding to this, Krishna said founders need to constantly observe how consumers use products, including how they adapt them beyond their original purpose. He pointed to the accessories people add to their tumblers and the different bottles they carry to offices and gyms as examples of opportunities that can emerge from everyday observations. "If you observe a person from morning to evening, you will get ideas. There is nothing magical about it. Just go around and observe," he said. Premium pricing needs product value Another challenge for emerging consumer brands is convincing customers to pay a premium when cheaper alternatives and established brands are already available. Khurana outlined two possible approaches: competing with established brands on the strength of a differentiated offering, or disrupting the market by providing comparable capabilities at a lower price through operational efficiencies. As a brand gains consumer trust, it can gradually move away from an initial penetration-pricing strategy and improve margins. "People are ready to pay if you have a quality product. The most important things are the build, the quality, the materials and the finish," said Krishna. For him, compromising on price simply to chase volumes is not necessarily the right strategy. A smaller but clearly defined customer base willing to pay for the product can be more valuable. Ultimately, building a lasting consumer brand requires more than visibility or an aggressive acquisition strategy. In a crowded consumer market, that may be the strongest competitive advantage a brand can build.

title: Freshworks posts $18.3M net profit in Q3 of 2026
content: Nasdaq-listed software-as-a-service (SaaS) company Freshworks reported a net profit of $18.3 million in the third quarter of 2026, compared with a loss of $4.7 million in the same period last year. Revenue for the quarter stood at $245.4 million, marking a 14% year-on-year growth. Freshworks also said it had crossed $1 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR) at the end of the third quarter, achieving the milestone ahead of its projection of reaching it by the end of 2026. “Our momentum upmarket accelerated, with new multi-product EX (employee experience) deals increasing over 35% and partners participating in more than half of our new business. Customers want a unified platform and single data model for service operations, and they are increasingly choosing Freshworks,” said Dennis Woodside, CEO of Freshworks. According to Freshworks, the number of customers contributing more than $100,000 in ARR stood at 1,821, an increase of 25% year-on-year. The number of customers contributing more than $50,000 in ARR rose 18% to 4,257, while those contributing more than $5,000 in ARR increased 5% to 25,498. The company said that mid-market and enterprise customers accounted for over 60% of its total ARR. Freshworks reported a net dollar retention (NDR) rate of 104%, unchanged from the second quarter of 2026, but down from 105% in the third quarter of 2025. For the fourth quarter of 2026, Freshworks has projected revenue in the range of $253.5 million to $254.5 million, translating into year-on-year growth of around 14%. For the full year 2026, the company expects revenue to be between $965 million and $966 million, representing growth of around 15%.

title: ShareChat parent Mohalla Tech records 40% rise in revenue for FY26
content: Mohalla Tech, the homegrown social media company that operates ShareChat, Moj and QuickTV, reported a 40% increase in revenue in FY26 to Rs 1,016 crore, compared with Rs 723 crore in FY25. The company said the growth was driven by its diversification into micro-dramas, which are monetised through both advertising and subscriptions. This added a third major revenue stream alongside its existing advertising and live-streaming businesses. Subscription revenue, driven by its micro-drama app QuickTV and Moj+, contributed Rs 293 crore in its first full year. Mohalla Tech said its annual recurring revenue (ARR) had already reached Rs 1,500 crore in the first half of FY27. It also expects to close FY27 with its first-ever full-year profit at the EBITDA level, with EBITDA of nearly Rs 25 crore. The company said its EBITDA losses narrowed by 58% to Rs 91 crore in FY26, compared with Rs 219 crore in FY25. It added that it had recorded positive cash flows for four consecutive quarters and positive EBITDA for two consecutive quarters by the end of the first half of FY27. “After a few years of strategic discipline, we have turned the corner in our path to profitability. A year ago, we had achieved the mission of building a sustainable core business and were shifting gears to accelerate growth. Now, we are EBITDA positive, generating cash, and funding the next phase of growth entirely from our own cash flows,” said Ankush Sachdeva, Co-founder and CEO, Mohalla Tech. While subscription revenue drove growth in FY26, the company said its advertising business was also regaining momentum. Ad revenue grew 40% year-on-year in Q2 FY27 and is expected to accelerate further during the festive season. According to the company, daily consumption of micro-dramas grew 6.5-fold over 12 months, crossing 1 billion [units] a day. “Our ads business in particular gained strong momentum during the last couple of quarters, and we expect it to pick up further in the upcoming festive months. Most importantly, we’re continuously improving profit margins while maintaining a strong revenue growth trajectory,” said Manohar Charan, Co-founder and CFO, Mohalla Tech. The company said f ree-to-watch and ad-supported micro drama has also widened its advertiser base, across ShareChat and Moj.

title: Canva job cuts affect over 1,200 employees as it restructures for AI era
content: Canva is undertaking a major workforce restructuring affecting 1,271 employees, or 22% of its workforce, as it reorganises its business to adapt to rapid technological change. The changes include redundancies, role changes and relocation requests, although the company has not disclosed how many employees will leave. Chief executive officer Melanie Perkins said the restructuring followed the company’s first slowdown in growth in a decade and reflected the need to rethink how it operates and organises its teams. In a note to employees published on November 4, Perkins described the development as the hardest moment in Canva’s 13-year history. She said, “New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use.” The memo did not explicitly blame artificial intelligence for the job changes. It also pointed to slowing growth and an organisational structure that had become fragmented as the company expanded. “After exploring a wide range of alternatives, I’ve come to the difficult conclusion that small changes won’t be enough. To set ourselves up for the next decade, we need to refound Canva, getting back to our roots of small, empowered teams with the freedom to make decisions, take ownership and focus on what matters most for our community,” Perkins wrote. Canva will combine its Product, Growth and Platform teams into a single Product organisation, reduce narrow specialisations and remove management layers. Sydney will become the main base for more product teams. From January, most hybrid employees are expected to work from an office for two to three days a week, depending on their location. Founded in Australia in 2013 by Perkins, Cliff Obrecht and Cameron Adams, Canva has grown into a global design platform. The company claims more than 25 crore people use its platform each month. It is now looking to expand beyond template-based design. Canva AI 2.0, introduced this year, allows users to create and revise layered, editable designs through conversations with an AI assistant. In October, the company also announced new AI tools and a design-focused model. In August Canva had reduced its 2026 revenue growth forecast to 20% from 30% after the cost of delivering AI features proved higher than expected. Competitors are also expanding their offerings. On November 3, Figma announced an AI feature that uses prototype interactions as context when generating code. Atlassian said in March that it would cut about 1,600 jobs, or 10% of its workforce, partly to fund greater investment in AI. Website platform Squarespace announced a separate 19% workforce reduction this week, citing the need to simplify operations. Regulation is evolving alongside technology. From August 2, transparency requirements under the European Union’s AI Act apply to certain AI systems. These include informing users when they interact with AI and ensuring AI-generated outputs carry machine-readable markings. Canva said departing employees will receive at least six months’ salary, healthcare coverage for 12 months in countries where it is provided, career support and access to $10,000 grants for those seeking to start a venture.

title: Indian startups with over $500M valuation grow to 51 despite low number of AI entities: Report
content: Indian startups with a valuation of over $500 million have increased to 51 in 2026, from 47 in the year-ago period despite lower number of artificial intelligence (AI) companies, a report said on Tuesday. The combined value of these 51 entities is about Rs 3.3 lakh crore ($34.1 billion), with an average valuation of about Rs 6,400 crore, and they employ over 60,000 people, as per the 2026 ASK Private Wealth Hurun India Gazelle Index report. The entities have reported combined revenue of Rs 33,233 crore, growing 50% year-on-year, the report said. Anas Rahman Junaid, founder and chief researcher, Hurun India, said the list includes three names engaged in AI, including Ema AI, Observe.AI and UnifyApps which is very low when compared with 54 in the US and 23 in China. However, despite this, the number of Indian gazelles, or the companies with over $500 million, has grown to 51 this year, he added. The lack of AI-themed companies is often cited as one of the biggest reasons for foreign investors withdrawing from the Indian public equity markets. The report said seven startups crossed $1 billion to become unicorns in 2026, with Twin Health's valuation rising to $2 billion from $700 million. Financial services and healthcare account for six of the seven. "It reflects an entrepreneurial base that is diversifying across sectors and geographies and building scalable businesses with the potential to compete globally," said Rajesh Saluja, Co-Founder, CEO & MD of ASK Private Wealth. Further, the report said AI and CleanTech are the largest of the three frontier sectors, with three startups each. AI group comprises Ema AI, Observe.AI and UnifyApps, and CleanTech comprises Carbon Clean Solutions, Lohum and Rayzon Solar. A total of 34 startups have moved up to unicorn status on the CGU Index since inception. Two startups were listed on the public markets, Shadowfax in January 2026 and Turtlemint in June 2026, the report said. FinTech is the largest sector with 13 startups, followed by SaaS and ecommerce with five each. Bengaluru is home to 17 startups in the list, ahead of NCR with 11 and Mumbai with eight. The report said 10 startups maintain a headquarters outside India--seven in the US, two in Singapore, and one in the UK. India ranks third globally in startups--behind the US and China. IIT Kharagpur is the most common undergraduate institution among startup founders with 13, followed by IIT Bombay and IIT Kanpur with six each, the report said. Further, IIT Bombay is the most common postgraduate institution among startup founders with seven, followed by IIM Ahmedabad with five. The report added that women founders are present across six startups, Prukalpa Sankar (Atlan), Shruti Aggarwal (StashFin), Sunita Sahney (Finova Capital), Amrita Sirohia (INDMoney), Pallavi Shrivastava (Progcap) and Nikita Prasad (GIVA).
