title: Sachin Tendulkar backs Hitwicket maker Metasports Interactive
content: Metasports Interactive, the Hyderabad-based maker of cricket strategy game Hitwicket, has brought cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar on board as a strategic investor. He will also serve as the game’s brand ambassador. Financial terms and valuation remain undisclosed. Existing backers include venture-capital firms Prime Venture Partners and Singapore’s Horizon Ventures, as well as cricket commentator Harsha Bhogle. This development is separate from the $20 million in user-acquisition funding it secured from London-based Metica in April. That earlier, non-dilutive facility was intended to fund marketing and international expansion without giving up equity. Metasports has not specified how Tendulkar’s investment will be deployed. It aims to reach 100 million downloads within three years. The company claims Hitwicket has more than 20 million users across 120 countries, revenue doubled in the six months before the announcement, and players spend an average of 51 minutes daily on the game. According to the company, more than 97% of its revenue comes from in-app purchases, or optional items bought within the game. Its wider ambition is to build mobile sports gaming franchises beyond cricket. Hitwicket is a multiplayer strategy title that puts tactical decisions ahead of reflexes. Players manage a virtual side and choose how to approach each ball. Tendulkar said it captures cricket’s strategic thinking, explaining that “Cricket has always involved reading the bowler, assessing the field and deciding the right approach for every ball.” He will also feature in the game and related content. Reddy said Tendulkar’s cricketing knowledge would help the team understand elite players’ decisions and refine gameplay. India’s gaming market offers a substantial audience, although converting it into globally competitive businesses and original intellectual property remains a challenge. The Game Developer Association of India estimates that the country had 511 million players and $1.04 billion in video-game revenue in 2025. Recent funding deals demonstrate investor interest across genres. Bengaluru-based Spill Games raised $10.5 million in October, led by Elevation Capital, while social gaming platform Matiks raised $10 million led by General Catalyst. Cricket-focused LightFury Games also secured $11 million from investors including Blume Ventures, V3 Ventures, MIXI and Times Internet. Policy is shifting too. The Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025, and its rules, effective from May 1, 2026, prohibit online money games while establishing a framework for e-sports and online social games, with user-safety and grievance-redressal requirements. Classification considers factors such as stakes, expected cash winnings and whether rewards can be converted outside a game.

title: India shines in Apple’s record September quarter
content: India emerged as a stellar growth market for Apple in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, registering an all-time company revenue record in the country. “We also set September quarter revenue records in both developed and emerging markets, in addition to an all-time record in India,” Apple Chief Executive Officer John Ternus said. The performance in India was propelled by a September quarter record for iPhone upgraders, with Worldpanel survey data ranking iPhone among the top-selling smartphone models in the country. Mac sales also set an all-time revenue record in India, driven by demand for the new MacBook Neo and MacBook Pro. Furthermore, Apple launched Apple Pay in India in this quarter in partnership with Axis Bank, extending digital payments to one of the world’s largest consumer markets. “We are optimistic about the long-term future of our services business,” Apple Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh noted. Global financials Moving to global business, Apple generated quarterly total revenue from operations of $114.48 billion, an 11.72% YoY increase compared to $102.47 billion in Q4 FY25. For the full fiscal year FY26, total revenue reached an all-time record of $478.83 billion, up 15.06% YoY from $416.16 billion, while full-year net profit reached $132.18 billion, up 18% YoY. Quarterly revenue comprised two distinct streams: Products revenue of $82.90 billion (72.42% of total) and Services revenue of $31.57 billion (27.58% of total). Across product categories, iPhone generated $57.58 billion (50.30% of total revenue), growing 17.46% YoY due to global upgrader records and demand for iPhone 18 Pro and the foldable iPhone Duo. Services achieved an all-time record of $31.57 billion, rising 9.82% YoY on record cloud, video, and payment revenues, with paid subscriptions topping 1.5 billion. Mac revenue jumped 23.68% YoY to $10.79 billion due to strong MacBook Neo adoption and global market share gains. Conversely, Wearables, Home and Accessories fell 7.91% YoY to $8.30 billion against tough prior-year comparisons, while iPad revenue declined 10.40% YoY to $6.23 billion due to supply constraints. Apple’s profit after tax rose 11.81% YoY to $30.71 billion, compared to $27.47 billion in Q4 FY25, assisted by a $0.05 per share tariff refund benefit. On a full-year basis, EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation), which measures operational cash profit, reached $171.49 billion, delivering an EBITDA margin of 35.81% on $478.83 billion in revenue. Expense drivers Managing total operations required $59.66 billion in total cost of sales, up 10.22% YoY. Total operating expenses jumped 20.58% YoY to $19.19 billion. Research and Development (R&D) represented the largest cost centre at $11.73 billion (61.13% of total operating expenses), surging 32.30% YoY from $8.87 billion as Apple accelerated investments in generative artificial intelligence (AI), such as Siri AI, and custom silicon. Meanwhile, Apple’s active installed base stood over 2.5 billion devices, with $28.10 billion in quarterly operating cash flow, and $137 billion in cash reserves. However, unprecedented memory cost inflation compressed profit margins, while supply limits on advanced nodes, cutting-edge semiconductor manufacturing chips, restricted device availability. “What we are seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented. And as we said earlier in the September quarter, we did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which were partly offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components,” Ternus explained. Supply chain bottlenecks also hampered shipments. “The Q4 constraints were primarily driven by the availability of the advanced nodes our SoCs are produced on. But as we have transitioned more of our lineup to the latest 2-nanometer technology nodes, our constraints on advanced nodes are easing,” Apple Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan said, detailing these operational challenges.

title: Google launches Dreambeans app in India
content: Google has launched Dreambeans, an experimental AI-powered app that creates personalised daily story collections, in India. Starting today, the app will be available in the country for users above 18 years. Developed by Google Labs, Dreambeans turns users' digital activity into personalised and illustrated stories about their interests and life. The app was first rolled out in the United States in September. “This could be everything from places to explore, new arts & crafts, or a reminder of upcoming local events. You can dive deeper into any story to learn more, bookmark for later, or easily share with others to spark inspiration," said Google in an official blogpost, adding that the app is designed to connect users with what matters without endless scrolling. The app is available on both android and iOS, and can be accessed across 14 languages, including Hindi, Bengali, Telugu, Marathi, Tamil, Urdu, Gujarati, Kannada, Punjabi, Assamese, and Nepali. Dreambeans creates curated stories using information from selected Google apps including Calendar, Gemini, Gmail, Photos, Search, and YouTube. "Share your feedback to make your stories even better over time," said Google. The app has a 'thumbs down' button to indicate that something is wrong with the content or is not relevant for the user. Users can also delete data anytime from the app via its settings. This deletes the data from the system as well.

title: India's data centre capacity set for 5x surge by 2030: Crisil
content: India's data centre industry is poised for an unprecedented investment boom, with installed capacity expected to increase five-fold to around 7.5 gigawatts (GW) by March 2030, attracting investments of more than Rs 3 lakh crore over the next four financial years, Crisil Ratings said in a report on Tuesday. The expansion, fuelled by generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), enterprise digitalisation and rising data consumption, is set to transform the country's digital infrastructure landscape. However, the industry's ability to translate demand into sustainable returns will depend critically on timely power connectivity, regulatory clearances and disciplined project execution. "Nearly half of the upcoming capacity is already committed under long-term contracts, limiting speculative development and reducing offtake risk," Crisil Ratings said. "Upfront tie-ups with hyperscalers, driven by cloud adoption and compute-intensive GenAI workloads, provide revenue certainty from the outset. This helps de-risk projects, even as the scale and speed of the planned build-out intensify execution requirements." Strong demand from global hyperscalers, driven by cloud adoption and increasingly compute-intensive GenAI workloads, is also supporting investment decisions and reducing offtake uncertainty. India's competitive cost structure is adding to its appeal as a data centre destination. Development costs are around 20 per cent lower than in several competing Asia-Pacific markets, reflecting relatively competitive land, construction and labour costs. Combined with lower power tariffs, this enables rental rates to be 30-35 per cent below those in peer markets. The availability of large campuses powered by renewable energy also strengthens India's proposition for hyperscalers seeking to meet sustainability commitments. Says Anand Kulkarni, Director, Crisil Ratings, "India's structural cost advantages further strengthen its attractiveness as a data centre destination. Development costs are around one-fifth lower than in several competing Asia-Pacific markets owing to more competitive land, construction and labour costs.” He further said, “Combined with lower power tariffs, this translates into rentals that are 30-35 per cent lower than in peer markets. The ability to develop large, renewable-powered campuses also aligns well with the sustainability goals of hyperscalers, reinforcing India's competitive positioning." However, the scale of the planned expansion is placing considerable pressure on power infrastructure. Nearly three-fourths of the approximately 6 GW of upcoming capacity is expected to be concentrated in Visakhapatnam, Mumbai and Hyderabad, Crisil said. By fiscal 2030, data centre capacity in these cities could be equivalent to around 80%, 60% and 20%, respectively, of their current peak electricity demand. This concentration makes timely grid connectivity and transmission capacity augmentation critical to avoiding commissioning delays and cost overruns.

title: Jewellery brand GIVA raises $100M from Multiples PE
content: Multiples Alternate Asset Management along with its co-investors, has led the $100 million funding round in jewellery brand GIVA. Founded in 2019, Bengaluru-based GIVA focuses on everyday wear, catering primarily to Indian consumers for both self-consumption and gifting occasions. The fresh capital will be used to strengthen its leadership team, expand manufacturing and deepen its offline presence. The brand offers a diverse portfolio spanning 92.5 silver, gold and lab-grown diamond jewellery. It follows an omnichannel distribution model through its own retail stores, D2C website and leading third-party e-commerce and quick-commerce marketplaces. Currently, the brand retails through 400+ stores across India and Sri Lanka. The latest fundraise is the largest investment in India's new-age jewellery market, according to the company. Ishendra Agarwal, founder & CEO, GIVA said, "Multiples’ backing is a strong endorsement of what we have built at GIVA since 2019, a high-growth, design-led fine jewellery brand that Indian consumers trust for everyday wear and gifting.” “As we enter our next phase, we are focused on scaling our omnichannel presence, strengthening our manufacturing capabilities and elevating the fine jewellery experience for modern Indian consumers. With Multiples’ experience in helping new-age businesses scale, we have the right partner for this journey. This $100 Mn+ round, the largest investment in India’s new-age jewellery market, gives us the strength to move faster.” The company also added that India's jewellery market is estimated to grow at around 6% CAGR to reach $124 billion by 2032. Multiples has also invested in brands such as Licious, ACKO, PVR and Arvind Fashions apart from in other sectors. Earlier this year, Multiples announced the close of a USD $430 million fund.

title: Beyond funding: Why every startup founder needs an insurance plan
content: Most founders are equity-rich and cash-poor, with household finances quietly tied to the venture: personal guarantees on business loans, savings deployed into the company, a spouse’s income covering monthly basics. That structure makes personal term insurance more urgent for a founder than for a salaried peer, not less. If the founder dies, the family inherits illiquid equity and live liabilities at the same moment, and only a large, immediate payout resolves that. The sizing rule also needs adjusting. The standard guidance of 10-15X annual income understates the need for entrepreneurs who deliberately pay themselves a modest salary. Anchor instead to household expenses, outstanding personal guarantees, and the real cost of the family’s next 15 years. Self-employed applicants should expect income documentation requests, ITRs, and bank statements rather than salary slips, and treat that as an administrative step rather than a reason to postpone. What Does ABSLI Super Term Plan Offer a Founder? The payout structure matters for founders carrying loan guarantees. A lump sum clears liabilities at once, while the monthly income option keeps a household running for a defined period, and ABSLI Super Term Plan allows the two to be combined, with between 10% and 90% of the sum assured taken as income and the balance as a lump sum. What is keyman insurance and who needs it? Ask your co-founder a direct question: if either of you died this quarter, does the company survive the next funding conversation? Investors ask themselves the same thing, which is why keyman insurance appears in diligence checklists and shareholder agreements. ABSLI Keyman Insurance Policy is a life insurance policy purchased by an employer on the life of a key employee, based on the insurable interest an employer has in that person. The payout gives the business capital to stabilise, hire replacement leadership, and reassure the cap table at the moment confidence is scarcest. For partnership firms, ABSLI Partnership Insurance Scheme addresses a related risk: on the death of an insured partner, the firm has liquidity available to purchase the deceased partner’s share, so working capital is not diverted and surviving partners are not required to bring in additional funds. Cover is assessed against the firm’s net worth, including each partner’s share of capital, share of profit and share in goodwill. How does employer-employee cover work for a startup team? This is the part that belongs in your next HR planning cycle. Under ABSLI Employer - Employee Insurance Scheme, the employer proposes and owns a policy on the life of an employee, and assigns it to the employee after a defined period. Assignment can be absolute, transferring ownership at issuance, or conditional, transferring ownership once terms set by the employer are met. Any company, proprietorship firm, LLP, trust, NGO or society with a genuine employer-employee relationship is eligible. The return on that spend is talent economics. Startups ask employees to accept risk, and benefits that protect an employee’s family are how a company signals it takes that trade seriously. The structure also matures with the company: the arrangement that covers a handful of employees becomes the foundation of the full benefits programme a later-stage HR lead will build. All products other than child plans can be offered under the scheme, and all riders other than Waiver of Premium can be attached. Which ABSLI solution fits which need? What should a founder do first? Buy personal term cover now, sized to household expenses and outstanding personal guarantees rather than declared salary, while age and health are on your side. Add keyman cover once the company has revenue or a valuation worth protecting. Put employer-employee cover in place for the team as an early, deliberate retention investment. Review all three annually, because cover set at seed stage rarely matches the liabilities of a Series A company. Disclose health, income and business details fully at proposal stage, since complete disclosure is what ensures a smooth claim later. Key Takeaways Founders need personal term cover first, sized to household expenses and personal guarantees rather than declared salary. ABSLI Super Term Plan offers three plan options, entry from 18 to 65 years and a minimum sum assured of Rs 25,00,000. ABSLI Keyman Insurance Policy allows a company to insure a key employee, with the company as the policy owner. ABSLI Partnership Insurance Scheme helps a firm fund the purchase of a deceased partner’s share. ABSLI Employer-Employee Insurance Scheme lets an employer insure employees as a welfare and retention measure. Premiums paid under Keyman and Employer-Employee arrangements may be claimed as a deduction under Section 37(1), subject to applicable tax laws. GST is not applicable on individual life insurance premiums. ABSLI settled 98.86%* of individual death claims in FY26. title: From prompt engineers to tool builders: Intuit’s Vignesh Subrahmaniam on building AI that acts
content: For the past few years, getting better results from AI meant learning to write better prompts. That is changing fast, as AI systems begin to reason, make decisions, and act across entire workflows on their own. At TechSparks 2026, YourStory’s flagship event, Dr Vignesh Subrahmaniam, Principal AI Scientist at Intuit, spoke with Adith Charlie, Managing Editor of YourStory and The CapTable, in a fireside chat titled ‘Beyond the prompt: Building AI that thinks, acts, learns’. Drawing on Subrahmaniam's experience of turning AI research into scalable systems, the two explored what builders need to rethink as intelligence becomes increasingly agentic. Teaching machines the game of business The session opened with a question for Subrahmaniam about what a typical day looks like for him. He was also asked to simplify the concepts of fintech and AI for the audience. He responded with a chess analogy, posing a question: if an algorithm were never taught the rules of chess but was shown a million completed games and their winners, could it deduce both the rules and the strategies most likely to lead to victory? His team at Intuit applies a similar approach to supporting small businesses, as the company serves both consumers and accountants. “How do we learn the game of business by looking at data, by looking at actual actions and outcomes that businesses are taking,” he said. The goal is to understand what helps a business win customers, grow quickly, and improve its cash flow. From prompts to tools The conversation then turned to the shift builders face, from years of learning to write smarter prompts to designing agents that are handed a goal and decide the steps themselves. Subrahmaniam placed prompt engineering in the long history of programming languages, from binary and assembly to Fortran, C, and Python. Large language models let anyone program using plain English. However, this method has limits. Researchers quickly understood that intelligence should not only be in the model. The model becomes an orchestrator, breaking a complex task into a series of actions and tool calls. The real intelligence moves into the tools it calls. Those tools must be built differently too, “not so that a human being can use them, or a software developer can use them, or anybody can use them, but in a way that an LLM orchestrator can really use them”. That means high-fidelity tools with highly deterministic output. For builders, the craft shifts from clever wording to dependable components that a model can call on again and again without surprises. The next frontier is beyond text On where new data will come from, Subrahmaniam was candid that learning from text is now largely a solved problem. The harder challenge is learning from multimodal sources and real-world actions. He pointed to how a small child learns mostly from what she sees, hears and observes, not from reading, and argued that bringing such real-world signals into AI systems is what will help models go beyond generating text to suggesting actions. That, he said, is the next frontier. Data quality still decides everything Looking ahead at the challenges for a regulated industry, he took the audience back 18 years, to one of the first machine learning labs in Bangalore, where he worked on logistic regressions and multi-layer perceptrons. The biggest problem then was not the algorithm. “Actually, it was data quality,” he recalled. That has not changed. Whether a team trains a simple regression or fine-tunes a transformer, “garbage in, garbage out” still applies. Enterprises that can collect, collate, and store data at the highest quality, he said, will have the edge. Consent and privacy from the floor In the short audience Q&A, an attendee asked how restrictions on where financial data can be stored affect Intuit’s work. Subrahmaniam called consent the heart of any learning system and cited the Framingham study, where residents of a Massachusetts town allowed doctors to follow their health over time, which shaped modern understanding of cardiovascular disease. Companies, he added, must also explain the benefits of data use to the wider community. What builders can take away As the conversation drew to a close, one thread ran through every answer: as AI moves from responding to acting, the foundations matter more than the interface. Prompts will remain a starting point, but the real work now lies in building dependable tools that agents can call on, feeding systems high-quality data, and earning the consent that lets them learn from it. For builders looking beyond the prompt, that is where the next wave of AI will be won.

title: From code to content: How AI could make India the world’s next story exporter
content: India spent the 1990s and 2000s becoming the back office of the world for code. At TechSparks 2026, a flagship event of YourStory , one founder asked whether the country can now do the same for stories. As AI makes video production more efficient and economical, his answer was a confident yes. The session, titled ‘Can AI turn India into a global content export hub?’ , began with the product showcase of Dolphin AI by Saurabh Pandey, Founder and CEO of Eloelo Group, and then moved into a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project. Why India has not yet exported its stories Pandey noted that India has long produced standout IPs such as Baahubali , Kantara , and RRR , but has rarely been an exporter. Japan did it with anime, South Korea with K-dramas, China with micro dramas, and the US with Hollywood. Each, he said, used content to build soft power. AI, in his view, changes the equation because the tools once available only to a few markets are now open to everyone. The opportunity also goes beyond films, to localized advertisements, commerce videos, and social media content for overseas customers. Dolphin AI: One suite from idea to final cut To make that case concrete, Pandey introduced Dolphin AI, Eloelo’s newest launch. The company began with live entertainment, moved into micro dramas with its Story TV app, and recently added a micro learning app called Master. Dolphin AI targets a familiar creator hurdle: making one AI video often means stitching together clips and edits from around 20 tools. Dolphin AI replaces that with an agentic chat and a set of templates. A simple prompt can produce a full video, with the suite handling context and continuity. It also integrates with Claude and ChatGPT through MCP, helping creators build longer AI videos. A short demo reel closed the showcase. Fireside chat: Removing the gatekeepers When Sharma joined Pandey on stage, she reacted to the demo with pride. “This is remarkable. This is real, and this is happening in India,” she said. The conversation first turned to adoption. Pandey said roughly 15,000 videos were created on Dolphin AI in eight days in its early access phase, entirely through organic discovery. He then explained why this matters for storytellers. High-end visual effects once meant massive budgets, and those budgets acted as a filter on who could tell ambitious stories. “With AI, with tools such as Dolphin AI, what we are trying to build is that you can ship content without any gatekeepers,” he said. He clarified that AI is not replacing actors but expensive locations, so a period drama no longer needs a real palace. With distribution now largely algorithmic, a storyteller in India can reach audiences in the US or Europe. Asked why India has lagged, Pandey did not blame creativity. He compared South Korea, with 52 million people and a content export economy of about $15 billion, to India’s 1.4 billion. “I would refuse to believe that we don’t have the creativity,” he said. In his view, technology, aspiration, distribution and capital must come together, and Indian builders have too often treated the local market as the only one that matters. The micro drama moment On whether micro dramas can finally work as a business in India, Pandey cited China, where the category reached roughly $8 billion in revenue last year and is now at a run rate of $10 billion to $11 billion, with a single platform earning more than China’s entire box office. In India, he said, the combined run rate of the top four or five players is north of Rs 5,000 crore, reached in about 18 months. Production costs have been the stumbling block, historically eating up 50-60% of revenue. AI, he argued, finally fixes the supply side. “This is that quick commerce moment of entertainment,” he said. Where the opportunity sits Pandey expects platforms to consolidate around two or three players, as food delivery and ecommerce did. Supply, however, will stay open. Eloelo launched 200 new micro dramas last month for its microdrama platform Story TV and works with about 90 production houses, a number he sees doubling. His advice for new entrants was to build on the supply side. Small, nimble AI studios of a few editors, promo producers and a line producer could supply platforms with micro dramas and OTT content. He urged writers and producers to treat AI as a brainstorming partner, and floated the idea of an AI-made Mahabharat . “The next Disney or the next big IP can be built now if the right supply engine comes in because the demand is very clear,” he said. The window to build Pandey said Eloelo, which has grown from one platform to five, is not eyeing an IPO soon and is focused on sustainable growth while it builds for India’s global ambitions. Sharma called his journey from a Flipkart employee to founder building for the world a reminder of what Indian aspiration can achieve. She urged the audience to tell their teams and networks that the window to build in this space is open. If India turned code into a global export, the session suggested, stories could be next.

title: WOI India launches venture studios, investor network, and startup support platforms at TechSparks 2026
content: Building a startup takes more than a good idea. Founders need capital, teams, market access, and practical support to turn their plans into businesses. At TechSparks 2026, WOI India launched a set of platforms aimed at addressing these needs, from venture studios that work alongside founders to services focused on sales, marketing, and investor connections. Amar Dixit, CEO of WOI India, led the launch with a video showcasing the organization’s existing initiatives and long-term plans. WOI India is the Indian arm of Dubai-headquartered WOI, a global ecosystem-development company. Its model covers infrastructure, capital, education, venture studios, community, and Centres of Excellence. Its flagship Startup Park in Bengaluru provides founders with access to workspace, mentorship, capital, and other support. Dixit invited entrepreneurs to visit Startup Park, an integrated hub and community centre in Koramangala, Bengaluru. He also outlined plans to expand the model, with more startup parks in the pipeline. Dayone Venture Studio: Building alongside founders Mazin Arbaz, Founder of Dayone Venture Studio, introduced the platform by addressing a common challenge for entrepreneurs: mentors can offer guidance and investors can provide capital, but who helps founders build their businesses? Operating under WOI, Dayone was founded by Arbaz, with Hashir Usman as CEO. The studio combines investment with hands-on support, working with startups from their early stages to turn ideas into viable businesses. Its work covers understanding customers, building brands, setting up systems and making the decisions needed to move a business forward. At TechSparks, Arbaz invited founders with business ideas, investors interested in co-building ventures and professionals looking to work with the studio to get in touch. Dayone aims to combine funding with practical business-building support, helping founders navigate the early stages of setting up and growing a company. Perform100X: Helping startups drive sales and marketing For Krishnakumar V, Co-founder and CEO of Perform100X, and Shanfaz C K M, Co-founder and Chief Strategy Officer, sales is a challenge startups need to address early. Perform100X is a sales and marketing accelerator operating as a Centre of Excellence. It brings together talent, strategy, technology, and execution to help startups turn products into customers, revenue, and sustainable growth. The platform aims to offer an alternative to working with multiple agencies and managing disconnected marketing activities. Its services include market analysis, data-backed planning, technology-enabled execution, and performance dashboards. Analyticsfy, its intelligence layer, brings reporting and performance insights into a single dashboard. Founders can access information through simple WhatsApp commands. Speaking at TechSparks, Krishnakumar said the team had spent the previous two days networking with founders and found that sales was one of the biggest challenges startups faced after raising investment. Perform100X aims to work as an extension of a startup’s team, aligning sales and marketing activities with its valuation criteria and investment plans. Krishnakumar also highlighted the platform’s reporting capabilities, which give founders visibility into strategies and execution without having to wait until the end of the month to assess performance. Point Zero: Supporting early-stage ecommerce brands Arshak N, Founder of Point Zero, introduced the venture studio, which aims to help Indian ecommerce brands navigate their early stages, when founders often lack the team, direction, and capital needed to get started. Point Zero works alongside entrepreneurs as a co-founder, providing a team, capital, expertise in brand building, product development, growth and operations, and shared playbooks. Founders can bring their own ideas to build founder-led ventures or lead studio-born brands developed through Point Zero’s research. The studio focuses on building brands with products that encourage repeat purchases, margins that can support growth, and a reason for customers to buy beyond price. It is mentored by brand builders including Bharat Sethi of Rage Coffee and Palash Arneja of BlaBliBlu. At TechSparks, Arshak said many ecommerce founders spend their first year building businesses alone, even though this is often when they need the most support. Point Zero aims to provide the teams, playbooks, capital, and direction needed to build and grow these businesses. Launched at TechSparks, the studio has set a target of achieving Rs 1,000 crore in combined revenue across its portfolio within the next three years. Applications are open to founders and investors interested in building ecommerce brands. VC Circle: Building a global investor network Hema Harshini, Business Head at VC Circle by WOI, is leading the platform's efforts to build a global network connecting investors, intelligence and opportunities across markets. VC Circle brings together fund managers, venture funds, family offices, high-net-worth individuals and institutional investors. Through curated roundtables, demo days, investor-focused reports and ecosystem engagements, it aims to help participants exchange ideas, identify emerging sectors and explore investment opportunities. At TechSparks, Harshini spoke about the platform’s first chapter, which included a roundtable on commercializing India’s next space economy. The discussion brought together government and industry representatives, including participants from NSIL, WICCI, COS and the Space Tech Foundation, alongside investors such as C Fund and Ivy Capital. VC Circle also launched its first report based on the roundtable, along with a magazine. Both were available at the TechSparks Startup Park booth. Harshini said the larger goal was to build a globally connected investor ecosystem that brings together capital, relationships, and intelligence to identify and develop opportunities. Founder Card: Connecting entrepreneurs to Startup Park Arun Das Janadaran, CEO of Startup Park, introduced Founder Card, a platform designed to help entrepreneurs access the wider startup ecosystem. Aimed at founders at different stages, Founder Card connects members with workspaces, mentorship, learning opportunities, investor networks, and other resources to help them build and scale their businesses. At TechSparks, Janadaran said successful entrepreneurs need more than ideas. They also need people, knowledge, and opportunities to turn those ideas into businesses. Founder Card, he explained, aims to make Startup Park’s ecosystem more accessible, giving entrepreneurs opportunities to connect, collaborate, and grow. With these launches, WOI India is bringing venture building, sales and marketing support, ecommerce development, investor connections and founder resources together within its startup ecosystem.

title: antimattr is building voice AI wearables that cut through the noise
content: When Sridipto Ghosh and Sirsha Chakraborty were developing the thesis for their startup, many advised them against venturing into hardware. But this didn’t deter them. “People said it was hard, that there were large companies in the hardware space, and that it was very difficult for a startup to build in this space. We continued building despite those perceptions,” says Ghosh. Their persistence eventually led them to start antimattr in 2025. The deeptech company is building a voice-first hardware interface for human-agent interaction that summarises conversations with clarity even in noisy environments. The conversations could be with anyone. Users can dictate to the wearable device directly or let it listen to a conversation with another person (offline or online). The technology would be able to pick up the conversation clearly despite ambient noise, says CEO Ghosh. He says its early incubation at Scaler Innovation Lab helped the startup get off the ground. “It gave us access to prototyping equipment such as 3D printers and soldering stations, which made it easier to iterate and keep developing the idea." The name ‘antimattr’ comes from the philosophy of challenging common notions or what people are generally taught. This year, the San Francisco-based startup was selected for Y Combinator’s current cohort, becoming the first India-origin wearable company backed by the accelerator. “One of our biggest learnings so far has been that you don’t need to have everything figured out before you start. You just need to keep moving and evolving. YC has accelerated this process for us at a global stage and pushed us further in thinking about what’s possible in human-machine interaction,” says Ghosh. Also Read Peak XV selects 18 startups for 12th Surge cohort, doubles down on AI and deep tech Wearable tech that is noise-proof One of antimattr’s projects is project mnemosyne, a voice-first hardware interface for human-to-agent (H2A) communication. Chakraborty, the startup’s CTO, says the barrier to adopting voice AI is not technical but the reality of noisy environments, where voice is not always usable. “For instance, dictating with clarity and accuracy while sitting in a noisy cafe is generally not possible. We are building an interface that makes voice usable everywhere, makes using it private, and solves H2A communication,” he says. The startup’s system pairs a ring with earphones. The earphones use proprietary voice isolation technology to block out background noise, allowing users to take a call from a loud place, such as a pub, or dictate with greater accuracy. The ring runs the software by capturing thoughts, controlling agents, and summarising conversations. Beyond this, the startup’s roadmap includes project soteria and project athena. The team believes the future of personal AI will be private and not dependent on the cloud—a private, local computer can run all your models and have all your context. “The next milestone towards this vision is project soteria, as true freedom begins with privacy and ownership. The final frontier for antimattr is project athena, which we envision as the machine that defines how humans function,” he says. Chakraborty says antimattr’s long-term vision is to build an ecosystem of devices for natural human-machine interaction. Also Read Deeptech is giving rise to new kinds of founders and bold ideas: VCs Unlike the general assumption, antimattr’s products are not always listening to humans. They record only when users deliberately trigger them. The CTO says the team retains the raw audio but does not use it to train any model. “We are currently pursuing SOC 2 and HIPAA compliance to bring enterprise -grade security to how data is stored and handled,” he says. Ghosh says more than 500 customers have placed pre-orders through its website. The beta version of mnemosyne is expected to launch publicly by December this year. The founders initially invested about Rs 25 lakh in the startup. They recently received a Rs 20 lakh equity-free grant from Nikhil Kamath’s WTFund. antimattr competes with startups such as San Francisco-based Bee. Ghosh says antimattr’s edge lies in its focus on the real-world challenges of using voice AI in noisy environments. “Nobody wants to shout at AI or be overheard. Even companies building hardware aren’t solving this ground-up for voice. We are building a full-stack interface that is tuned for voice and allows users to use voice anywhere,” Ghosh says. Edited by Swetha Kannan

title: Code is no longer scarce: Hostinger’s Auksė Žirgulė on what founders should build instead
content: A founder in Srinagar recently built a website and an application on Hostinger in very little time. When building software takes that little effort, the question for every business shifts from whether it can build to why anyone would choose what it builds. That shift was the subject of a fireside chat at TechSparks 2026 in Bengaluru, YourStory’s flagship event. Auksė Žirgulė, VP of Product at Hostinger, spoke to Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, about what happens when every business can build its own software. From building to running a business Žirgulė began with how the questions customers bring to Hostinger have changed. Publishing a website was once a hard task for non-technical people, and the company’s vision has been to help everyone succeed online. Now that AI has removed much of that barrier, founders are no longer asking how to build. They are asking how to attract clients, drive revenue and run the business. Fragmentation is part of the problem. A new founder may buy a domain on one platform, set up email on another, and run campaigns on a third, ending up with five subscriptions and five logins. When something breaks, the founder turns into a technician or integration specialist. Hostinger’s answer is to take care of the full flow and to bring AI agents into it. Where the advantage lies If code is no longer scarce, the edge moves to understanding the customer. Founders need to know exactly which problem they are solving and test the product as early as possible. Innovation, Žirgulė argued, does not mean inventing something new. Apple did not invent the mobile phone or the touch screen, yet the iPhone won by delivering the best customer experience. She also drew on the book ‘Monetizing Innovation’ to make a point many builders forget in their rush to test: a great product does not always make a great business. Thinking about how a product will reach the market has to start early. That is why she calls customer obsession the thing that should not change. “Customer obsession is the foundation, and I know that now AI is everywhere, but this is the part we need to keep,” she said. She does not mean a survey sent by AI over email, but honest conversations. Sharma shared a lesson from the Bharat Project’s travels through Bihar, eastern Uttar Pradesh, Assam and Chhattisgarh. The team expected people to respond by email or WhatsApp, but many were watching and observing them on Facebook. Customers, she noted, are not always where a founder assumes they are. Judgment and trust in the age of agents As agents take on more decisions, the question is who makes the final call. For now, Žirgulė said, it is still the founder. “AI can do a lot, but the founder says the last word,” she said. Trust, she added, has to be earned. She shared a story of an agent at Hostinger that agreed to a conference over email, leaving the CEO to learn of his own participation on LinkedIn. Her takeaway was to treat an agent like a new joiner. “I’m looking at this as a new colleague,” she said, which means testing its work and watching how it behaves before giving it more responsibility. That trust is also what worries her most, even as she is excited by how quickly the technology is moving. Adoption and markets differ Žirgulė noted that selling approaches vary widely from one market to another, citing India and Brazil, so products have to adapt. Sharma observed that the AI conversation in tech circles can look very different from the world outside them. Žirgulė agreed that adoption cycles differ and that those who are not yet convinced need to be educated on AI’s value. What the audience asked Audience questions covered where to stop automating, whether customer expectations will rise, and how non-technical founders can write good prompts. Žirgulė said agents must be tested and observed closely before more is automated, and that rising expectations mean products with strong UX and quality will win. If launching software as quickly as the Srinagar founder did becomes the norm, the session suggested that what will set businesses apart is knowing the customer, owning the final judgment, and earning trust, whether from a user or an AI agent. Code may no longer be scarce, but those three still are.

title: Crypto’s next chapter: Regulatory sandboxes, AI co-pilots and the rise of derivatives
content: Crypto investing is evolving beyond its early hype cycles. Regulation, investor awareness, risk management and new technologies are changing how people trade digital assets, all while raising pertinent questions about what responsible participation should look like. At TechSparks 2026, Rajagopal Menon, Vice President at WazirX; Satish Mishra, CTO of Pi42 and SharkExchange; and Sharat Chandra, Founder of EmpowerEdge Ventures, joined Swetha Kannan, Deputy Editor at YourStory, to discuss the changing crypto landscape, the need for regulatory clarity, and the growing role of AI in trading. A new crypto landscape emerges India’s crypto market has historically been a dynamic space, growing rapidly during the 2021-22 bull run, where Menon noted that WazirX’s spot markets processed close to $48 billion in transactions during that period. This was succeeded by the taxation measures introduced in the subsequent Budget that changed the market significantly. According to Menon, the resulting environment of these changes has placed Indian exchanges at a disadvantage compared with foreign platforms. Domestic exchanges must deduct tax at source (TDS) and operate within the 30% tax framework, while foreign exchanges have not faced the same requirements, he argued. “I think a stable environment or a better environment would be that the same rules apply for everybody, so that Make in India is made for Indian exchanges,” he shared. Menon also pointed to a shift in trading activity. As spot trading volumes declined, futures and derivatives began gaining traction. He expects this segment to see significant adoption in India. Regulation that makes room for all players Moving to the question of regulation, Chandra shared that exchanges had helped educate investors about different crypto assets and the importance of understanding risks, but that gaps in the regulatory framework remained. “I think once this space is regulated, that can lead to a lot of capital inflow to the country,” he said. Chandra pointed out that while exchanges are required to follow KYC norms, there are still gaps when it comes to verifying identities as assets move on-chain. He suggested that regulatory sandboxes could help address some of these challenges. SEBI and IFSCA already have sandboxes to encourage innovation in the capital markets, but digital asset native fintech players have not yet been given the go-ahead to participate. He also highlighted the potential of tokenisation, pointing to the tokenisation of corporate bonds as an example. For now, participation is limited to institutional players. Chandra suggested that opening up regulatory sandboxes to more web3 fintech companies could help them test new ideas, improve existing processes and play a bigger role in the tokenisation journey. Crypto infrastructure: Built for endurance Unlike traditional financial markets, crypto trades 24 hours a day, seven days a week. For tech teams, that means monitoring systems, managing risk and responding to incidents without the predictable downtime offered by market closing hours. Mishra described how trading activity on crypto platforms can pick up during evenings and weekends, partly in response to movements in US markets. This places continuous demands on observability, alerts and leverage monitoring. His experience building a spot trading exchange also showed how quickly demand for derivatives can outpace infrastructure development. At Pi42, the team took a different approach from the outset, building a platform specifically for derivatives rather than adapting a spot-trading system. Production incidents, Mishra noted, had occurred over weekends when systems could not keep pace with demand. The experience underlined the need to build infrastructure around crypto’s round-the-clock operating model. Beyond the hype: When risk management is embedded in processes As more people enter the crypto market, investor education and effective compliance become increasingly important. Menon pointed to WazirX’s ‘Gangs of Cryptopur’ campaign, which aims to help investors understand what they’re trading. He also spoke about taking a disciplined approach to crypto, comparing the historical returns of different asset classes with Bitcoin. His advice was to think long term rather than treat crypto as a series of short-term bets. For exchanges, making the process easier for users is just as important as maintaining compliance checks. Mishra explained that KYC can be frustrating when an application fails and users have to start all over again. Technology can make this simpler by letting users pick up where they left off and clearly explaining what needs to be corrected. He added that genuine users are generally less likely to be bothered by compliance checks than those trying to get around them. The aim is to make the process smoother for users while retaining the checks needed to identify suspicious activity. Putting AI to work in crypto: regulation, education, innovation AI is also changing how traders research markets and assess potential trades. Menon said WazirX has introduced an AI-powered feature that scans more than 300 tokens to spot those showing bearish momentum. WazirX AI - India’s first AI-powered crypto agent is a conversational co-pilot that handles advanced, multi-step requests, including technical indicators such as the Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) and Relative Strength Index (RSI), and offers recommendations for users to consider. Traders must confirm their chosen strategy before the AI places an order with stop-loss and take-profit parameters. Menon sees AI as a way to analyse large volumes of market data and spot patterns, but he also highlighted that AI should support decisions rather than make them for users. Mishra also urged traders to backtest AI-generated strategies and monitor their performance before using them in live markets, saying “If you ask AI to give you a strategy and then run with it, make sure that you are also observing it so as soon as it goes wrong, you can unplug it.” Chandra noted that regulatory implications will depend on how AI is used. Educational tools could be treated differently from systems that offer personalised investment advice, which could fall under investment-adviser regulations. He also stressed the need for AI systems to be trustworthy, explainable, auditable and fair. What comes next for crypto? As the crypto landscape changes with new regulations, AI disruptions and evolving investor expectations, Menon, Chandra and Mishra were asked what would represent the next phase of the sector. For Menon, it was futures and derivatives. Mishra agreed, noting that derivatives have continued to grow and address specific needs within the crypto ecosystem. Chandra pointed to another emerging possibility: compute futures, with developments such as the launch of compute futures by CME in the US indicating how new asset classes could emerge at the intersection of AI and digital assets. As the market evolves, the discussion highlighted three interconnected priorities: clearer regulation, stronger infrastructure and more informed use of AI. The next phase of crypto investing in India will depend not just on new products and trading opportunities, but also on how effectively the ecosystem manages risk and builds trust.

title: Two Point O raises $10M led by Transition Venture Capital
content: Two Point O Capital (TW.O), an AI-powered, full-stack clean energy deployment platform for commercial and industrial (C&I) businesses, has raised $10 million in a funding round led by Transition Venture Capital. Existing investor Omnivore and angel investors Chiranjeev Singh Saluja and Sudhir M Reddy also participated in the round. TW.O said it will use the funds to expand into new asset classes, including battery energy storage systems (BESS), and deepen its presence in existing segments such as solar, energy efficiency and wastewater treatment. The capital will also support its expansion into sectors with significant energy and water requirements, including data centres, automotive, pharma, manufacturing and healthcare, the company said in a statement. Founded in 2024 by Archit Mehrotra, Karan Bhutani, Manya Ranjan, and Shashidhar Reddy, TW.O helps businesses adopt clean energy infrastructure by bringing together financing, technology and end-to-end project execution. “This funding will accelerate our vision to become India’s first and largest multi-asset and multi-solution platform enabling adoption of clean energy by C&I customers,” said Karan Bhutani, CEO and Co-Founder of Two Point O Capital. TW.O partners with OEMs and EPCs across India. Its existing clientele includes the likes of Premier Energies, Godrej, JK Tyre, Morepen Pharma, Wipro, Phoenix Mills, and several other large commercial and industrial customers. According to the startup, it has grown its assets under management by 1.5x consistently every quarter over the last 3 quarters and uses a proprietary AI/ML-enabled platform for solutioning, underwriting and asset monitoring. “Two Point O removes the capex barrier, accelerating the adoption of clean energy solutions. The industry often underestimates the complexity of integration across a fragmented ecosystem with multiple stakeholders. By taking end-to-end ownership of execution, Two Point O enables customers to focus on their core business rather than managing the build,” said Yashodhara Bakliwal, VP, Investment at Transition Venture Capital.

title: Weekly VC funding stays subdued at $115M; Prosus gets CCI nod for Navi investment
content: Dear Reader, AI investments are beginning to translate into measurable business gains , with companies reporting stronger earnings and improved operational efficiency. Santander said its AI initiatives generated €194 million ($216 million) in business value in the first nine months of 2026, while Novartis and Standard Chartered reported profitability improvements. Meta credited AI with boosting advertising revenue, while Google Cloud’s revenue more than doubled to nearly $31 billion in Q3, highlighting the growing commercial returns from the technology. Closer home, Dutch investment group Prosus is a step closer to acquiring a stake in Sachin Bansal-led Navi, after the Competition Commission of India (CCI) approved the proposed deal . The approval follows Navi’s $100 million fundraise from Prosus in August, marking the Bengaluru-based fintech’s first institutional capital raise. The deal will deepen Prosus’ presence in India’s digital financial services market. In other news, Binance says it has replenished approximately 95% of the $6.3 billion in assets stolen in a major security breach, using company funds and reserves. The exchange has begun restoring cryptocurrency withdrawals in phases after completing security checks, while working to source the remaining 5% of less-liquid tokens. Binance has reiterated that users will not bear the financial losses. Meanwhile, countries at the UN’s COP17 biodiversity summit have agreed on a roadmap to accelerate nature conservation by 2030. The plan calls for reducing harmful subsidies and increasing conservation funding, although a significant financing gap remains a challenge to meeting global biodiversity targets. In today’s newsletter, we will talk about Weekly VC funding stays subdued at $115M India needs greater control over app distribution: Indus Appstore and Eloelo Here’s your trivia for today: What was the name of the very first internet search engine, created in 1990? (Scroll down for the answer) Funding Weekly VC funding stays subdued at $115M Venture capital funding into Indian startups remained subdued in October, with the absence of large-value deals weighing on overall inflows. The trend continued in the final week of the month, with startups raising $115 million across 29 deals. The largest transaction was a $15 million investment in healthtech startup Cent, while AI startups accounted for two of the deals. As 2026 draws to a close, the funding environment is expected to remain largely unchanged, with hopes of a recovery shifting to 2027. Key takeaways: Startups raised $115 million across 29 deals in the last week of October, up from $96 million in the previous week, but large-ticket investments remained elusive. Healthtech startup Cent led the week's transactions with $15 million, followed by AI infrastructure startup Simplismart and AI startup Live2.ai, which raised $14 million each. AI funding activity showed early signs of momentum, with two pure-play AI startups securing investments. However, the broader funding environment is expected to remain subdued through 2026. TechSparks India needs greater control over app distribution: Indus Appstore and Eloelo India’s app-first economy has yet to unlock the full potential of its digital goods market, with distribution barriers and high platform commissions limiting opportunities for developers. At TechSparks 2026, Indus Appstore’s Priya Narasimhan and Eloelo Group’s Sagar Gaonkar argued that India needs greater control over app discovery, distribution and billing. They also highlighted how AI-ready platforms, localised experiences and affordable pricing could help bring the next 500 million users online. Key takeaways: India needs a stronger digital goods marketplace, as high commissions of 15–30% charged by dominant app stores make it difficult for developers to sell lower-priced digital products. Digital sovereignty extends beyond chips and AI models to three critical layers: app discovery and distribution, monetisation and billing, and data trust and consent. AI could reshape app discovery and content personalisation, while platforms need to offer locally relevant experiences and flexible pricing to tap India's next 500 million digital users. News & updates EV Manufacturing: EKA Mobility has expanded its manufacturing footprint with six new facilities across Pune and Pithampur, taking its network to 11 plants with an annual capacity of over 40,000 electric vehicles. The expansion, backed by investments exceeding Rs 3,500 crore, comes as the company reports 1,243% year-on-year growth in H1 FY27 and an order book of over 11,000 buses. Global EV push: BYD recorded its sixth consecutive month of year-on-year sales growth in October, selling 4.9 lakh vehicles, up 11% from a year earlier. Overseas shipments surged 102.8% to 1.7 lakh units, helping offset sluggish domestic demand and intense price competition in China. What you should watch out for The Bengaluru Skill Summit 2026, organised by the Department of Skill Development, Entrepreneurship and Livelihood, Government of Karnataka, will take place from November 3 to 5 at The Lalit Ashok, Bengaluru. Devcon 8, Ethereum’s flagship global developer conference focused on blockchain infrastructure, decentralised applications, Web3 and the future of the Ethereum ecosystem, will take place in Mumbai from November 3 to 6, 2026. title: How Zocket is building the brain behind enterprise marketing
content: For the last three years, enterprise AI has been told one story: pick the most powerful model and you win. Every launch brought a new benchmark, a bigger context window, and a sharper reasoning score. Boardrooms debated which model to bet on as if it were a once-in-a-decade infrastructure decision. That story is running out of road. The gap between the leading models is narrowing every quarter, and most enterprises can now access near-frontier intelligence through a single API call. When everyone has access to the same brain, the brain stops being the advantage. The next battle in enterprise AI will be won in context: the proprietary knowledge, history, signals and judgement that tell a model what your business actually needs. Models are becoming the engine. Context is becoming the fuel, the map and the destination. The model is becoming a commodity Consider how quickly the landscape has shifted. A capability that felt magical 18 months ago, such as summarizing a 100-page contract or writing production-ready code, is now table stakes across multiple providers. Open-weight models have closed much of the gap with proprietary ones. Inference costs keep falling. Switching from one model to another, once a painful migration, is increasingly a configuration change. This is the classic arc of any foundational technology. Electricity, cloud computing and bandwidth all followed it: a period of scarcity and differentiation, followed by abundance and standardization. Nobody today wins because they have a better power supply. They win because of what they build on top of it. For enterprise leaders, the implication is uncomfortable but liberating. If your AI strategy rests mainly on which model you chose, your competitors can replicate it in a weekend. A durable advantage has to come from somewhere else. What ‘context’ really means AI models are powerful, but intelligence alone is not enough to understand how an enterprise operates. What makes AI genuinely useful is the context surrounding every decision: the brand, its customers, its business priorities, and the processes that govern how work gets done. For enterprise marketing, context goes beyond feeding information into a model. It means connecting four critical layers of intelligence: Data context: Customer behavior, campaign performance, product information, consumer interactions, and historical trends. These signals help AI understand what is working, what is changing, and where opportunities exist. Brand and institutional context: Brand guidelines, tone of voice, positioning, compliance requirements, past decisions, and business priorities. This is the knowledge that ensures every AI-generated action reflects the organization it represents. Workflow context: Understanding how marketing operates across teams, from creative development and campaign execution to approvals, governance, and reporting. AI needs to recognize not just what to do, but how decisions move through an organization. Real-time context: Consumer sentiment, emerging market trends, competitor activity, and live campaign performance. This allows AI to respond to changing conditions rather than relying entirely on historical information. The challenge is that most AI tools operate with only fragments of this intelligence. A creative tool may understand brand guidelines but lack campaign performance data. A media platform may optimize spending without understanding consumer sentiment. A research tool may identify emerging trends without connecting those insights to the next marketing decision. The result is fragmented intelligence across an increasingly connected marketing ecosystem. This is where Zocket's Brand Brain introduces a different approach. Rather than treating every marketing function as an isolated AI workflow, Brand Brain brings brand knowledge, consumer intelligence, performance signals, and governance into a shared context layer that powers specialised AI marketing capabilities. The underlying principle is simple: AI becomes more valuable when it understands not just the task it has been asked to perform, but the business behind it. For enterprises, that is the shift from AI that generates outputs to AI that can support informed, consistent, and connected marketing decisions at scale. Why context is the moat that lasts Models can be bought. Context has to be built, and that is precisely why it is defensible. First, context is proprietary by nature. No competitor can download your ten years of customer interactions or the hard-won lessons of your last hundred campaigns. Second, context compounds. Every decision an AI system makes, and every outcome it observes, becomes a new context that sharpens the next decision. An organization that starts capturing this loop today will be meaningfully ahead of one that starts in two years. Third, context is hard. In most enterprises, valuable knowledge is scattered across CRMs, spreadsheets, ad platforms, email threads and the heads of a few senior employees. It is siloed, inconsistently labelled, and often outdated. Getting it into a form an AI system can reliably use requires investment in data infrastructure, governance and integration, work that is unglamorous but decisive. This is why so many enterprise AI pilots look impressive in a demo and disappoint in production. The model was rarely the problem. The missing piece was context: the system simply did not know enough about the business to make the right call. "Enterprises often ask us which model is best. The better question is how quickly your systems can turn scattered data into something an AI can trust and act on. The model is the easy part to swap. The context layer, with its integrations, retrieval and feedback loops, is what takes real engineering, and it is where performance is won or lost," says Mukund Srivathsan, Co-founder and CTO, Zocket Also Read The Zocket Story: Building Brand Brain, the context and orchestration layer for AI-native enterprise marketing A view from marketing and advertising At Zocket, this shift is seen most clearly in marketing, where AI adoption has been fast and the cost of generic output is immediately visible. Any model today can generate an ad headline, a product description or a campaign plan in seconds. But a generic headline is not a good headline. A good one reflects the brand's voice, speaks to a specific audience segment, learns from which creatives converted last month and adapts to what is trending on each platform this week. The difference between an ad that performs and one that burns budget is almost never the raw writing ability of the model. It is the context behind the prompt. The same is true for budget allocation, audience targeting, and performance optimization. An AI agent that understands a brand's historical cost per acquisition, its seasonal patterns, its margins and its competitive landscape will consistently outperform a more powerful model working blind. The biggest gains for marketers come not from upgrading the model but from enriching what the model knows. This is why Zocket believes the future of AI in marketing is agentic and context-rich: systems that continuously learn from a brand's own data and outcomes, rather than tools that start from zero with every request. "Every brand now has access to the same AI. What it does not have is the same understanding of its customers. Our focus at Zocket is helping businesses turn their own data and results into an AI that gets smarter about them every single day. That is the advantage nobody can copy,” says Karthik Venkateswaran, Co-founder and CEO, Zocket What enterprise leaders should do now If context is the new battleground, the playbook changes. Five priorities stand out. Treat context as a strategic asset. Audit where your most valuable knowledge lives and who owns it. Customer data, performance history, and institutional rules deserve the same rigour as financial data. Stay model-agnostic. Build architectures that let you swap models as the market evolves. Lock-in to a single model is a risk; lock-in to your own context is an advantage. Close the feedback loop. Design AI systems that capture outcomes, not just outputs. Knowing which recommendation worked, and why, is what makes context compound over time. Invest in the plumbing. Data integration, retrieval systems, governance, and access controls are not back-office chores. They are the foundation of AI performance. Encode judgement, not just data. Capture the rules, guardrails, and preferences your best people apply instinctively, so AI can apply them consistently at scale. The winners will be the ones who know the most The first chapter of enterprise AI was about access: who could get their hands on capable models and put them to work. That chapter is almost at an end. The next one will be about understanding whose AI knows their customers, their markets, and their own business most deeply. In that world, the question in the boardroom shifts from "Which model are we using?" to "What does our AI know that nobody else does?" The companies with a compelling answer, built on rich, connected, and continuously improving context, will set the pace for their industries. Models will keep getting better, and that is good news for everyone. But because they are getting better for everyone, they cannot be what sets you apart. Context can. The enterprises that start building it seriously today will not just use AI more effectively. They will own an advantage that no model upgrade can buy. To learn more, visit www.zocket.com

title: How the open-source route helped Uzair Ali land global roles
content: Indian engineers no longer have to relocate abroad or go through several rounds of resume screening and interviews to bag global roles. Increasingly, open-source public code is paving the way for that. Public code is a record anyone can read and inspect, and hiring teams are actively using it to assess one's real-world engineering skills. It includes open-source contributions, public repositories (like GitHub), and code samples that hiring managers can evaluate. This is how Uzair Ali landed internships at various global companies and eventually became a founding engineer at a US-based fintech startup. As a college student at the Kalinga Institute of Industrial Technology in Bhubaneswar, Ali was building a tool to monitor server logs. He shared his repository of work in open source on X, which caught the attention of the CTO of Dukaan, an Indian mobile-first, do-it-yourself ecommerce platform , leading to an interview at the firm. Ali joined Dukaan as a backend intern in January 2022 in Bengaluru. This was an early lesson in the value of making his work visible to the world. It helped his project reach someone who might otherwise have not seen his resume. Ali's career path did not follow a straight line through a typical hiring funnel at big tech companies. After a stint at Dukaan, he interned at HackerRank and FamPay while still being in university. After graduating, he joined Civo, a London-based cloud infrastructure provider. Twenty-four-year-old Ali is now an engineer at Flip Laboratories, a San Francisco-based fintech startup. He works from India. In an interaction with YourStory , Ali says all his career moves from being a backend engineer to AI work and now to being part of the founding team at Flip are largely thanks to his open-source contributions. Ali reasons that open-source code helps software maintainers see how people works over months, while the reviews show how they handle feedback. Now anyone with an internet connection can pick a project, fix what is broken, and receive feedback and reviews. Over time, this history builds a credible repository of one's work in a way a resume cannot, says the techie. Ali's GitHub profile has a number of pull requests merged in various open source projects such as LiteLLM, a widely used open-source LLM gateway. A pull request is a request from others to merge a code into their projects, and this is reveiwed jointly by those who create the code and those who would like to integrate it. Ali's most visible work is on Agno, an open-source framework for building AI agents. It has more than 42,000 stars on GitHub. He also has contributions in major codebases including Terraform, Crossplane, and IntelOwl. A codebase is a complete compendium of source code, configuration files, and supporting resources used to build, test, and run a software system or application. Today, Ali is part of the founding team at Flip Laboratories, which has built Flip, a proactive AI agent to manage the finances of Americans. Flip acts like a personal finance assistant operating directly inside users' messaging apps (such as iMessage). The startup recently raised a $1.4 million pre-seed round from investors including a16z speedrun, Pear VC, The House Fund, and Cory Levy. For Ali, the thread connecting all his experiences—as a student developer, an intern building cloud tools and an AI framework, and as a founding engineer at a startup—is work that other people can see. Open source was not a shortcut to an interview or a job; it was a proactive way to make his learning and work visible beyond his college, city, and country. Edited by Swetha Kannan

title: NTT DATA explores expansion in Mangaluru and Udupi, meets Priyank Kharge
content: Karnataka wants its next wave of technology investments to reach beyond Bengaluru, and global IT companies are being encouraged to look towards its coastal cities. NTT DATA is exploring plans to expand its operations in Karnataka, with Mangaluru and Udupi emerging as potential areas of focus. The company shared its expansion plans during discussions with Karnataka IT, BT and Rural Development Minister Priyank Kharge on November 2, 2026. The discussions covered new areas of collaboration, technology investments and opportunities to strengthen the company's presence in the state. NTT DATA, which recently acquired Karnataka-based Niveus Solutions and WinWire, cited the availability of skilled talent as a key advantage in expanding its operations, particularly along the coast. Beyond Bengaluru takes centre stage Priyank Kharge highlighted the state's Beyond Bengaluru programme, which aims to develop technology ecosystems across Karnataka by extending investments, infrastructure and employment opportunities to emerging technology clusters. “Through our Beyond Bengaluru programme, we are building strong regional technology ecosystems by investing in skilling, infrastructure and progressive policies. Our focus is on taking investments and opportunities to where the talent is,” he said. He added that the government wanted to work closely with industry to develop solutions that could accelerate growth across Karnataka's emerging technology hubs. Data centres, cloud and digital infrastructure on the agenda The meeting also explored opportunities under Karnataka's Sustainable Data Centre Policy and potential collaboration with NTT DATA across data centres, cloud services and digital infrastructure. Moreover, Kharge outlined plans for a cable landing station in Mangaluru, which is expected to strengthen the state's digital infrastructure, and discussed how NTT DATA's expertise could support the project. The minister also encouraged the company to explore opportunities beyond cloud services in sectors such as biotechnology, healthcare, life sciences and automotive manufacturing. These areas align with Karnataka's existing industrial and research ecosystem. Startup collaboration and new technology opportunities Startup incubation and innovation were also part of the discussions. Priyank Kharge also mentioned the recently launched Government First programme, which allows startups to pilot their solutions with public sector departments. He invited NTT DATA to partner with the initiative and contribute to Karnataka's startup ecosystem. The meeting was attended by senior government officials, including Dr N. Manjula, Secretary, Department of Electronics, IT, BT and S&T; Dr Avinash Menon Rajendran, IAS, Director, Department of Electronics, IT and BT and Managing Director of Karnataka Innovation and Technology Society (KITS); and Sanjeev Gupta, CEO of KDEM. NTT DATA was represented by Charlie Li, President and Global Head of Cloud, AI and Security; Ayman Husain, Worldwide Managing Director and VP, Google Business Unit; and Shashir Shetty, Chief Growth Officer. With Mangaluru and Udupi being discussed as potential expansion destinations, Karnataka is looking to extend its technology footprint beyond Bengaluru and bring more specialised technology investments to its coastal region.

title: Clinics On Cloud raises $12.5M to expand microclinic network
content: Healthtech company Clinics On Cloud has raised $12.5 million in Series A funding from Dubai-based Model42, a health and wellness growth platform powered by Enlightened Minds Investments. The Pune-based firm said it will use the funding to strengthen its artificial intelligence capabilities, expand research and development, and grow its connected microclinic network. It also plans partnerships with healthcare providers and technology companies to integrate new screening tools and AI applications. The United Arab Emirates will be its global hub, with planned expansion into Africa, the United States and Southeast Asia. Founded in 2018, Clinics On Cloud builds technology-enabled healthcare access points. Its Health ATMs are compact screening stations combining connected medical devices, health checks and digital reports, alongside AI-assisted insights and telemedicine. Its portfolio also includes Health Lounges, Box Clinics and Mobile Medical Units for hospitals, workplaces, housing communities and underserved areas. Founder and chief executive officer Abhay Agarwal said the company had spent eight years guided by the belief that “quality healthcare should never depend on someone’s PIN code”. The investment, he said, would help take that vision overseas, with the opportunity lying in “making these innovations accessible to people, wherever they are”. Clinics On Cloud claims more than 3,500 deployments, over 12 million health screenings and operations in eight countries. Its systems have been used in government health centres, hospitals, corporate sites, rural communities and Indian defence establishments, including the Army, Navy and Border Security Force. The funding comes amid a more selective investment climate. Venture Intelligence data showed Indian health-tech startup funding fell to $447 million in 2025 from $707 million in 2024. However, capital continues to flow into specialised models. In October, preventive-health startup Cent raised $15 million in a Series A led by Blume Ventures and South Park Commons. In July, radiology AI company CARPL.ai secured $10 million in a round led by the International Finance Corporation. Meanwhile, public digital infrastructure is also expanding. By May 2026, the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission had crossed 90 crore digital health accounts and 100 crore linked health records. Initiatives announced in June, including digital clinic-management tools and common data standards, aim to make health information easier to exchange.

title: Deeptech startups gain VC attention as India’s investment landscape evolves
content: India’s deeptech startup ecosystem is witnessing growing investor interest, with themes such as technological sovereignty, import substitution, AI infrastructure and advanced manufacturing emerging as key investment opportunities. After years of limited access to early-stage capital, deeptech ventures are increasingly attracting funds willing to back them from the pre-seed stage, signalling a shift in the country’s venture capital landscape. During a panel discussion at TechSparks 2026, an incubator, early stage venture capital firm and a late stage investor provided interesting perspectives on the evolving investment landscape in India, particularly in the areas of artificial intelligence and deeptech.
