Priyanka Agarwal Chopra, Managing Partner and CEO of IIMA Ventures, said deeptech had traditionally been a challenging investment segment because of its high risks and longer gestation periods, which often did not align with conventional venture capital timelines. “When we started, our founding vision was to address gaps in India's innovation and entrepreneurship ecosystem, particularly in markets and sectors where private sector capital was not available,” she said. IIMA Ventures was among the early investors in India's deeptech ecosystem, supporting companies in areas that were then categorised as high technology. Chopra said two major themes currently driving deeptech innovation in India are technological sovereignty and import substitution. She added that while investing in deeptech at the early stages was once a relatively isolated proposition, more funds are now showing interest in supporting companies even at the pre-seed stage. The growing focus on building indigenous technology capabilities is also creating opportunities for Indian startups to address domestic requirements while developing products for global markets. Anaina Malik, Partner at VU Venture Partners, said AI infrastructure would be an important investment opportunity as India expands its AI application ecosystem. She emphasised that infrastructure development should receive attention alongside application-led innovation. Malik also identified agriculture and advanced manufacturing as underserved sectors with considerable potential for technological disruption. She said the firm was looking at startups addressing India's domestic requirements as well as companies building products and solutions for international markets. According to her, the boundaries between domestic and global markets are increasingly dissolving, with international capital also showing greater interest in investment opportunities emerging from India. Meanwhile, Sandeep Sinha, Co-founder and Co-CEO of Oister Global, said India's deeptech ecosystem had matured considerably, with several companies that began their journeys eight to 10 years ago now reaching commercial readiness. He pointed out that many of these ventures had already addressed significant technology and research and development risks and were generating revenues from both domestic and international markets. Sinha said deeptech companies were increasingly demonstrating the ability to create value through revenue growth, margin expansion and market expansion. The emergence of commercially viable businesses with greater revenue visibility represents an important development for investors evaluating the sector. While acknowledging that the funding ecosystem remains somewhat fragmented, he described the current activity as 'chaos by design', adding that the increased movement of capital and investors over the past 18-24 months had brought deeptech into sharper focus. The panellists also highlighted the importance of founder capabilities in determining investment decisions, particularly at the early stages when financial and operating data are limited. Chopra said investors at the early stage place considerable emphasis on four parameters: founder depth, founder-problem fit, the unique insight of the entrepreneur and the market opportunity. Sinha, meanwhile, stressed the need for founders to build predictable businesses and diversify their customer base rather than depend excessively on a single customer, irrespective of its importance. Beyond AI On investment sizes, Malik said VU Venture Partners' initial cheque sizes remained between $250,000 and $1 million. However, the firm had increased its follow-on investments, choosing to stay invested for longer and support founders through different stages of growth. She added that evaluating AI startups had become more challenging because of the large number of companies identifying themselves as AI businesses. Consequently, the firm was placing greater emphasis on understanding the underlying technology through deeper due diligence. Despite the growing investor focus on AI and deeptech, Chopra cautioned entrepreneurs against assuming that opportunities in other sectors had diminished. Consumer businesses, fintech and retail continue to offer substantial opportunities, supported by strong domestic demand. She emphasised that India's startup ecosystem has room for multiple business models and sectors, and encouraged founders to pursue opportunities they are genuinely passionate about.

title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 02, 2026)
content: From AI-powered, full-stack clean energy deployment platform, Two Point O Capital (TW.O), raising $10 million in a funding round led by Transition Venture Capital, to Competition watchdog CCI approving Dutch investment group Prosus' proposal to acquire a stake in Sachin Bansal-led fintech firm Navi, here are the latest developments across sectors. Featured Stories Two Point O raises $10M led by Transition Venture Capital Two Point O Capital (TW.O), an AI-powered, full-stack clean energy deployment platform for commercial and industrial (C&I) businesses, has raised $10 million in a funding round led by Transition Venture Capital. Existing investor Omnivore and angel investors Chiranjeev Singh Saluja and Sudhir M Reddy also participated in the round. TW.O said it will use the funds to expand into new asset classes, including battery energy storage systems (BESS), and deepen its presence in existing segments such as solar, energy efficiency and wastewater treatment. Read more Latest News Prosus investment in Sachin Bansal's Navi gets CCI nod Competition watchdog CCI has approved Dutch investment group Prosus' proposal to acquire a stake in Sachin Bansal-led fintech firm Navi Ltd, paving the way for the investment group to deepen its presence in India's digital financial services sector. "The proposed combination involves the acquisition of certain shareholding in Navi Ltd (target) by MIH Payments Holdings BV (acquirer)," the regulator said in a release. The Competition Commission of India (CCI) said it has approved the proposed deal. Read more Funding News ValueQuest Tristar Fund raises over Rs 2,100 Cr for advanced manufacturing ValueQuest Tristar Fund, a private equity fund that backs India’s advanced manufacturing sector, has received more than Rs 2,100 crore in commitments from investors. It reached this within 15 months of its first close, beating both its original target and the full greenshoe (the extra amount a fund is allowed to raise above its target). The fund invests in aerospace, defence, precision engineering and manufacturing linked to the energy transition. Read more Other News Razorpay Wins Final IFSCA Licence to Run Cross-Border Money Movement from GIFT City Razorpay has received its final Payment Service Provider licence from the IFSCA, following in-principle approval in April 2026. The licence lets it move money in and out of India from GIFT City under a single regulatory framework. Its infrastructure supports global investing, international collections, settlements and multi-currency accounts, with banking integrations live with RBL Bank and ICICI Bank. Investment platforms can integrate once, cutting timelines from months to two to three weeks. The move responds to rising demand, as Indian residents put $2.65 billion into overseas stocks and debt in FY26, up 56 per cent year on year. Arrowhead AI launches Fletch, a voice model built for India and Southeast Asia's multilingual conversations Arrowhead AI, a Bengaluru-based voice AI company, has launched Fletch, an in-house text-to-speech model for multilingual customer calls. It supports 14 languages, switches between them mid-sentence and offers 12 emotion styles. Fletch reports 80 milliseconds of latency and starts speaking in under 100 milliseconds. Already powering over one million calls a day for clients such as Axis Bank and RBL Bank, it claims roughly 30% better pronunciation accuracy on selected names and terms, a figure the company stresses is not an overall call-resolution gain. Arrowhead is adding Malay and Indonesian support ahead of Singapore FinTech Festival 2026. BikeWo Green Tech signs MoU with Eden Green Energy to explore electric mobility opportunities BikeWo Green Tech Limited has signed a strategic Memorandum of Understanding with Eden Green Energy Private Limited to explore collaboration in electric mobility and sustainable transportation. The companies will look at opportunities in EV fleet solutions, vehicle leasing, charging infrastructure, and workforce, rider and operational management. BikeWo brings expertise in leasing, infrastructure and business development, while Eden contributes workforce and operational strengths. Eden's Managing Director said the partnership aligns with plans to expand dedicated electric fleets and charging networks in Tamil Nadu, including Chennai and Tiruchirappalli. Both firms aim to build scalable, zero-emission mobility solutions. Fibe launches UPI payments on its App after NPCI third-party provider approval Digital lending platform Fibe has launched its UPI offering following NPCI approval to operate as a Third-Party Application Provider. The service is open to consumers across India, including those who are not existing Fibe customers. Users can pay through bank accounts, RuPay Credit Cards and eligible credit lines, all within a single UPI experience. The launch adds an everyday payments layer to Fibe's range of products, which includes the Fibe Axis Bank Credit Card, third-party FDs and Loan Against Mutual Funds. Group CEO Akshay Mehrotra said the aim is to give users greater choice, control and value in every transaction. DHL Express appoints Sandeep Juneja to lead South Asia and India business DHL Express has appointed Sandeep Juneja as Senior Vice President for South Asia and Managing Director for India, effective 1 November 2026. He succeeds R. S. Subramanian, who moves to Blue Dart as Managing Director. Juneja joined DHL Express in 2004, has sat on the India Management Board since 2007 and has led the commercial function since 2013. He will focus on customer partnerships, people and sustainable growth, and will also oversee Nepal, Bhutan, the Maldives, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh. Asia Pacific CEO Ken Lee said Juneja brings the market knowledge and customer relationships needed for the next phase of growth. Nagaland University-led study proposes framework to evaluate AI tools for preserving India's cultural heritage A research team led by Nagaland University, with scholars from institutions in Tamil Nadu, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka, has proposed a framework to evaluate how AI can help preserve manuscripts, endangered languages, oral traditions and historical records. It assesses tools across nine areas, including text recognition, translation, cultural context and ethics, combining technical checks with expert and community review. The researchers stress that AI should support, not replace, archivists, linguists and cultural custodians, since technical accuracy does not guarantee cultural accuracy. They recommend piloting the framework across different collections, scripts and dialects. The findings appear in Acta Innovations. Thyrocare launches India's first pregnancy kit with bundled lab confirmation test; Yami Gautam named brand ambassador Thyrocare Technologies has entered the pregnancy testing segment with the Thyrocare Pregnancy Kit, which it says is India's first to include a quantitative laboratory confirmation. Priced at Rs 60, the kit contains a rapid at-home test and a voucher for a Beta hCG blood test at Rs 399, half the regular Rs 800, with home sample collection included. Users book the test by scanning a QR code, and the voucher is valid for six months. Actor Yami Gautam is the brand ambassador. Thyrocare's MD and CEO Rahul Guha said the kit pairs a quick home answer with clinical confirmation. ICICI Lombard's Startup Shield forum helps Bengaluru startups build resilience against emerging business risks ICICI Lombard General Insurance hosted "Startup Shield – The Risk Readiness Forum" in Bengaluru on 27 October 2026 to help startups prepare for emerging risks. Karnataka has 24,026 DPIIT-recognised startups, and the discussions covered AI-driven threats, cyber and data security, employee wellness, professional indemnity, directors and officers liability, asset protection and business interruption. Founders, investors, CXOs and risk professionals attended, and ICICI Lombard experts shared real-world case studies. Anand Singhi, the company's Chief for Corporate, International, Banca and Government Business, said risk preparedness is increasingly a marker of business maturity that influences how investors and enterprise partners assess a company. Avendus appoints Sumit Agarwal as Managing Director and Head of Equity Corporate Finance Avendus has appointed Sumit Agarwal as Managing Director and Head of Equity Corporate Finance, Investment Banking, reporting to Karan Sharma, Head of Investment Banking at Avendus Capital. He will lead the firm's equity capital markets execution, strengthening its ability to deliver end-to-end IPO mandates and follow-on offerings. Agarwal has over 18 years of experience and has led more than 100 transactions, including IPOs, FPOs, QIPs, InvITs and rights issues. He joins from Kotak Mahindra Capital and previously worked at ICICI Securities. Sharma said Agarwal brings deep execution expertise and strong institutional relationships that will broaden the firm's ECM capabilities. Xflow launches SaaS subscription management tool for businesses to pay global vendors like AWS and OpenAI Cross-border payments company Xflow has launched SaaS Subscription Management, letting businesses pay and track global subscriptions such as AWS, OpenAI, Figma and Slack in one place. Companies pay Xflow via SWIFT in USD or through NEFT/RTGS in INR, and use a USD virtual card for all subscription payments. The tool addresses failed recurring payments on domestic cards and scattered renewals across teams and currencies. CEO Ashwin Bhatnagar cited industry estimates that over 30 per cent of card-based recurring payments fail in India, and said Xflow is already processing millions in volume since launch. Blume Ventures' Amit Gajaria praised the service. (The copy will be updated with the latest news through the day)

title: ValueQuest Tristar Fund raises over Rs 2,100 Cr for advanced manufacturing
content: ValueQuest Tristar Fund, a private equity fund that backs India’s advanced manufacturing sector, has received more than Rs 2,100 crore in commitments from investors. It reached this within 15 months of its first close, beating both its original target and the full greenshoe (the extra amount a fund is allowed to raise above its target). The fund invests in aerospace, defence, precision engineering and manufacturing linked to the energy transition. So far, it has backed four companies: Hi-Q Electronics makes critical circuit boards for aerospace and defence. Rangsons Aerospace builds fluid distribution systems and satellite communications equipment. Waaree Energy Storage Solutions focuses on battery energy storage. Trusted Aerospace & Engineers (TASE Global) is a precision engineering firm that serves several industries and manufactures across borders. To pick its investments, the fund combines in-depth sector research with a mapping of industrial value chains. This helps the fund find specialised manufacturers that stand to gain from long-term industry growth and from key turning points in their own businesses. “India is at the beginning of a multi-decade transformation in advanced manufacturing. But sector growth alone does not guarantee investment returns. The real differentiator is identifying the right businesses at the right stage of their evolution. The work we do upfront gives us the conviction to partner with strong promoters and deepen our exposure as they deliver against milestones,” said Aniket Dharamshi, Co-Founder and Managing Partner, ValueQuest Investment Advisors. “In advanced manufacturing, competitive advantage is built over years through process expertise, rigorous customer qualification and consistent delivery on quality and reliability. Once a supplier becomes integral to a customer’s critical programs, replacing it can involve significant time, cost and execution risk. We seek businesses that can build on these capabilities to deepen customer relationships and translate industry growth into sustained, profitable growth,” said Dr. Arvind Ananthanarayanan, Partner, ValueQuest Private Equity. ValueQuest Private Equity is also raising its SCALE Fund II, which will invest in established businesses with clear competitive advantages and visible routes to an exit for investors. ValueQuest Private Equity is the private equity arm of ValueQuest Investment Advisors. It manages over Rs 6,000 crore across two investment strategies, three funds and co-investments. ValueQuest Investment Advisors manages about $3.4 billion across public and private markets.

title: MobiKwik posts Rs 11.83 Cr profit in Q2 of FY27
content: MobiKwik reported a net profit in the second quarter of FY27, compared with a loss in the year-ago period, marking its fourth consecutive profitable quarter and its highest-ever quarterly profit. The fintech company posted a net profit of Rs 11.83 crore for the July-September quarter, against a loss of Rs 28.61 crore in Q2 FY26. Revenue rose 9.4% year-on-year (YoY) to Rs 295.70 crore. MobiKwik attributed the quarter’s performance to higher gross merchandise value (GMV) growth and improved margins. “We believe that the operating leverage in our business model will compound as we evolve into an AI-first company. Our continued focus on cost optimisation and operating efficiency is further strengthening our operating model and will drive profitability as we scale,” said Bipin Preet Singh, MD & CEO, MobiKwik. According to MobiKwik, its payment business recorded a 35% year-on-year (YoY) growth in gross merchandise value (GMV) to Rs 59,677 crore in Q2 FY27. Consumer payments GMV grew 27% YoY to Rs 46,375 crore, while lending disbursals rose 34% to Rs 1,082.6 crore during the quarter. The company’s registered user base increased to 196.3 million in Q2 FY27, compared with 183.5 million in the corresponding quarter last fiscal. MobiKwik is also accelerating the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) across engineering, lending, customer experience, and risk management. According to the company, AI now generates 92% of its code, helping accelerate go-to-market initiatives by 55%. Its Help LLM resolves 91% of customer queries, while fraud detection is entirely AI-led. The fintech company added that its AI-powered collections platform facilitates 55% of early collections and has improved collection rates by 33%. Voice AI has also helped achieve 30-40% higher customer connect rates.

title: OYO parent PRISM’s revenue rises 35% to Rs 2,814 Cr in Q1 FY27
content: IPO-bound PRISM, parent entity of hospitality chain OYO, has posted a consolidated profit after tax (PAT) of Rs 353 crore in the first quarter ended June, registering 17% growth from Rs 301 crore in the year-ago period. The quarterly profit included a deferred-tax credit of approximately Rs 244 crore, according to the company's audited financials. PRISM's revenue from operations increased 35% to Rs 2,814 crore in the first quarter of FY2026-27, compared with Rs 2,078 crore in the corresponding quarter last year, the audited financials showed. The company's Gross Booking Value grew 30% to nearly Rs 9,600 crore in the same period. Growth was broad-based across its hotels and vacation homes businesses. PRISM's hotel segment bookings grew 30% year-on-year, while the vacation homes business recorded 28% growth in bookings. Addressing shareholders at the company's Extraordinary General Meeting (EGM) in early October, PRISM Founder Ritesh Agarwal said, "What is encouraging is that this momentum has continued into the first quarter of FY27. Our performance across hotels and vacation homes has demonstrated improving gross margins and higher operating earnings, even as we invest in expanding our brands and strengthening customer demand." "We are continuing to grow our business while generating healthy operating earnings. We are seeing the benefits of the investments we have made over the past few years in technology, brands and distribution capabilities, while continuing to invest quite aggressively," he had said. In his EGM address, Agarwal highlighted the importance of the company's geographically diversified business, with North America remaining a key market following the acquisition of G6 Hospitality. He said G6 alone contributed approximately Rs 14,000 crore in Gross Booking Value during FY26. Other profitability indicators also strengthened in the June quarter: EBITDA rose 24% year-on-year to Rs 760 crore, while adjusted EBITDA, net of lease expenses, increased 35% to Rs 589 crore. Its common technology platform is built centrally and replicated across markets, supporting pricing, distribution, reservations, customer service and property management. PRISM is also embedding AI in pricing and workflows; its Grace AI general manager supports operations at several hotels in Western markets. Separately, an October 26 addendum filed with SEBI cut the proposed IPO fresh issue to up to Rs 3,350 crore and earmarked Rs 2,512.5 crore for repayment or prepayment of borrowings through a subsidiary, while removing the proposed pre-IPO placement. With inputs from PTI.

title: Customers withdraw $3.6B after largest theft in Binance's history
content: Binance witnessed a massive increase in outflows, with customers withdrawing $3.6 billion from the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange after the largest theft in its history, which has been linked to North Korea. According to media reports, customers withdrew $3.6 billion of assets from Binance as it reopened on Sunday following the theft of $6.3 billion on Thursday. The company had suspended all transactions following the incident. "Binance began restoring withdrawals in phases at 06:00 UTC on November 1, 2026," the company posted on X on Sunday, three days after it froze assets in the wake of the theft. "By 12:36 UTC, withdrawals had resumed for all 15 networks and assets in the initial phase. After an initial spike, withdrawal volumes have declined and are stabilising as expected, while deposit volumes have remained substantial," it said. According to Binance, customers deposited $1.01 billion and withdrew about $4.649 billion in assets. Most of those transactions occurred in the first few hours after trading was restored, it added. The outflow of $3.64 billion represents 2.1% of $171 billion in total assets under its management, the company said on Sunday. "Our team continues testing rigorously the remaining networks and assets. We know how important safe and reliable access to your funds is and will share details of the next phase as soon as we can. Rest assured that market conditions are stable,” Binance said in a post on X. The company said that it would cover all losses that occurred during the hack and that it had worked with other cryptocurrency firms to freeze about USD 3 billion in stolen assets, according to a The New York Times report. The paper said that the cybersecurity analysts and the FBI have attributed the theft to North Korea, which has targeted cryptocurrency companies for years, taking advantage of vulnerabilities in their infrastructure to steal assets. "The hackers may have used artificial intelligence technology to accelerate their attack, according to the crypto analytics firm Chainalysis, which said that the attackers processed 'thousands of transactions in a short period'," the NYT report said. Changpeng Zhao, a co-founder of Binance, said, "Trust isn’t earned by what you say in good times. It’s earned by what you do in hard times." According to the NYT, he also warned customers to beware of online scammers making bogus offers of compensation.""

title: Ambani tops Forbes' global billionaire gainers list with $7B wealth jump as Reliance shares soar
content: Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani has emerged as the world's biggest billionaire wealth gainer, adding over $6 billion to his fortune in a single day, as shares of his flagship company surged following a stronger-than-expected quarterly earnings performance. According to Forbes' Real-Time Billionaires list, Ambani's wealth increased by 7.85%, or $6.3 billion, making him the biggest gainer globally in the latest update to the ranking on November 2. The gain was substantially ahead of the second-biggest wealth accretion on the list, with Spanish retail billionaire Amancio Ortega adding $1.7 billion, followed by China's Zhong Shanshan at $1.5 billion. The gains pushed Ambani to No.23 spot on the world billionaire list, making him the richest Indian ahead of Gautam Adani, who was ranked at No.26 with a wealth of $79.12 billion, according to the Forbes listing. Ambani had a wealth of $88.8 billion, according to Forbes. The sharp increase in Ambani's wealth coincided with a rally in Reliance Industries shares, which jumped 11.6% on Monday, marking their strongest trading session in more than six years. The stock closed at its day's high and was the biggest gainer on the benchmark Nifty 50 index. The rally followed Reliance's September-quarter results, which showed a 40.6% year-on-year increase in consolidated net profit to Rs 25,548 crore, significantly ahead of analyst expectations. Stronger refining and petrochemical margins, alongside improved profitability at its telecom business Jio, helped drive the earnings growth. The results reinforced investor confidence in Reliance's two major earnings engines - its oil-to-chemicals business and digital services - even as profitability in its retail business remained under pressure. The company's refining core earnings surged 68%, while Jio Platforms' core earnings rose 16.6% during the quarter. "Mukesh Ambani chairs and runs $125 billion (revenue) Reliance Industries, which has interests in petrochemicals, oil and gas, telecom, retail, media and financial services," Forbes said. Reliance was founded by his late father Dhirubhai Ambani, a yarn trader, in 1966 as a small textile manufacturer. After his father's death in 2002, Ambani and his younger sibling, Anil, divided the family empire. Reliance's telecom and broadband service Jio Platforms got listed in October 2026, achieving a market capitalisation of $137 billion, which made it the country's second-most valuable company after its parent. Ambani's three children joined the board of Reliance in 2023. Son Akash heads Jio; daughter Isha oversees retail and financial services; and younger son Anant is in the energy business. In 2026, Ambani announced plans for a $110 billion investment in AI infrastructure to be built across the country over the next seven years, the publication added.""

title: EKA Mobility expands manufacturing footprint
content: Electric mobility firm EKA Mobility has inaugurated six manufacturing facilities across Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh in a bid to scale production of electric buses, trucks and smaller commercial vehicles as India expands fleet electrification. The company said the six plants in Pune and Pithampur are part of a 11-facility network spread across 120 acres, with annual capacity for more than 40,000 electric vehicles and investment exceeding Rs 3,500 crore. The facilities cover vehicle assembly, engineering, battery enclosures, seating and interiors. EKA claims 1,243% year-on-year growth in H1 FY27. It also asserts an order book of more than 11,000 buses. Founder and Chairman Sudhir Mehta emphasised the importance of affordability and accessibility, saying, “Until we make it accessible and affordable for all, we will not have achieved our vision, and no amount of technology matters if it does not reach the people who depend on it every day.” Competition, however, is intensifying. VAHAN-based figures show that India registered 2,944 electric buses between January and June 2026, a 40% increase year-on-year. Switch Mobility led with 830 registrations, followed by JBM Auto with 635 and PMI Electro Mobility with 574. Pinnacle Mobility Solutions, the company behind EKA, registered 171, accounting for 5.8% of the market. Meanwhile, Government policy is supporting this expansion. The PM E-DRIVE scheme, whose outlay increased to Rs 11,900 crore in August 2026, earmarks Rs 4,391 crore for 14,028 electric buses and Rs 500 crore for 5,643 electric trucks. The scheme has been extended for most segments until March 2028. A separate PM-eBus Sewa payment-security programme supports the deployment of more than 38,000 buses, addressing concerns around delayed payments to operators. The Rs 25,938-crore production-linked incentive programme also seeks to strengthen domestic advanced automotive technology manufacturing.

title: Prosus investment in Sachin Bansal's Navi gets CCI nod
content: Competition watchdog CCI has approved Dutch investment group Prosus' proposal to acquire a stake in Sachin Bansal-led fintech firm Navi Ltd, paving the way for the investment group to deepen its presence in India's digital financial services sector. "The proposed combination involves the acquisition of certain shareholding in Navi Ltd (target) by MIH Payments Holdings BV (acquirer)," the regulator said in a release. The Competition Commission of India (CCI) said it has approved the proposed deal. MIH Payments Holdings BV does not undertake any business activity other than holding investments in its portfolio companies, which operate in India, the watchdog added. Prosus is a global consumer internet group and one of the world's largest technology investors. It is majority-owned by the South African multinational mass media company Naspers. Bengaluru-based Navi is the holding company of the Navi Group, founded by Bansal in 2018 after leaving Flipkart following its sale to Walmart. The fintech firm provides a range of financial services, including digital payments, lending, insurance, and mutual funds. In August, Navi announced that it had raised $100 million from Prosus, marking the company's first institutional capital raise and strengthening its position as it looks to scale its digital financial services businesses. Deals beyond a certain threshold need regulatory approval, which monitors unfair business practices and promotes fair competition in the marketplace.

title: Beyond AI: Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026 to spotlight new technologies, markets and opportunities
content: For technology entrepreneurs, staying ahead increasingly means looking beyond their immediate business environment. New technologies are emerging rapidly, industries are converging, and opportunities for partnerships, investment, and market expansion are often found at the intersection of different ecosystems. This makes technology-focused platforms that bring together businesses, innovators, investors, researchers and global technology communities particularly valuable. Bengaluru Tech Summit (BTS) 2026 , taking place from November 17–19 at Bangalore International Exhibition Centre , is one such platform worth keeping on the radar. The 29th edition of BTS will bring together tech companies, startups, investors, R&D institutions, and global technology ecosystems across a wide range of sectors. The participation of global technology giants, Indian conglomerates, unicorns, and soonicorns creates an environment where entrepreneurs can gain a broader understanding of where their industries are headed while identifying potential business connections . The convergence of the global tech ecosystem The international dimension is equally significant. Technology communities from 75+ countries, including Sweden, Italy, Australia, Poland, USA, Israel, Spain, Japan, China, Germany and South Korea, will participate across the expo, conference and special events. This creates an opportunity to engage with ecosystems beyond India for businesses or startups looking to understand international markets, explore collaborations, or simply broaden their technology network. The grand co-location of embedded world India, organised by Nuernberg Messe India , brings embedded technologies into sharper focus at BTS 2026. With embedded systems increasingly underpinning applications across electronics, automotive, industrial technology and connected devices, its presence adds another important dimension to the technology landscape represented at the summit. AI and robotics will take centre stage at BTS 2026 with the AI & Robotics Pavilion , led by Bharat fi.AI , spotlighting emerging innovations and advancements shaping the future of these transformative technologies. Future makers in focus For startups and emerging businesses, BTS 2026 offers opportunities that go well beyond the exhibition ﬂoor. Through workshops, masterclasses, mentoring sessions, pitching opportunities and product launches , entrepreneurs can gain practical insights, showcase their innovations, connect with potential investors, and explore new business opportunities. The Future Makers Conclave further brings together founders, investors, and industry leaders, creating a platform for meaningful conversations around innovation, funding, and scaling businesses. Together, these initiatives aim to help entrepreneurs expand their networks, gain visibility, and build connections that can accelerate their growth. Focus areas at BTS 2026 The breadth of sectors represented is another reason the summit stands out. From IT & deeptech, frontier tech, fintech, health & biotech to electro-semicon, cybersecurity, data centers and Global Capability Centres (GCCs) , the summit explores technologies transforming businesses and creating new avenues for growth. It also looks beyond conventional technology domains to emerging opportunities in electric mobility, circular economy, orange economy, and edtech , highlighting how innovation is reshaping industries, opening new markets, and creating possibilities for entrepreneurs. For businesses looking to identify emerging trends, explore cross-sector opportunities and understand where the next wave of growth may come from, this diversity makes BTS 2026 a valuable platform for discovery, collaboration, and business development. The future belongs to entrepreneurs willing to imagine, innovate, and take the next step. Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026 is an opportunity to exchange ideas, discover fresh perspectives, and forge connections that can open new doors. Because sometimes, a single conversation, a new perspective or an unexpected connection can be the beginning of something extraordinary. Register Now

title: Omio founder’s advice to entrepreneurs: Find a problem worth solving and stick with it
content: AI has made it easier to build products, but entrepreneurs still need to decide what to build and whether they can stay committed long enough to turn an idea into a sustainable business. For Naren Shaam, Founder and CEO of ﻿ Omio ﻿ Omio Group, the answer is to solve difficult problems, stay focused, and avoid chasing the next big thing. Speaking at TechSparks 2026, Shaam spoke about building Omio, which operates across 56 countries, and why Indian entrepreneurs should think globally from the beginning. “If I were to rebuild Omio today, I would start here because there is so much growth and opportunity in India today. But the principles remain the same. You need to go after really hard problems and focus on solving them for a very long time,” he told YourStory . Shaam founded Omio after identifying a problem in global transportation: operators had separate systems for trains, buses, and ferries. After moving to Germany , he spent two and a half years working on the supply side before launching the company's first product. “Building a billion-dollar business is really hard. The stories of companies going from zero to a billion dollars very quickly are rare. Don’t get inspired by the exceptions as for most, it is a daily grind,” he said. Also Read Google Cloud’s Gemini voice AI wants to do more than just talk Think global from day one Shaam believes entrepreneurs need not wait until they have succeeded in India before expanding overseas. While some businesses cater to local needs, sectors such as education, healthcare, and deeptech offer opportunities across markets. “If your problem statement is already global, you should start early. We entered 30 countries in our first three or four years, even though people told us to win Germany first. That bet, despite the capital required and the mistakes we had to correct, probably helped make us become the company we are today,” he said. AI has also made international expansion easier. Shaam recalled that when Omio expanded in Germany, it employed around 30 people to handle translations. That work is now done by AI. However, lower barriers to entry also make it easier for competitors to copy products. Shaam believes entrepreneurs must therefore be more careful about where they invest their time and resources. “The onus moves from bias to action to judgement: what should I focus on? Which industry has a bigger moat? What will that moat look like 10 years from now? Starting is easy now but choosing what to pursue and committing to it is the hard part,” he said. Also Read Swiggy’s Q2: Net loss drops nearly 16%, revenue rises 36%; What sells? The celebrity or the product? AI may change distribution, but trust remains important Shaam said AI agents could change digital commerce, including how people book travel. However, widespread adoption will depend on bringing down costs and finding sustainable business models. “Consumers need these agents to be very cheap before they penetrate the market. There is a cost barrier and a business-model problem to solve. I see this as a major transformation and not an overnight event,” he explained. Even as more transactions move to AI agents, Shaam believes businesses will still need to deliver reliable services in the physical world. “Real life happens outside the internet. If an agent buys something or orders food, people need to trust that it will arrive every single time. Businesses that can solve these operational problems at scale will have something valuable to build on,” he said. For aspiring founders, his advice was to focus on solving a problem rather than on the appeal of becoming an entrepreneur . “Find a great problem. Don’t become an entrepreneur simply because you want to be one. This is a journey with long periods of darkness, and you need to be passionate enough about what you’re solving to keep going,” Shaam concluded.

title: Come for capability, not just capacity: Why Europe is looking to India for tech partnerships
content: Countries around the world are investing in their own semiconductor capabilities, AI models, and critical infrastructure. But building everything independently is neither practical nor always necessary. The challenge is to balance strategic sovereignty with international collaboration. This was the focus of a panel titled 'New tech alliances: Why the world's startups need India, and India needs the world' at TechSparks 2026 in Bengaluru on October 15. The discussion explored how Indian startups could work with international technology ecosystems and how global partners could build stronger ties with India. The panel featured Dr Angela Honegger, CEO and Consul General, Swissnex India (Switzerland); Jacobus Johannes 'Jaap' Veerman, Consul-General of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in Bangalore; and Peter Winther-Schmidt of the Consulate General of Denmark in Bangalore. The three representatives discussed programs that help startups access research, funding, markets, and partnerships across India and Europe. Balancing sovereignty and collaboration “We have to avoid equating strategic sovereignty with technological independence,” Winther-Schmidt said. While defence and security require a degree of sovereignty, he argued that areas such as talent, research, and technical interoperability benefit from international cooperation. He cited the European Union’s digital identity wallet, which he said is being built on the Indian technology stack with support from India. Veerman agreed that countries should identify what is critical to their own ecosystems while remaining open to partnerships. “I don't believe in isolation,” he said, emphasising the importance of finding the right partners. Honegger also stressed the need for cooperation. “If we want a fighting chance, we have to collaborate,” she said. Switzerland: Connecting research with startups Honegger described Swissnex as a science consulate with six locations worldwide, including Bengaluru. Its programs cover student and researcher exchanges, joint research funding for Swiss-Indian teams, bilateral startup exchanges, and market-validation camps. Under its startup program, 10 startups from each country visit the other to explore opportunities. She cited Suind, a company working across AI, drones, and agriculture, as an example of cross-border collaboration. Founded by a Swiss and an Indian entrepreneur, Suind initially opened a subsidiary in Bengaluru before switching the locations of its headquarters and subsidiary. “Technically, they are an Indian startup with a Swiss arm,” Honegger said. She encouraged Indian deeptech founders to consider moving part of their research and development operations to Switzerland while retaining their headquarters and manufacturing in India. Switzerland Innovation Parks, she said, offer access to research facilities, specialized technology platforms and public funding for joint R&D with Swiss institutions. Bengaluru-based robotics startup CynLr has already opened a subsidiary in one of these parks. Honegger also highlighted Apertus, Switzerland's open-source large language model, as an example of efforts to develop public AI infrastructure and prevent control of the technology from becoming concentrated “in the hands of a few corporates”. The Netherlands: Partnerships across the semiconductor industry Veerman spoke about the Netherlands’ semiconductor partnership with India, signed a couple of months earlier. The agreement covers semiconductor design, photonics, and advanced packaging, alongside manufacturing. He also said Dutch semiconductor equipment company ASML is establishing a presence in India. The Dutch consulate recently brought 17 startups to Semicon India as part of its efforts to strengthen technology ties between the two countries. Veerman also highlighted Brain Bridge, a programme connecting Dutch and Indian universities with Dutch companies already operating in India. Five Indian medtech startups have been selected for grants to explore opportunities in the Netherlands, while a cybersecurity mission is also being planned. “We look at Bangalore as the Silicon Valley of Asia,” Veerman said. Denmark: Supporting joint development “The key word for us is co-development,” said Winther-Schmidt, outlining Denmark’s approach to working with Indian startups. He highlighted the country's Water Challenge, which brings 10 selected Indian startups to Danish universities to work on AI-led water-cleaning solutions. The startups subsequently pitch their ideas to investors, with seed funding available. Denmark’s Green Strategic Partnership with India is also being renewed and expanded to include spacetech, deeptech, and defence technology. Winther-Schmidt pointed to a recent memorandum of understanding between DTU and IIT Madras, alongside efforts to bring venture capital and private equity investors from both countries together through a “financing bridge”. He also mentioned the Danish Impact Fund, which primarily provides loans for solutions that have a positive environmental impact. What Indian startups should keep in mind The three representatives offered practical advice for Indian founders looking to enter European markets. Winther-Schmidt urged startups to identify a specific market rather than approach Europe as a single destination. “Don't treat Europe as a single destination,” he said. He advised founders to validate their value proposition before entering a market, invest time in building relationships, and be willing to share their solutions with local partners rather than being overly protective of them. Honegger called for greater willingness among Indian companies to take risks when working with international startups. She wanted to see “more risk appetite... to become a co-creator and not just a receiver of innovation”. Swiss startups, she explained, often find that discussions with potential Indian partners end after a free pilot project. She argued that companies should be more willing to share the financial and operational risks of developing new technologies. The solution, she said, was to “share the risk that comes with innovation on multiple shoulders”. During the audience interaction, an 11-year-old founder asked how smaller companies could navigate European regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The panel advised startups to prepare early, choose their target markets carefully, and seek guidance from local partners, consultants, and consulates. India as a partner for capability Winther-Schmidt said Danish companies had traditionally viewed India primarily as a market that offered scale. But that, he argued, was only part of the opportunity. “You don’t come to India for capacity, you come actually to India for capability,” he said. He also emphasized that international partnerships should involve learning on both sides. “We don't have so much we can teach India... We can learn as much from them,” he added. Edited by Teja Lele

title: Waiting for an AI law is a poor compliance strategy
content: A bank has an AI system in place to flag suspicious transactions and take the call to freeze accounts. While the workflow has a human sign-off in place, clearing around 400 cases a day has resulted in the approval system becoming a formality. So, when a wrongly-frozen account takes the system to court, the bank becomes unable to prove what the human actually reviewed. This, unfortunately, is no longer a hypothetical scenario. On July 2, 2026, the Supreme Court of India quashed orders passed by the National Company Law Tribunal and the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal in the Pooja Ramesh Singh v. Jammu and Kashmir Bank Ltd. case . The orders had rested on citations generated by an AI tool and attributed to the Supreme Court itself. This directed the Bar Council of India to constitute a committee to prescribe disciplinary norms for advocates who file AI-generated citations. This is a business story as much as a legal one. Despite two tribunals and several rounds of proceedings, the parties had to carry the cost of a machine error that no human caught before filing. No AI statute was required to reach that outcome. Ordinary law, applied by judges, did the work. The regulators are moving faster than the legislature For most Indian companies, the sharper edge is coming from sectoral regulators rather than from the bench. In early June this year, the Reserve Bank of India gave banks and other regulated entities until June 30 to submit gap assessments on frontier-AI cyber risk. Instead of having the CISO to file the note, the RBI had asked the board to sign one. Later, on June 24, the RBI publicly released a draft 'Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management' to establish a comprehensive enterprise-wide model governance framework for the financial sector. Here 'models' extend to third-party models, AI, and machine learning (ML) systems used by commercial banks, small finance banks, payments banks, NBFCs, and other financial institutions. So if a lending decision is influenced by a model licensed from a vendor, the model risk sits on the one putting the AI system to use and not the vendor who built it. Meanwhile, India's legislative position is still a work-in-progress. On October 8, 2026, Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw had assured that the time has come for India to get an AI law. In a first step towards this, the government will be launching a consultation paper on regulating artificial intelligence. However, any business that is treating a pending law as its compliance milestone has their sequencing backwards. Even when the statute arrives, it can only land on top of existing case laws and sectoral circulars, not in place of them. Regardless of what law comes into place, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act takes full effect on May 13, 2027. Businesses will be held accountable even if the data is being processed by an external vendor as the DPDPA will be applicable wherever an AI system handles personal data. What does this ask of a business? Behind all the legal vocabulary, the requirements across all the domains are the same—one needs to show their working. For any consequential decision made by an AI system, organisations must be able to have the visibility regarding which model produced the output, what data it drew on, whether a retrieval step was involved, who reviewed it before it went out, and whether that record still exists six months later. Multiple Indian firms have written a policy, appointed a committee, and deployed systems but can still not answer any of the above questions. This is clearly an architecture question before it is a policy-related one. Recording the model version, prompt, retrieved data and human sign-off for every AI decision is only cheap if it is thoughtfully designed for. It can, however, become close to impossible to reconstruct afterwards. It is important for businesses to question an AI vendor before procuring a model. Does the system record which model version handled each request? Can that record be exported and retained? Where does inference physically happen? What happens to inputs after processing? Where in the workflow is a human required to act? Vendors that cannot answer plainly are transferring risk to the buyer. Build the record now There is not much point in waiting for an AI law. AI adoption is already in full swing, and when unprepared, the chain is only waiting to break. In the case of the tribunal matter, that chain broke at the review step. In an RBI-regulated entity, the chain is most likely to break earlier, at provenance, if nobody logged which version of which model scored the application. The current strategy, albeit unglamorous, is to ensure that the record of every AI-assisted decision made can survive being read aloud. So while the law may still be pending, the question is not. When it does come, the answer will have to exist already. (The article has been authored by Ramprakash Ramamoorthy, Director - AI Research, Zoho Corporation) (Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of YourStory.)

title: How Tagbin’s BRIXX uses AI to simplify building design and planning
content: Cost overruns, project delays, and disconnected design processes remain major challenges in India’s construction industry. At TechSparks 2026, ﻿ Tagbin ﻿ Co-founders Saurav Bhaik and Ankit Sinha, the company's CEO and CTO, respectively, demonstrated how their AI-powered product, BRIXX, aims to address these problems. BRIXX brings architectural drawings, building information modelling (BIM), mechanical, electrical and plumbing (MEP) systems, and project costing into a single workflow that users can control through natural-language prompts. “Construction is one of the least digitized industries, despite its scale. The two major problems we are trying to solve are cost and time overruns. Design systems often operate separately, with architectural drawings, MEP plans, and cost estimates unable to communicate with one another,” Bhaik said. He explained that conventional design processes rely heavily on two-dimensional drawings. BIM adoption, meanwhile, remains limited because the software requires specialised expertise to use. Building regulations that differ across states and municipalities add to the complexity. BRIXX aims to simplify the process by allowing users to describe a building in plain language or upload an image as a reference. The platform then generates building models, incorporates applicable regulations, estimates project costs, and creates construction schedules. Also Read MiCoB has built over 650 3D-printed structures across 13 states From prompts to building models During the demonstration, Sinha showed how BRIXX could use an image reference to generate a three-dimensional building information model complete with structural elements, foundations, and excavation plans. The system also incorporated MEP components, including electrical layouts, plumbing, and heating, ventilation and air-conditioning systems. “BIM is daunting because every discipline has its own experts and tools. What we are trying to build is a solution that brings the entire ecosystem into one tool and lets you simply talk to it,” Sinha said. Unlike conventional 3D visualisations, BIM models contain information about individual building elements, including structural properties and fire ratings. During the demonstration, BRIXX also took soil-bearing strength and the water table into account while generating foundations and excavation plans. Sinha then showed how users could modify designs through additional prompts. In one example, he asked the system to add a tower connected by a skybridge. The platform regenerated the model to reflect the changes. Also Read Ankit Maheshwari: AI, architecture and impact Bringing design, execution, and costs together Another part of the demonstration showed how BRIXX could coordinate different building systems. Changes that would traditionally require revisions across several drawings could be made through a single prompt. “Every element in the building needs to be accounted for, from columns and beams to electrical systems, excavation, and labour. All of this comes together in the bill of quantities. The idea is to connect the entire process, so design changes, technical requirements, and costs are reflected in one place,” Sinha said. The demonstration ended with a bill of quantities (BOQ) that estimated the showcased project’s cost at approximately Rs 95 crore. Edited by Megha Reddy

title: Pixxel deepens US push with dedicated federal subsidiary
content: Bengaluru-based spacetech startup Pixxel has established Pixxel Federal, a US subsidiary aimed at expanding its business with American civilian, defence and intelligence agencies. The move reflects the growing role of privately operated satellites in government operations, from national security and resource mapping to environmental monitoring. It also signals Pixxel’s ambition to move beyond supplying specialised satellite imagery towards offering a broader combination of sensing technologies, software, and satellite systems. The subsidiary will build on the company’s existing engagements with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) and the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO). “The US government market represents a significant opportunity for Pixxel as we expand our capabilities beyond hyperspectral imaging into advanced sensing technologies, software, and satellite systems,” said Pixxel's founder and CEO Awais Ahmed, adding that the new unit will enable it to work more closely with federal agencies, understand their mission requirements, and deliver solutions tailored to their needs. A key part of the company’s offering is hyperspectral imaging, a technology that captures reflected light across hundreds of narrow wavelength bands, including those beyond the visible spectrum. Different materials absorb and reflect light differently, producing identifiable patterns known as spectral signatures. These can help distinguish minerals, vegetation, and other materials in ways that conventional satellite imagery may not. The US Geological Survey uses hyperspectral surveys to identify minerals, soils and vegetation, illustrating the technology’s potential in resource exploration and environmental research. Pixxels sees applications in defence and intelligence, including camouflage detection, terrain assessment, and identification of activities of interest. Other potential uses include locating critical minerals and rare earth elements, monitoring crops, and tracking environmental changes. Allyson Jenkins, who previously led Pixxel’s public-sector business, has been appointed the CEO of Pixxel Federal. The subsidiary’s board includes retired US Army Lieutenant General Ray Palumbo, former Northrop Grumman executive Patrick M. Antkowiak, and former senior intelligence official Frank X. Avila. Pixxel also plans to establish an office in the Washington, DC, metropolitan area. The company’s government relationships have developed over the past two years. In September 2024, Pixxel was selected for NASA’s Commercial SmallSat Data Acquisition Programme, a multi-provider arrangement through which the agency purchases commercial Earth-observation data. In May 2026, the NRO named Pixxel, alongside EarthDaily and ICEYE under its Strategic Commercial Enhancements initiative to expand access to commercial sensing capabilities. The wider industry is moving in the same direction. US policy has long encouraged government agencies to use commercial remote-sensing capabilities where practical, while retaining national-security safeguards. More recently, the Department of Defense and US Space Force have outlined strategies to integrate commercial space services into national security operations.

title: Hero MotoCorp to increase EV capacity to 80,000 units per month by Q2 FY28
content: India's largest two-wheeler maker Hero MotoCorp plans to increase the production capacity of its Vida electric two-wheeler to 45,000 units by March-end and further boost it to 80,000 units by the second quarter of FY28, according to a senior company official. Hero MotoCorp CEO Harshavardhan Chitale said supply is a constraint, with dealer inventory of just around one day. "Our dealer inventory continues to be low. We are working with a dealer stock of just about one day, which shows that we are still capacity constrained and there is a strong demand for our product," he said. The automaker's electric two-wheeler capacity was at 15,000 units per month at the end of the financial year 2026. The capacity currently stands at 30,000 units. "We have already doubled the capacity. We are well on our way to take it to 45,000 units a month in the fourth quarter. Looking at the demand, we are expanding further, which will take our capacity to over 80,000 units a month by the second quarter of FY28," he said. The electric two-wheeler market is witnessing strong demand with penetration exceeding 20% in the scooter segment. As per the data from FADA, registration of electric two-wheelers jumped 33% in the Navratri period to 75,758 units, while the total two-wheeler registration fell almost 3% to 8.34 lakh units. TVS Motor is the market leader, followed by Bajaj Auto, Ather Energy and Hero MotoCorp. All the top four OEMs are ramping up their capacity to meet the surge in demand. Both TVS and Bajaj are increasing capacity to 80,000 units per month by March, while Ather is targeting around 95,000 units capacity by July-September with its new facility. "Right now the industry as a whole is definitely capacity constrained. There is far more demand. As and when anyone brings on capacity online and if the product is good, there is an immediate bump up in share," Chitale said. Hero MotoCorp's capacity ramp comes as the automaker looks to expand its Vida distribution. Currently, it is selling Vida at around 700 of its retail outlets. "When we put it in the context that we have close to 8,500 points of sale, there is a lot more retail expansion that is going to come to further drive the growth," he added.

title: Govt notifies National Social Security Board for gig, platform workers
content: The government has notified the National Social Security Board for unorganised workers and gig and platform workers, which will design, monitor, and recommend targeted welfare schemes to bridge the social security gap. Gig workers are those who perform work or participate in a work arrangement and earn from such activities outside the traditional employer-employee relationship. Platform workers are those who engage in work through or with online platforms. In a move towards ensuring comprehensive social security for India's massive informal workforce, the Ministry of Labour & Employment has notified the constitution of the National Social Security Board for Unorganised Workers and Gig & Platform Workers, a ministry statement said. Established under the statutory framework of the Code on Social Security, this marks a historic shift by integrating digital gig and platform professionals into India's formal welfare architecture, the ministry said. The Board will be presided over by the Union Minister for Labour & Employment and comprise representatives from the Central and state governments, prominent aggregator companies, employers, civil society organisations, workers' unions, and gig and platform worker associations. The Board is mandated to design, monitor, and recommend targeted welfare schemes to bridge the social security gap for millions of gig and platform workers, alongside traditional unorganised workers. The National Social Security Board shall meet at least thrice a year and observe the rules of procedure relating to the transaction of business at its meetings, as prescribed by the Central government. The National Social Security Board shall recommend to the Central government the framing of suitable schemes for different sections of unorganised workers, gig workers and platform workers. The board will advise the Central government on such matters arising out of the administration of this Code as may be referred to; It will monitor such social welfare schemes for unorganised workers, gig workers and platform workers administered by the Central government. It will review the record keeping functions performed at the state level and also review the expenditure from the fund and account. It will also undertake other functions as are assigned to it by the Central government from time to time.

title: India needs a digital goods marketplace and control of its distribution layer, say Indus Appstore and Eloelo
content: India’s app-first economy still lacks a thriving marketplace for digital goods, and fixing that is as much a question of sovereignty as of technology, according to speakers at the 17th edition of YourStory’s TechSparks. Speaking on a panel titled “India’s digital economy 2.0: Public tech, AI sovereignty, and the next 500 million”, Priya Narasimhan, Chief Business Officer at Indus Appstore, said the country’s mobile-first habits should have produced a large digital goods market, but have not. She blamed distribution monopolies held by Google and Apple and the economics of their 15% to 30% billing commissions, which make lower-priced digital products unviable. Web stores, the other route, suffer from user friction and low reach, she said. Narasimhan argued that digital sovereignty is about how and where consumers meet technology. She named three layers India must control: discovery and distribution through app marketplaces, monetisation and billing, and a data trust and consent framework. She pointed to the Epic Games and Google dispute in the US as proof of what happens when developers depend on gatekeepers. She stressed, however, that sovereignty does not mean rebuilding every base layer. The aim, she said, is to plug into global technology on India’s terms. Sagar Gaonkar, CTO of Eloelo Group, said India’s strengths lie in its data, its cultural variety and its creative and platform-building talent. Chips and large language models can be built upon, he said, with value added for India and then exported. He added that security cannot be an afterthought as more tools are hosted outside the country. On AI, Gaonkar said it helps microdrama platforms decide what to greenlight before a frame is shot, and personalise what viewers see. He also pointed to stories that adapt to a viewer’s preferences. Narasimhan said app stores must become hybrid platforms: simple and familiar on the surface for most Indians, and addressable by AI agents at the back end, so that developers can scale whether users tap an icon or ask a chatbot. Both speakers challenged the idea that Bharat is a low-spending audience. Narasimhan recalled that PhonePe’s gold category scaled only after it allowed purchases of Rs 10 a day. Gaonkar said Indian users are value-conscious rather than unwilling to pay, and need a softer landing to experience a product before paying. Narasimhan also urged founders to talk to users rather than rely only on analytics. Responding to audience questions, Narasimhan said Indus aims to cut the commission burden on developers, and rejected the suggestion that Indians do not value digital goods, citing microdramas, OTT and gaming. She said platforms should not let discovery become purely pay-to-play. On fraudulent installs, she said vetting combines automated checks with human review and constant monitoring, but admitted that no system is foolproof.

title: Binance estimates $6.3B impact from security breach, freezes $3B in crypto assets
content: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has estimated the total impact of a major security incident at around $6.3 billion, with approximately $3 billion worth of affected digital assets frozen on-chain in coordination with blockchain partners. In an update issued on October 30, 2026, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume said its preliminary investigation suggested that the incident may have originated from a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer. The attacker allegedly used the access to enter a service container and submit unauthorised withdrawal transactions. However, a subsequent investigation uncovered additional points of breach, indicating that the attack was more complex than initially suspected. "This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it. We are still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them," the company said in a statement. Binance CEO Richard Teng, in a separate communication to users, clarified that the attacker had not simply exploited an engineer's permissions and that the incident was not a single "one-click" action. He added that the investigation had not attributed responsibility to any individual. The exchange said it had found no evidence of any compromise involving wallet private keys. Binance has estimated the total impact at approximately $6.3 billion, of which around $3 billion worth of assets have been frozen on-chain so far in coordination with blockchain partners. Binance has temporarily suspended withdrawals while undertaking a security revamp of its withdrawal service and related addresses. It has also revoked authorisation for the affected address and engaged law enforcement agencies and blockchain intelligence firms to trace and recover the funds. The exchange said deposits remain unaffected and continue to operate normally. It added that outflows had ceased after it paused withdrawals. Binance expects to resume withdrawal services within 45 hours as it completes the security checks and remediation process. Assuring customers that their assets remain safe, Binance said it would cover all losses arising from the incident through its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and the company's own funds. "We'll share a detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and every fact is verified," Teng said, adding that the exchange would also publish an updated Proof of Reserves once the remediation process was complete. Binance said its teams were working closely with law enforcement agencies and blockchain intelligence partners to identify those responsible and recover the affected assets. The company has urged users to rely exclusively on its official communication channels for further updates as the investigation progresses. (The copy has been updated with the latest developments)
