title: How Stelcore helps brands go global without building everything from scratch
content: Selling internationally can open new markets for a brand. But behind every order lies a web of logistics, payments, product certifications, customs rules, and local compliance requirements. As businesses expand, managing these moving parts across countries can become a challenge of its own. This is where Stelcore Group steps in. At TechSparks 2026, Founder and Chairman Bharat Mandot explained how the company connects trade infrastructure, compliance, and technology to help brands navigate global markets. One integration for multiple markets “Stelcore is about trade infrastructure, compliance infrastructure, and technology for global markets,” Mandot said, describing how the company supports brands entering international markets. Stelcore says it has worked with more than 30,000 brands and sellers from India over 14 years of operations. It has a presence in more than 14 countries, including the US, Canada, the UK, Europe, the UAE, Singapore, Australia and South Korea. Rather than requiring brands to establish a separate entity in every destination market, Stelcore brings together importing, storage, payments, last-mile delivery and returns. When an order arrives through a marketplace or a brand’s direct-to-consumer (D2C) store, the system coordinates warehouse allocation and delivery. Stelcore’s local entity can act as the seller of record and importer, handling applicable compliance and logistics requirements. Mandot described the model as a way to give brands international reach through one operating partner, without having to rebuild the process for every new market. Compliance before the shipment moves Cross-border commerce involves more than getting products from one warehouse to another. Brands must also meet destination-market requirements for product registration, packaging, labelling, certifications and technical documentation. Mandot demonstrated Stelcore’s compliance assessment tool, which allows sellers to select a destination country and product category to identify relevant tests, reports, import procedures and certifications. “The tool is free of cost,” he said, explaining that sellers can assess requirements for a product category across different countries in 10 to 15 minutes. The platform also provides a central repository for product information, including HSN codes and other market-specific details. This can help brands respond to queries from logistics providers and customs authorities, reducing the risk of shipments being held up over documentation. Mandot distinguished between business and product compliance. While businesses can choose different arrangements, such as working with a distributor or a local entity, product compliance remains necessary regardless of the operating model. Connecting the entire order journey Stelcore’s technology brings order processing, warehouse allocation, and last-mile delivery into one view. Brands can access this information through an application programming interface (API) and build their own management systems around it. The platform also supports services such as tax registration, VAT, customs procedures, intellectual property support, and payment reconciliation. For brands entering unfamiliar markets, the challenge is not simply finding customers. It is building the operational infrastructure to serve them consistently. Stelcore’s approach is to connect these moving parts through one operating partner, helping businesses expand internationally without having to assemble every layer themselves.

title: D2C brands don't need an AI team to get discovered and grow, says Shopflo
content: AI assistants are becoming shopping destinations, but keeping up with them can stretch lean teams. Shoppers are beginning to turn to AI assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude to discover products, compare options and make buying decisions. For direct-to-consumer (D2C) brands, this raises a new question: how do they stay visible as shopping behaviour changes, without building an in-house AI team? At TechSparks 2026, Mihir Shah, Chief Business Officer at Shopflo by Pine Labs, presented two ways the company aims to help brands tackle this challenge: agentic commerce, which connects product catalogues to AI-powered discovery and shopping surfaces, and AI agents that help businesses improve growth and operational efficiency. “You don't need an AI team to figure out growth or efficiency for you. You need Shopflo,” Shah said. Getting products in front of AI shoppers Brands have spent years building visibility through search engines, marketplaces, and social media. AI assistants are adding another discovery channel, where shoppers can describe what they need and receive product recommendations. Shopflo's agentic commerce offering aims to make participating brands' catalogues available across AI-native platforms, including ChatGPT, Claude and other emerging interfaces, said Shah. Through integrations, the company streams product catalogue information to these surfaces, allowing shoppers to discover relevant products and, where supported, proceed towards checkout. For instance, a shopper looking for festive gifts under Rs 2,000 could discover products from a participating brand through an AI assistant. Shopflo's integration with Pine Labs' payments infrastructure is designed to support transactions through these experiences. Shah argued that brands will need to look beyond traditional discovery channels as consumer behaviour evolves. However, AI visibility does not replace search engine optimisation (SEO), which continues to contribute to website traffic. AI agents put growth decisions in context Discovery is only one part of running a D2C business. Brands must also balance conversion rates, average order value, returns, customer retention and profitability, often using separate tools for each function, said Shah. Shopflo's Growth Orchestrator, which Shah said was available in beta, aims to bring these decisions together. Brands can define their priorities, whether that means pursuing growth or protecting profitability, and receive recommendations based on their store's performance data. During the demonstration, Shah showed how the system could identify a drop-off between address entry and payment, suggest a fee-transparency banner and propose an experiment to test whether the change improves conversions. Brands can review recommendations, set limits and approve experiments before scaling them. They can also decide how much autonomy to give the agents. “How much or how little to use the agents is under your control,” Shah said. For D2C businesses working with lean teams, the proposition is less about adopting every new AI tool and more about making existing growth decisions easier to manage. Shopflo's approach combines AI-led discovery with tools that help brands act on their own business goals, while leaving the final decisions in their hands.

title: Too much code, too little shipped: Why AI needs a software factory
content: AI can generate code faster than ever, but getting it tested and reviewed and into production is a different challenge. Engineering teams are increasingly using AI agents to write code, fix bugs, and build features. But faster coding does not necessarily mean faster software delivery. As code generation accelerates, reviews pile up, testing slows down, and teams struggle to coordinate the growing volume of changes. At TechSparks 2026, Tushar Mathur, CEO of Forge Code, explored this problem in his session, Anatomy of a software factory. He explained how AI-native engineering organisations can move beyond automating individual coding tasks to building systems that manage the entire software development lifecycle. “Just because code is becoming easy and faster to generate doesn't mean your overall SDLC becomes faster,” Mathur said. From coding assistants to software factories The traditional software development process focused heavily on writing code efficiently. Teams spent time defining requirements, preparing specifications and designing architecture to reduce the effort needed during implementation, he said. With AI taking over more coding work, the bottlenecks are moving elsewhere. Mathur described how organisations can end up with large volumes of pull requests awaiting review, longer testing cycles and more bugs than existing regression suites can catch. Hiring more engineers or running more AI agents is not necessarily the answer. More people can increase coordination costs, while adding agents without effective feedback loops can generate code that overwhelms the systems responsible for reviewing and testing it. “The reason why this happens is because there's no signal,” Mathur said, explaining why simply connecting automated steps does not create an effective software factory. An assembly line that learns Mathur presented Forge Code as a software factory that coordinates AI agents across the development lifecycle. The process begins with triaging requests, creating specifications and implementing features. Agents then verify changes before they move towards deployment, with human engineers stepping in when decisions or feedback are needed. The system also monitors production, using the resulting insights to inform future tasks. This creates a feedback loop in which the factory can identify problems, improve its workflows and generate new work from what it learns. Mathur said Forge Code was running around 100 agents in the background during his presentation, working on features, compatibility and bug detection. He outlined six principles for an effective software factory: autonomous operation, scalability, cost efficiency, measurability, self-improvement and alignment with business goals. The last principle is particularly important. Instead of treating every request as a coding task, the factory should work towards outcomes such as improving customer retention or meeting compliance requirements. Teams can then prioritise features based on the value they deliver. Engineers become supervisors In this model, engineers spend less time directing every task and more time monitoring outcomes, reviewing signals and improving the system. Business leaders can also contribute requests and priorities directly, allowing the factory to translate organisational goals into a development backlog. Writing code faster is great. Shipping better software is the real win. For engineering teams, the trick is turning AI-powered speed into reliable products, measurable gains and business results.

title: Delhivery reports net profit of Rs 41 crore in Q2 of FY27
content: Logistics company Delhivery reported a net profit of Rs 40.63 crore during the second quarter of FY27, compared to a loss of Rs 50.49 crore in the same quarter of the previous fiscal year. Revenue rose 19.8% to Rs 3,066.38 crore from Rs 2,559.3 crore in the year-ago period. Delhivery, in a statement, said it could register a strong performance despite the pressure of inflation. Express parcel volume recorded a 32% YoY growth touching 325 million shipments for the second quarter. The part truck load segment recorded a 14% YoY growth. The logistics company said its new businesses are ramping up faster than originally planned. Delhivery Local, an on-demand, intracity logistics and courier service, is now live across eight cities and is on track to exceed its previous guidance of an annual revenue run rate of Rs 250 crore by Q4FY27, along with improved contribution margins. Financial Service has also begun early monetisation of its vendor ecosystem, and is developing co-lending partnerships to broaden financial access to vendor partners through an asset-light approach, the company said. Delhivery said early investments in AI are beginning to bear fruit, with improved sales productivity and customer onboarding and faster resolution of claims and disputes and fraud detection. Delhivery Robotics, an inhouse automation lab, has commenced production of customised autonomous vehicles for in-facility movement operations. It has also begun testing robotics systems across under-the-roof operations, in partnership with global leaders in the physical AI domain. Delhivery expressed confidence going into the second half of the fiscal year, despite a volatile macro environment due to rising fuel prices, labour availability issues, and multiple statutory changes. It said its network service levels heading into the festive season have been the best, with improved profitability.

title: India’s new-age manufacturers to benefit from $3 trillion global AI investment cycle: Avendus Capital
content: India’s new-age manufacturing sector could benefit significantly from a $3 trillion global AI infrastructure investment cycle, according to a report by Avendus Capital. The investment banking firm has identified defence and aerospace, space technology, robotics and automation, semiconductors, energy transition, and advanced materials as the sectors poised to drive India’s next phase of industrial growth, offering key opportunities for domestic companies. The report highlighted 2027–28 as a critical period for commercialisation as companies move from policy support and project approvals towards production. The opportunity is being driven by rising global investments in AI infrastructure, increasing demand for energy infrastructure, and growing geopolitical security concerns. India’s domestic demand, engineering talent and policy framework could help manufacturers reduce import dependence and build globally competitive capabilities. “India's new-age manufacturing opportunity is substantial, but its right-to-win manifests in select segments,” said Koushik Bhattacharyya, Managing Director and Head of Industrials Investment Banking at Avendus Capital. With more than 80% of the $3 trillion AI infrastructure investment yet to be deployed globally, India has an opportunity to capitalise on its domestic demand base, engineering capabilities, and policy support, he said. Semiconductors and space technology are among the segments showing significant growth potential. India’s semiconductor consumption is projected to more than double from $49.5 billion in 2025 to $106.5 billion by 2030, creating opportunities in chip design, packaging, testing, and specialised materials. India’s space economy is expected to expand more than threefold, from approximately $13 billion in 2025 to $44 billion by 2033. Domestic defence production is projected to reach around $31.6 billion by 2030, while the robotics market could grow nearly fourfold to $4.6 billion by 2030, supported by wider adoption and import substitution. The report also expects India’s clean-energy manufacturing ecosystem to move further upstream over the next five years. By the end of the decade, the country could establish an integrated solar manufacturing chain spanning ingots to modules, several gigawatt-hour-scale battery cell plants, and commercial production of indigenous electrolyser stacks and rare-earth-free motor technology. Advanced materials represent another emerging opportunity, with rising domestic demand and heavy import dependence creating scope for local capacity building. Recycling is expected to scale first, followed by battery materials, while rare-earth magnet manufacturing could advance with policy support. The coming years will test India’s ability to translate these opportunities into commercially viable manufacturing capabilities, the report said.

title: 7 Things emotionally intelligent people do differently
content: Emotional intelligence is not about staying calm all the time or knowing exactly what to say in every situation. It is about understanding your emotions, recognising how others feel, and choosing how to respond rather than reacting impulsively. In everyday life, emotional intelligence can influence how we handle disagreements, build relationships, respond to criticism, and navigate difficult situations. People who develop this skill are often better equipped to communicate clearly, understand different perspectives, and manage their emotions constructively. The good news is that emotional intelligence is not simply something you are born with. Many of its essential skills can be practised and strengthened over time. 7 Things emotionally intelligent people do differently 1. They pause before reacting When someone criticises them, disagrees with them, or says something hurtful, emotionally intelligent people try not to respond immediately out of anger. They understand that an emotional reaction can sometimes make a difficult situation worse. Instead of sending an impulsive message or saying something they might regret, they give themselves time to process what happened. For example, if a colleague points out a mistake, they may initially feel embarrassed or defensive. Rather than immediately arguing, they consider whether the feedback is useful and how they can respond constructively. Pausing does not mean ignoring your emotions or pretending that nothing bothers you. It means allowing yourself to feel an emotion without letting it make every decision for you. The lesson: You cannot always control what you feel, but you can practise choosing how you respond. 2. They try to understand before judging Emotionally intelligent people recognise that their perspective is not the only possible explanation for a situation. When someone behaves unexpectedly, they try to understand the circumstances before making assumptions about their intentions. For instance, if a friend takes hours to reply to a message, it is easy to assume that they are losing interest or deliberately ignoring you. However, they might be dealing with work, family responsibilities, or something they have not shared. Instead of immediately jumping to conclusions, emotionally intelligent people leave room for other explanations and communicate when clarification is needed. This does not mean excusing repeated disrespect or ignoring unhealthy behaviour. It means distinguishing between what you know and what you are assuming. The lesson: Understanding another person's perspective can prevent unnecessary misunderstandings and help you respond more fairly. Also Read 5 Books that uncover the reasons behind emotional exhaustion 3. They can admit when they are wrong Admitting a mistake is not always easy. It can challenge your pride, make you feel uncomfortable, or force you to reconsider something you strongly believed. However, emotionally intelligent people understand that being wrong does not make them less valuable. When they hurt someone, misunderstand a situation, or make a poor decision, they try to acknowledge their role instead of shifting all the blame onto others. A genuine apology involves more than saying, "I'm sorry you felt that way." It means recognising the impact of your actions, taking responsibility where appropriate, and making an effort to behave differently. They also understand that an apology does not automatically entitle them to forgiveness. Rebuilding trust often requires consistent actions over time. The lesson: Taking responsibility for your mistakes is a sign of self-awareness, not weakness. 4. They set boundaries without feeling obligated to explain everything Emotionally intelligent people understand that being considerate does not mean making themselves available to everyone at all times. They recognise their limits and communicate them clearly. If they are exhausted, overwhelmed, or unable to take on another responsibility, they can say no without turning the decision into a lengthy justification. For example, they might tell a friend, "I care about you, but I don't have the energy for a conversation tonight. Can we talk tomorrow?" This approach respects both their own needs and the other person's feelings. Healthy boundaries also apply to work, family expectations, personal time, and emotional availability. They help people maintain relationships without constantly ignoring their own well-being. Setting boundaries does not mean becoming selfish or indifferent. It means understanding that care and availability are not the same thing. The lesson: You can care about other people without taking responsibility for every expectation they have of you. 5. They listen to understand, not just to reply In many conversations, people spend more time preparing their responses than listening to what the other person is saying. Emotionally intelligent people try to avoid this habit. They pay attention to the speaker's words, ask questions when something is unclear, and consider the feelings behind the message. For example, when a friend talks about a difficult day, they do not immediately offer advice or compare the experience with their own. They might first ask, "Do you want me to help you figure it out, or do you just need someone to listen?" This simple question can make conversations more supportive because it acknowledges that different people need different kinds of help. Active listening also involves noticing when your assumptions are influencing your interpretation of what someone says. The lesson: Sometimes, the most helpful response is not advice but the willingness to listen without rushing to fix everything. 6. They do not depend on everyone's approval Emotionally intelligent people care about their relationships, but they do not treat universal approval as a requirement for feeling secure. They understand that people have different expectations, values, and opinions. As a result, not everyone will agree with their choices, and that disagreement does not automatically mean they have done something wrong. For instance, choosing a different career path, declining an invitation, or expressing an unpopular opinion may disappoint someone. Emotionally intelligent people can consider that person's perspective without automatically abandoning their own judgement. They remain open to constructive criticism while recognising that criticism is not always accurate or fair. This balance helps them make decisions based on their values rather than constantly changing themselves to avoid disappointing others. The lesson: You can value other people's opinions without allowing those opinions to define your self-worth. 7. They recognise that other people's emotions are not always their responsibility Emotionally intelligent people can show empathy without assuming they must fix every uncomfortable feeling another person experiences. They understand the difference between supporting someone and taking complete responsibility for that person's emotional state. For example, if they respectfully decline a request and the other person becomes disappointed, they can acknowledge that disappointment without automatically reversing their decision. Similarly, if a friend is upset, they can offer support while recognising that they cannot control how the friend processes the situation. This does not mean ignoring the consequences of their own actions. If they have caused harm, taking responsibility matters. The distinction is between being accountable for your behaviour and trying to manage every emotion someone else feels. Learning this difference can make relationships healthier and reduce the pressure to keep everyone happy. The lesson: Empathy means caring about how others feel, not believing you must control how they feel. Final thoughts Emotional intelligence is often reflected in small, everyday decisions: pausing before responding, listening without interrupting, admitting mistakes, and setting boundaries respectfully. These behaviours do not mean emotionally intelligent people never feel jealous, angry, insecure, or overwhelmed. They experience difficult emotions like everyone else. The difference is that they can gradually learn to recognise those emotions and respond to them more thoughtfully. You do not have to master all seven habits at once. Start by noticing one situation in which you tend to react impulsively, seek approval, or struggle to express your needs. With practice, greater self-awareness and more thoughtful communication can help you build healthier relationships with both yourself and the people around you.

title: IG Defence, Oman’s MSA Global explore production of drone systems
content: India’s IG Defence and Oman-based MSA Global have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to explore the co-development and local manufacture of drone and counter-drone systems for Oman and the wider Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC). The agreement links India’s defence-export ambitions with Gulf security concerns, but remains exploratory and does not confirm an order, factory or deployment. Reuters reported in October that Iran and allied groups had carried out at least 135 drone and missile attacks against 84 infrastructure sites across Gulf Arab states since the United States and Israel began bombing Iran in February. “The evolving security environment in the Gulf reinforces the importance of strengthening indigenous defence capabilities and developing resilient regional manufacturing ecosystems,” MSA Global chairman Col M. S. Atwal (Retd.) said. The MoU was exchanged during the India-Oman Defence Industry Cooperation Seminar in Muscat in October. India and Oman already have established defence ties, including joint exercises involving all three branches of India’s armed forces. IG Defence, formerly known as IG Drones, said discussions will cover three systems. KAL is described by the company as a one-way attack unmanned aerial system with a stated range of up to 1,000 kilometres. BAJ is an unmanned aerial interceptor intended for counter-unmanned aircraft system (C-UAS) use, while JWALA is a micro-missile system under development for counter-drone applications. “Our partnership with MSA Global reflects our vision of taking India's indigenous defence technologies to global markets through strategic industrial collaboration,” IG Defence Chief Executive Officer Bodhisattwa Sanghapriya said. The agreement comes as India’s defence exports reached Rs 23,622 crore in the 2024-25 financial year, up 12.04% from the previous year. On October 26, India also approved in principle Rs 2,12,000 crore in military acquisitions, including counter-drone systems and long-range attack drones. Other companies are responding to similar demand. In May, France’s CS Group won a NATO contract to supply two counter-drone systems for its Brussels headquarters. In August, US firm Powerus announced a separate contract for counter-drone technology to protect Middle Eastern energy infrastructure.

title: AI that speaks, codes and takes action: Inside Google Cloud’s Gemini masterclass
content: Imagine handing AI 80,000 files and getting back a presentation with charts, images and a clear narrative. Or asking it to build a detailed 3D scene using code, without dedicated rendering software. These are examples of AI moving beyond answering prompts to taking on complex tasks. At TechSparks 2026, Rajesh Shivani, Head of AI Customer Engineering for Digital Natives, Startups and ITES at Google Cloud, demonstrated how Gemini is being used across voice AI, autonomous agents and software development. His masterclass explored how businesses can move from using AI for answers to delegating work to it. From chatbots to autonomous coworkers AI tools initially gained traction through chat interfaces that answered questions. The next stage is agentic AI, where systems can plan tasks, access information, and use tools to act on a user’s behalf. “An agent is nothing now but a model plus a harness,” Rajesh said, describing the infrastructure around a model that manages memory, context, permissions and task execution. Building useful agents requires four elements: a goal, clear instructions, relevant knowledge and tools to act on that knowledge. A company’s internal data is particularly important because general-purpose models may not have access to its specific processes or customer information. Shivani also discussed Google’s Open Knowledge Format (OKF), which aims to give organisations a structured way to make information accessible to AI agents. Voice AI takes on real-world tasks Voice was one of the key demonstrations. A system developed for Singapore-based Grab helped passengers and drivers coordinate airport pickups despite language barriers. The demo highlighted how voice AI could support interactions across more than 85 languages. Another example showed AI dubbing an English video into Marathi and Malayalam while matching lip movements and facial expressions. Such capabilities could help businesses produce multilingual training material, marketing videos and customer communications with fewer production steps. “Voice is becoming the new user interface,” Rajesh Shivani stated, pointing to the growing role of voice-based interactions for customers and employees. He also showcased a virtual banking assistant created for Citibank’s retail banking experience. In the demonstration, the AI avatar explained options for a maturing certificate of deposit and submitted a renewal after the customer selected a 12-month term. AI that builds, checks and creates Beyond voice, Shivani highlighted Google’s tools for coding and cybersecurity. Antigravity helps developers build applications, while CodeMender can identify code vulnerabilities, generate patches and test them in a sandbox. In one demonstration, Gemini analysed 80,000 files from NASA’s open archives, including Mars weather readings and helicopter telemetry, and produced a presentation using a supplied template and design guidelines. Another demo showed a model generating a detailed 3D library scene using Python and NumPy, without dedicated rendering software or external assets. For businesses weighing the cost of AI adoption, Shivani stressed that the most powerful model is not always necessary. “You don’t need to have a frontier model for everything,” he said, explaining why simpler tasks can use faster, lower-cost models. Preparing businesses for AI agents As agents take on more work, businesses will need to rethink how their systems handle permissions, security, costs and automated activity. Shivani urged organisations to consider a future in which agents, not just people, interact with their systems. Developers, he suggested, could increasingly become managers of agents rather than handling every step themselves. The challenge is no longer simply choosing a capable AI model. It is giving agents the right knowledge and tools, while ensuring they can complete tasks reliably and safely.

title: Lighthouse Communities Foundation lists on BSE’s Social Stock Exchange to scale youth livelihoods
content: For many young people, finding a job begins long before they enter a classroom. Understanding their strengths, identifying career options and building the confidence to pursue them can be just as important as acquiring skills. Lighthouse Communities Foundation (LCF), a non-profit working to improve livelihood opportunities for underserved youth, has marked its listing on the Bombay Stock Exchange’s (BSE) Social Stock Exchange (SSE). The listing follows a public issue of Zero Coupon Zero Principal (ZCZP) instruments held from September 30 to October 14, 2026. The foundation marked the milestone with a bell-ringing ceremony at BSE on October 29, attended by government officials, corporate partners, philanthropic organisations and its leadership. A new route to fund social impact The listing gives Lighthouse Communities Foundation access to a regulated platform through which corporates, corporate social responsibility (CSR) partners and impact-focused supporters can fund its work. ZCZP instruments differ from conventional investments. They pay no interest and return no principal, meaning subscribers contribute towards defined social outcomes rather than receiving financial returns. The platform also requires organisations to report how funds are used and the progress achieved. “Models that combine career guidance, skilling and employer linkages, supported by transparent funding, are exactly what our youth need to find stable livelihoods,” said Manisha Verma, IAS, Additional Chief Secretary, Skills, Employment, Entrepreneurship and Innovation Department, Government of Maharashtra, who attended the ceremony as chief guest. The listing comes as LCF looks to expand a model that combines government infrastructure and corporate support to deliver livelihood programmes. Helping young people find the right career path LCF’s Lighthouse programme begins by helping participants understand their aspirations and strengths before they choose a vocational training pathway. The foundation works with partner organisations offering courses aligned with available employment opportunities. Since its establishment in 2015, LCF has reached more than 2.9 lakh young people across six states. Its Lighthouse programme operates 51 centres, with women accounting for nearly 60% of enrolments. According to the foundation, 77% of placed youth remain employed a year after placement. The model brings together state and local governments, which provide infrastructure, and corporate partners, which fund operations and implementation. Dr Ganesh Natarajan, Co-Founder and Chairman of LCF, said the listing was an important milestone in the organisation’s work with underserved youth. “Ringing the bell at BSE today is a proud moment for everyone who has been part of the Lighthouse journey, from our young people and partner organisations to the corporates and governments who backed us early,” he said. He added that LCF aims to reach one million young people nationally, helping them choose and build the careers they aspire to. Pune is the next focus for expansion The proceeds from the issue will support LCF’s work in Pune, with a target of helping 500 young people develop career awareness, confidence and job-readiness skills to access sustained livelihoods. In Maharashtra, the foundation works with the Skills, Employment, Entrepreneurship and Innovation Department and the Directorate of Vocational Education and Training under a memorandum of understanding signed in January 2023. Its initiatives include a Lighthouse centre at ITI Mulund and Model Career Centres in Thane and Nagpur. The partnership has provided career counselling to more than 5,500 young people, skilling to over 2,075 and placement support to more than 3,200. The next phase is expected to extend the programme to additional Model Career Centres and industrial training institutes, including those in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar and Amravati. Lighthouse Communities Foundation will report its progress through the Social Stock Exchange’s disclosure framework. For the foundation, the listing creates an opportunity to connect funding with measurable outcomes as it works to expand access to meaningful and sustained livelihoods.

title: NIT Rourkela scientists develop lead-free light-emitting materials for safer lighting and security applications
content: Researchers from the National Institute of Technology Rourkela (NIT Rourkela), in collaboration with researchers from IIT Guwahati, IIT Bombay, and NISER Bhubaneswar, have developed new materials that can emit different colours of light under ultraviolet (UV) light exposure. These materials respond to changes in heat and moisture and can have applications in security systems, sensors, and lighting technologies. The research investigated bismuth-based compounds as safer alternatives to lead-based photoluminescent materials, which are widely studied for their light-emission properties but raise significant environmental and health concerns because of lead toxicity. Many materials used for producing light contain lead, which is harmful to human health and the environment. To find a safer alternative, the researchers have investigated bismuth-based compounds, a class of compounds containing both organic and inorganic components, which can offer useful light-emitting properties without relying on lead. Prof. Saroj L Samal, Associate Professor, said, “The most interesting aspect of this material is its ability to undergo reversible structural transformation in response to heat and moisture, accompanied by change in its light emission properties.” This discovery has the potential for protecting important documents and products from counterfeiting. For example, special inks containing the developed material can be used on certificates, signatures, and security labels. Their light-emitting properties could be checked under UV light after controlled heating, which could help verify whether an item is genuine. It could also be useful in humidity sensors. Since its light emission changes with moisture, it may help monitor humidity in food packaging, storage facilities and other places where moisture levels need to be controlled. Further studies will focus on developing efficient and stimuli-responsive luminescent materials for anti-counterfeiting, improving the sensitivity and reliability of sensors, and optimising the performance of white-light-emitting diodes. These efforts could help translate the findings into practical technologies for optical security, environmental monitoring and cost-effective, energy-efficient lighting.

title: Why better data could be the key to AI-driven food R&D
content: Picture a product developer creating a plant-based protein drink for three different markets. The product concept is clear; the information needed to build it is not. Supplier specifications are locked inside PDFs. Trial results sit in spreadsheets. Regulatory requirements arrive by email. Even a single ingredient can carry a different name in each document: “haldi” in one file, “turmeric” in another and “Curcuma longa” in a regulatory note. None of these files is wrong. The problem is that the information is scattered. As a result, the developer spends more time searching, matching, and verifying data than working on the product itself. This has become common across food, beverage, and wellness R&D. Creating a product is no longer only about getting the taste and texture right. It is also about managing and connecting an ever-growing volume of data. Why the data load keeps growing Food product development is becoming more complex, and food safety sits at the centre of that complexity. The World Health Organization’s 2026 estimates, which cover 42 foodborne hazards, found that unsafe food caused an estimated 866 million illnesses and 1.5 million deaths worldwide in 2021. Chemical hazards accounted for 73% of these deaths, with inorganic arsenic and lead alone responsible for 42% and 31% of chemical-related deaths, respectively. The economic toll is just as stark: WHO puts the productivity lost to foodborne disease at $310 billion in 2021. The challenge multiplies when companies develop products for several markets at once. Each market brings its own allergen rules, contaminant limits, permitted claims and labelling norms, and the ingredients themselves vary. In wellness products, for instance, the composition of a botanical can shift with its source, harvest season and processing. With every new ingredient, supplier and market, the volume of information that must be checked and connected keeps growing. Giving data a common language The answer is not another database. It is a shared vocabulary with the relationships built in, which is exactly what an ontology provides. FoodOn, an open food ontology described in npj Science of Food in 2018, was created to tackle a familiar problem: food data siloed across disparate languages and data dictionaries. Still actively maintained, it now contains tens of thousands of classes covering food products, their plant and animal sources, and the processes used to make them. Inside a company, the principle is simple. Turmeric is turmeric, whatever name appears in a spreadsheet, supplier document or regulatory file. An ontology can link that one ingredient to its specification, supplier lot, test results, claims and market requirements. Instead of merely matching keywords across thousands of documents, AI can recognise that different names refer to the same ingredient and connect it to the details that matter. A question such as “Which approved ingredients could breach the lead limit in Market B?” then shifts from a slow, manual exercise to a rapid, data-driven check. Where GenAI fits Generative AI can read supplier documents, scan scientific literature, suggest alternative ingredients and help draft R&D reports. But when information is fragmented, AI can miss important connections or produce answers that are hard to verify. In some cases, it may generate details that sound plausible but are simply not true. An ontology can help address this by grounding GenAI in structured, connected facts. Rather than guessing from loose text, the model can draw on linked information about an ingredient, its supplier, its test history, the rules it must satisfy and the claims made for it, and show where each answer came from. This makes AI outputs easier to check and, ultimately, easier to trust. The ontology provides the map; GenAI makes that map usable. Safety built in, not bolted on In most organisations, even when quality checks run throughout development, some risks only become visible late, once a finished batch reaches the lab. Connected data can bring those risks into view at the design stage. If a developer selects a rice-based protein, the system can flag a potential inorganic arsenic risk well before a pilot batch is made, since rice absorbs arsenic from soil and water more readily than most other cereals. If a recipe changes, implications for allergens and cross-contact can surface immediately. This matters because many foodborne illnesses are preventable, and catching risks upstream reduces rework, delays and costly product recalls. The scientist stays in the loop AI can produce a formulation that is confident and wrong. It cannot taste bitterness, feel grittiness or predict how a blend will behave after months in a humid warehouse. Consider one high-protein beverage project. The AI recommended a pea protein isolate with added calcium and a stabiliser system, a combination that met every target for protein, nutrition and ingredient constraints on paper. In the lab, however, the proteins aggregated after heat processing, leading to visible settling and a chalky mouthfeel. The team had to rework the mineral load and the stabiliser system before the formulation could move forward. The working rule is simple: AI proposes; scientists decide. Every suggestion should trace back to a source, be tested at the bench and be signed off by a qualified person. This matters most in safety and regulatory decisions, where accountability cannot be delegated to software. What comes next The future of food R&D is not about robot chefs. It is about shorter development cycles, because no one has to waste time hunting for information. It is about keeping institutional knowledge within the organisation, even after a scientist moves on. And it is about building safety and compliance into a product from day one, rather than adding them at the end. The messy, unglamorous work of cleaning, naming and connecting data will decide who gets real value from AI. The advantage may not go to the company with the most powerful model, but to the one whose data both people and machines can understand. (Vicky Dodani is the Co-founder of Agrizy) (Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of YourStory.)

title: How to get corporate gifting right across multiple cities
content: Sending Diwali gifts to a handful of employees or clients is relatively simple. Sending hundreds of gifts to recipients spread across different cities is another matter. Addresses need to be verified, budgets finalized, packaging standardized and deliveries timed to arrive before the festival. A missed shipment, incorrect address or last-minute change can quickly complicate the exercise. For businesses managing large-scale Diwali gifting, the key is to plan early, coordinate the details and ensure that every recipient has a consistent experience, regardless of location. Start with a detailed recipient list The first step is to organize all recipient information in one place. This should include names, delivery addresses, contact numbers, and any other information required to complete the delivery. For employee gifting, it may also be useful to group recipients according to city or office location. Client and partner lists can be organized separately so that different gifting requirements are easier to manage. Checking the information before placing the order is important. Incorrect or incomplete addresses can create delivery problems, particularly when gifts are being sent to several cities. Personalize where it matters Large-scale gifting does not have to feel completely impersonal. Businesses can add small details that make gifts feel more thoughtful. A personalized greeting card, recipient name or company message can add a sense of occasion without making the process significantly more complicated. For key clients or long-term partners, businesses may choose a more customized gift, based on the relationship. The goal is to find the right level of personalization for each recipient group while keeping the overall process manageable. Use bulk ordering to simplify the process When a business is managing a large number of recipients, placing individual orders can quickly become time-consuming. Bulk ordering can make the process more organized, particularly when the same or similar gifts are being sent to multiple locations. A single gifting plan can cover product selection, quantities, packaging, and delivery requirements. This also makes it easier for the internal team to monitor the overall budget and track the progress of the campaign. Businesses planning corporate Diwali gifts can also establish recipient categories in advance, making it easier to decide which gift goes to which group. Keep packaging consistent Packaging plays an important role in professional Diwali gifting. When gifts are being sent to different cities, consistent packaging can create a unified brand experience. The same box style, colour scheme, greeting card or branding element can be used across the entire order. This helps ensure that recipients receive gifts that feel like part of the same Diwali campaign, even if they are in different locations. Packaging should also be practical enough to protect the contents during transportation. Fragile products or items sensitive to heat may need additional consideration. Set a clear budget Diwali gifting costs can increase quickly when the recipient list is large. Setting a budget before selecting products helps businesses narrow down suitable options. The budget can be divided by recipient category. For example, employee gifts may have one price range, while client or business-partner gifts may have another. It is also useful to account for packaging, delivery, and personalization costs rather than looking only at the product price. Track every shipment Once the Diwali gifts are ordered, tracking becomes one of the most important parts of the process. A simple tracking sheet can include the recipient, city, order status, and delivery status. This allows the business team to quickly identify delayed or unsuccessful deliveries and take action where required. For larger gifting programmes, having one person or team responsible for monitoring the campaign can make communication much easier. It also prevents different departments from working with separate or outdated recipient lists. Decide what the gift should include The next step is deciding what will go into the Diwali gift. Businesses have several options, from traditional sweets and dry fruits to chocolates, snacks, candles and curated hampers. The choice can depend on the recipient group. Employee gifts may follow one format, while important client or partner gifts may have a different product mix. A consistent selection across cities can make large-scale gifting easier to coordinate. At the same time, businesses can create different categories of gifts based on the relationship with each recipient. This balance can help maintain consistency without making every gift identical. Plan for different delivery locations Sending gifts across multiple cities requires attention to delivery coverage and timelines. Businesses should confirm whether the selected gifting provider can deliver to all the required locations and understand how long each delivery may take. This becomes especially important during Diwali because demand for gifting and delivery services can increase significantly around the festival. Businesses can group orders by city and create a delivery schedule before placing them. This makes it easier to track which gifts have been dispatched, which are in transit, and which have already reached the recipients. Start planning before the festive rush One of the easiest ways to make multi-city Diwali gifting smoother is to start early. Early planning gives businesses more time to finalize recipient details, compare gifting options, approve designs, and schedule deliveries. It also leaves room to handle unexpected issues, such as an incorrect address or a product becoming unavailable. Waiting until the last few days can limit the available options and put additional pressure on both the business team and the delivery network. Making multi-city Diwali gifting easier Diwali gifting across several cities requires more planning than a small personal gifting exercise, but the process becomes manageable when it is treated as a structured campaign. A clear recipient database, suitable gifts, consistent packaging, planned delivery schedules, and proper tracking can help businesses coordinate gifting across locations. The aim is not simply to send gifts to as many people as possible. It is to create a consistent and thoughtful festive experience, even when recipients are spread across different cities. title: Why women should build their front row; AI automation and its impact on jobs
content: Dear Reader, India’s ambition to achieve defence self-reliance gets a big boost. Sarvam has inked a five-year agreement with the defence ministry to develop AI tech for the armed forces. The Bengaluru-based AI company will design, develop and deploy AI applications for operations, training, and decision-support, and also provide follow-on technical assistance. The deal envisages shared foundation models, agentic infrastructure, and geospatial and perception systems. In other news, the high-stakes boardroom battle at the Tata Group continues. Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata has challenged the resolution to reappoint N Chandrasekaran as the chairman of Tata Sons. The resolution was passed at the board meeting of the Tata conglomerate’s holding company on September 17. According to sources, Noel has called the reappointment “void”, arguing that it was taken out of turn and was not on the meeting’s agenda. Meanwhile, as it reshapes its workforce amid heavy AI investments, Microsoft is offering employees an exit option. The American tech major has announced a voluntary exit programme for eligible employees in India, the US, the UK, and Canada. The package includes one month’s base salary for each completed year of service, besides health insurance and career transition services. Globally, around 60,000 employees are eligible for the programme. Microsoft has about 23,000 employees in India. However, it’s not clear how many would be eligible in the country. Lastly, Wall Street is closely watching the upcoming Big Tech earnings, which could serve as testimony to AI growth in an otherwise turbulent market. In today’s newsletter, we will talk about Why women should build their front row AI automation and its impact on jobs Here’s your trivia for today: At what temperature do Fahrenheit and Celsius match? (Scroll down for the answer) Women in Tech Kripa Venkatachalam of Cadence urges women to build their front row As part of our Women in Tech series, Kripa Venkatachalam, VP, India Technical Field Organisation & Global Customer Success at Cadence Design Systems, reflects on gender barriers, changing workplace policies, mentorship, and the importance of having people who egg you on. Her career spanning more than two decades has taken her through diverse roles across companies, including LSI Logic Corporation, Synopsys, GlobalFoundries, and Siemens EDA. Today, as VP, India Technical Field Organisation & Global Customer Success at Cadence Design Systems, she has what she calls a “front-row seat” to how the world’s chips are designed in India. Key takeaways: Kripa believes women need to seek support, leverage their network, and not always put the burden on themselves. “You have to make your family work for you, your workplace work for you, your society work for you. You have to lean in and take the help,” she says. At informal forums in Cadence, she often speaks about the need for people, especially women, to create their own front row—people cheering for them. “The front row has to assure you. Organisations and managers have to look closer, look harder, and encourage women forward,” she reiterates. As she looks ahead, Kripa resists the idea of tying her ambitions to a title. She describes her career as a jungle gym rather than a ladder, an image she credits to Sheryl Sandberg. <Funding Alert> Startup: Cent Amount: $15M Round: Series A Startup: Simplismart Amount: $14M Round: Series B Startup: Live2.ai Amount: Rs 130 Cr Round: Pre-Series B TechSparks Capital no longer creates jobs: Yatish Rajawat of Hundred Million Jobs At TechSparks 2026, K Yatish Rajawat, Co-founder of Hundred Million Jobs, a non-profit initiative to create 100 million net jobs in India over the next decade, said MSMEs, data laws, entrepreneurship and reskilling will shape the next wave of employment in the country. Key takeaways: Rajawat identified three trends reshaping the economy. One, the old formula, wherein Rs 100 crore of investment generates around 10,000 jobs, no longer holds, said Rajawat. Schemes such as the production-linked incentive are tied to capital rather than employment, he added. The second trend is the impact of AI and automation. AI is already affecting white-collar work across sectors. MSMEs, which he called the country’s largest job engine, are also losing jobs to automation. The third is platform consolidation. Rajawat argued that dominant ecommerce and social media platforms hold consumer data, which new entrepreneurs need, and this kind of monopoly prevents new businesses from succeeding. If entrepreneurship stalls, so does job creation, he said. title: ‘Cope harder’: Vaishnaw defends India's iPhone PLI scheme
content: Assembling iPhones makes great headlines for India. Owning the supply chain is where the real power lies. Apple assembled around 55 million iPhones in India in 2025, a 53% increase from 36 million units in 2024. The country now accounts for about a quarter of Apple's global iPhone output, according to a Bloomberg report. The growth has strengthened India's position as an alternative manufacturing base to China. While skeptics question whether snapping together foreign components delivers true high-tech independence, the government points to ₹3.25 lakh crore in tax collections and 12 lakh new jobs as proof that the PLI scheme is already paying off handsomely. Vaishnaw counters criticism with tax and employment figures The debate intensified after a Bloomberg Opinion video questioned whether India should replicate China's manufacturing model. It highlighted India's dependence on imported components and the cost of government subsidies supporting phone production. Union Electronics and IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw responded on X on October 27, defending the government's Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for mobile manufacturing. According to the figures he shared, the government had paid Rs 19,000 crore in incentives, while direct tax collections reached Rs 25,000 crore. The sector had also generated Rs 3 lakh crore in Goods and Services Tax (GST) collections. Mobile PLI stats as follows: Government incentive paid: Rs 19,000 Cr. Direct tax collected: Rs 25,000 Cr. GST collected: Rs 3,00,000 Cr. Electronics manufacturing employs 25 Lakh people; mobile manufacturing alone employs 12 Lakh. Cope harder!! https://t.co/G3bDU6ldGg — Ashwini Vaishnaw (@AshwiniVaishnaw) October 27, 2026 Vaishnaw also cited employment figures, saying electronics manufacturing supported 25 lakh jobs, including 12 lakh in mobile phone manufacturing. He ended his post with the pointed remark, “Cope harder!!” The figures form the government's case for continuing to support domestic manufacturing. However, tax collections and job creation are only part of the discussion. India's iPhone growth comes with a supply chain challenge India's expanding role in Apple's manufacturing network is a significant development. In 2025, the country assembled around 55 million iPhones, up from 36 million in 2024. Apple also began assembling all variants of its iPhone 17 line-up in India, including the Pro and Pro Max models, according to The Times of India. Yet assembling a finished product is different from manufacturing all its components locally. India continues to depend on imports for several critical parts, including processors, memory chips, displays, camera lenses and batteries. This matters because the economic value generated by manufacturing depends partly on how much of the supply chain operates within the country. Greater domestic production of components could help Indian suppliers capture more value while reducing reliance on overseas manufacturers. The next test is building more of the iPhone in India The government's manufacturing push now faces a more demanding test: turning higher production volumes into a deeper domestic electronics ecosystem. That means expanding local component manufacturing, bringing more suppliers into the country and strengthening research and design capabilities. These steps could help India progress beyond final assembly and establish a more substantial presence in global electronics supply chains. India's iPhone production growth demonstrates that the country can attract large-scale manufacturing. Whether that translates into lasting economic gains will depend on its ability to build more of the technology and supply chain behind each device.

title: From Homemade Badi to GomatiRoots: Shital Kumari Secures Funding
content: Key Takeaways GomatiRoots is building a brand around Bihar's traditional badi. The startup received Rs 1 lakh in funding through YourStory's Shuru Kar initiative. Shital Kumari's startup is connecting rural women with markets. The company generated Rs 32 lakh in revenue in its first financial year. Last September, in 2025, the Bihar Idea Festival concluded at Bapu Sabhagar in Patna. YourStory launched the festival under its initiative, The Bharat Project , in collaboration with the Bihar Industries Department and the Chandragupt Institute of Management, Patna (CIMP). The objective was to take entrepreneurship beyond metropolitan cities and select groups of people, reaching young people in smaller towns and villages and helping them turn their business ideas into reality. Shital Kumari was among those present at the event. She wanted to start her own business but had several questions. What business should she start? How would she get started? Where would the money come from? And what would happen if her efforts failed? Life had already exposed her to numerous challenges. Taking the risk of starting a business was not easy, but she decided to take a step towards turning her idea into reality. Nearly a year later, Shital's efforts reached an important milestone. Through YourStory's Shuru Kar initiative, she received funding of Rs 1 lakh for her startup , GomatiRoots . The funding came from Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project. For Shital, the amount represented more than financial support; it was also a sign of confidence in her idea. Through GomatiRoots, Shital aims to give Bihar's traditional badi and other indigenous food products a distinct identity. She wants badi, a traditional lentil-based food product that has been part of Indian households for generations, to establish itself as a trusted brand in the market. Building a Business Amid Challenges To understand Shital's entrepreneurial journey, it is important to look back at her early life. She grew up in Bihar and completed her education at government institutions. She studied up to Class 10 at Shri Guru Gobind Singh Girls High School, completed her intermediate education at RPM College, and earned an honours degree in Physics from the College of Commerce. She wanted to pursue a BTech degree, but that dream did not materialise. Nevertheless, she continued her education and later completed an MA from Nalanda Open University. A friend helped her with Rs 4,500 to pursue her studies. In 2018, her life took a major turn when she lost her younger brother. Following his death, her family moved to Muzaffarpur. As the family struggled to cope with the loss, Shital lost her mother during the COVID-19 pandemic. After her mother's death, the responsibility of caring for her younger siblings fell on her shoulders. She moved to Patna to support her family and began looking for work. Over the next two to three years, she took up video editing, taught children, and even sold lychees whenever necessary. Throughout this period, she continued preparing for the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) examination . During this time, she learned about the Bihar Laghu Udyami Yojana , a state government initiative designed to support small entrepreneurs. She applied for the scheme and received Rs 50,000 as the first instalment. She also received training to start her business. Later, she received a second instalment of Rs 1 lakh. In addition, she took a loan of Rs 2 lakh and laid the foundation for GomatiRoots in Patna. Speaking to YourStory, Shital says, "There were several phases in my life when taking care of my family was the most important responsibility. After my mother passed away, looking after my younger siblings became my priority. I worked in video editing, taught children, and even sold lychees. At the same time, I continued preparing for the UPSC examination. When I learned about the Bihar Laghu Udyami Yojana, I felt that perhaps I finally had an opportunity to start something of my own. I did not have much money, but I decided to begin with whatever resources I had." How Her Mother's Homemade Badi Inspired a Business GomatiRoots did not begin with a long-standing business ambition. Instead, the idea emerged from a deeply personal experience. After her mother's death, Shital often missed the badi her mother used to make. When she began looking for a similar product in the market, she could not find one that matched the taste and quality she remembered. Some products raised concerns about adulteration, while others did not offer the varieties she preferred. What began as a personal search soon revealed a potential business opportunity. Shital started researching the market, speaking to people, and learning more about badi. During her research, she observed that while India had several well-established pickle and papad brands, badi had not achieved the same level of recognition. Yet, in Bihar and many other parts of India, lentil-based badi is a regular part of everyday meals. It is eaten with lentils, vegetables, and other dishes, and the tradition of making it at home has continued for generations. Despite its popularity, badi often remains a locally produced food item rather than a recognised packaged brand. Shital believed that the product could establish a stronger market presence if it were made available throughout the year with consistent quality and better packaging. This insight gradually shaped the idea behind GomatiRoots. For her, badi was more than a food product. It represented memories of her mother, the taste of home, and an opportunity to bring Bihar's culinary traditions to a wider audience. Shital says, "The idea of building a brand around badi was not something I had thought about since childhood. After my mother passed away, I looked for a product in the market that tasted like the badi she used to make. That was when I realised there was a need for a reliable brand. I studied the market and spoke to people. There are several pickle and papad brands, but I did not see the same kind of identity for badi. I felt that if we could make it available throughout the year with consistent quality, people would embrace it." Turning Traditional Flavours Into a Brand GomatiRoots started with badi, but its product range has since expanded to include several traditional varieties. These include urad dal badi, moongori, chana dal badi, Bihari masala badi, and kohrauri. The company also offers traditional fryums such as tisiyori and tilauri. Through these products, Shital aims to bring greater recognition to flavours that have long been part of households and local communities. One of the biggest challenges in this business is the seasonal nature of badi production. Traditionally, making badi depends heavily on sunlight and weather conditions. Unfavourable weather can affect both production and product quality. Ensuring that customers receive a consistent product throughout the year is therefore not easy. Shital has tried to address this challenge through research and experimentation. Her goal is to ensure that customers receive the same quality every time they purchase a product, regardless of the season. According to Shital, the business has received encouraging customer feedback within its first year of operations. Repeat orders from retail shopkeepers, in particular, have strengthened her confidence. These orders indicate that customers are not simply trying the product once but are willing to buy it again. However, maintaining this trust requires continuous improvements in production, packaging, and storage. Shital says, "Making badi available throughout the year is one of our most important priorities. Traditionally, it has been prepared according to the weather and availability of sunlight. But if we want to build a brand, customers must receive consistent quality every time. We have conducted research at our level and improved our production methods. Over the past year, we have received repeat orders from shopkeepers. When customers tell us that our products taste like homemade food, that means a lot to us." Limited Capital, a Larger Market, and New Challenges GomatiRoots initially relied on government scheme assistance and a loan to get its operations started. With limited resources, Shital had to account for every expense carefully. Purchasing raw materials, developing packaging, delivering products to retail outlets, and building brand awareness all required money. Rather than expanding in multiple directions at once, she chose to grow the business gradually. The company currently generates revenue by supplying products to retail stores, restaurants, and cloud kitchens, as well as selling directly to customers. GomatiRoots products are available at more than 50 stores in Patna. The company is also working to expand its presence in other districts of Bihar through distributors. Its products are available on Amazon, Flipkart, and JioMart. Customers can also place orders through the company's website, gomatiroots.com. In addition, the business reaches customers directly through exhibitions, fairs, and canopy stalls. Funding Through YourStory's Shuru Kar Initiative During its first financial year of operations, GomatiRoots generated revenue of Rs 32 lakh. Shital is now looking to expand into larger retail networks and quick-commerce platforms. However, entering large retail stores and organised markets requires a reliable supply chain. The business must also address product shelf life, packaging, and storage requirements. Shital is working to overcome these challenges. She also plans to bring more people on board to strengthen e-commerce operations and direct-to-consumer sales. She says, "We started the business with very limited capital. In the beginning, we had to account for every rupee. We had production and packaging expenses on one side and the challenge of reaching retail stores on the other. Large retail companies also want to know whether a brand can maintain a consistent supply. We are gradually strengthening our sales record and distributor network. We intend to use the Rs 1 lakh funding received through YourStory's Shuru Kar initiative for working capital and marketing as well." Connecting Women's Work With Market Opportunities GomatiRoots' ambitions extend beyond increasing product sales. Shital wants women and small producers who make traditional food products in Bihar to benefit from access to larger markets. Some of the company's products are prepared in collaboration with rural women's self-help groups (SHGs). These include different varieties of tisiyori made with flaxseed, potatoes, and rice, along with rice-based tilauri and kohrauri. The women already have experience preparing these traditional foods. GomatiRoots aims to help them connect with buyers and access wider markets. Shital is also in discussions with JEEViKA , Bihar's rural livelihoods initiative. She was invited as a buyer to the Saras Mela and now hopes to establish long-term partnerships to source traditional products directly from JEEViKA Didis . Her objective is to ensure that the women receive fair prices for their products and gain access to regular income opportunities. In the future, she also wants to work with farmers in Bihar so that the lentils used to make badi can be cultivated locally, allowing farmers to benefit from the business. Over the next three to five years, Shital hopes to take GomatiRoots beyond Bihar and into major cities across India. Her plans include expanding into large retail stores, online marketplaces, and quick-commerce platforms. The company also hopes to open its own store and eventually export its products internationally. Alongside expansion, Shital wants to formalise business operations, obtain the necessary licences, increase production capacity, and make better use of available business support schemes. One of her long-term goals is to create year-round work opportunities for up to one lakh women associated with JEEViKA's self-help groups. For now, this remains an ambition that she hopes to pursue as the business grows. Shital says, "I want the growth of GomatiRoots to translate into higher incomes for women in Bihar. Many women here have excellent skills in preparing traditional food products, but they lack the means to reach larger markets. If they receive regular work and fair prices, their efforts can gain greater recognition. We also want to work with farmers so that the lentils used in badi can be grown in Bihar itself. My dream is to take these flavours across the country and around the world." The Road Ahead Shital Kumari's story is not about building a business with abundant capital, an established market, and plenty of resources from the outset. She found her way forward while managing family responsibilities, took up different jobs, and used support from a government scheme to establish her business. The Rs 1 lakh funding she subsequently received through YourStory's Shuru Kar initiative has further strengthened confidence in her idea. Her search for the badi her mother used to make helped her identify a gap in the market, one she is now working to address through her brand. GomatiRoots still faces several challenges. It must increase production while maintaining quality, strengthen customer trust, and build a more organised business to compete in larger markets. However, Shital has a clear goal: she wants badi to become more than a product associated with a particular household or region. She wants customers to recognise the brand by name and purchase it with confidence. Entrepreneurship in India is often associated with large investments and technology startups. But the story of GomatiRoots, which emerged from Bihar, offers a different perspective. Its foundation is not a new technology but a traditional food product that has been part of everyday meals for generations. The real challenge lies in adapting that product to market requirements, building a trusted identity, and creating income opportunities for the people involved in its production. For Shital, the journey is still in its early stages. She dreams of a day when someone in any part of India looking to buy lentil-based badi will think of GomatiRoots. The coming years will determine how far this ambition takes her. For now, her journey demonstrates that entrepreneurship does not always require an entirely new idea. Sometimes, the beginnings of a business can be found in the familiar flavours of home. Hokar Nidar Shuru Kar.
