title: Why India’s flying taxi revolution begins with electric air ambulances
content: For most deeptech entrepreneurs, the hardest lesson is not solving complex physics but overcoming their own technical fascination. Professor Satya Chakravarthy, Founder and technical lead of The ePlane Company, explained this clearly at TechSparks 2026 , YourStory's flagship event. “The biggest challenge that a deep tech entrepreneur normally would face is what I call the technology trap,” he said. “We have to actually ask the question who cares, and the moment you actually ask the question who cares... even your wife doesn’t care.” Chakravarthy, an aerospace professor at IIT Madras, founded the company to develop electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, or eVTOLs. These are battery-powered flying vehicles capable of hovering, taking off, and landing vertically without a runway. In a sector often driven by academic prestige, Chakravarthy insists that financial fundamentals must lead engineering ambitions. For deeptech startups, companies built on breakthroughs in science and engineering, long development timelines and heavy capital commitments mean that technological novelty alone cannot survive. In aerospace, he notes, becoming a unicorn is merely the minimum baseline, and founders must build business cases capable of reaching decacorn scale through healthy revenues and margins. The inspiration for ePlane stemmed from a visit to Toulouse, France, where Chakravarthy discovered that 50 smaller aircraft manufacturers existed alongside global giants. “If there are 50 plane companies in France, maybe plane making is not so difficult... why don’t we give a shot at it?” he recalled. Coming from an academic institution accustomed to international standards, he aimed to build a world-class aircraft directly out of India. The air ambulance strategy To avoid the economic traps that have sunk rival aviation ventures, ePlane has designed a phased commercial rollout. Instead of launching directly into intracity air taxis, which represent a high-volume but low-margin business, ePlane is prioritising electric air ambulances. Emergency medical transport offers higher profit margins at lower production volumes, providing early positive cash flow while supply capacity scales up. This approach also solves the challenge of demand modulation, preventing consumer frustration when early aircraft supply is limited. “First of all don’t let the bubble grow in the first place... be realistic about what is the customer that you can actually cater to,” Chakravarthy explains. Deploying five air ambulances in a congested city like Bangalore transforms emergency healthcare without overwhelming fleet capacity. Only after establishing economic stability will ePlane expand into short-haul air cargo and urban air taxis, where commuters can achieve a five-to-eightfold reduction in travel time for roughly double the cost of an Uber ride. Global standards, Indian economics Crucially, Chakravarthy rejects the notion that Indian innovations must settle for discounted quality. Because gravity and flight dynamics are identical everywhere, aircraft must satisfy rigorous international regulatory benchmarks, such as those set by the Directorate General of Civil Aviation. Building to global safety standards while keeping production costs low creates a distinct export advantage. As Chakravarthy asserts, “what’s good for India is good for the world.” Engineering decisions at ePlane have been tailored specifically for practical certification and urban operation. The team deliberately avoided the tilt-rotor mechanism, a design where propellers rotate between vertical hover and horizontal flight, because single points of mechanical failure complicate regulatory approval. Instead, they selected a multi-rotor layout backed by redundant systems to ensure a straightforward path to certification. Public anxiety regarding urban air mobility is often misplaced when compared to everyday transit risks. Aviation regulators demand a failure rate of less than one in a billion before granting commercial approval. “If you are driving a car, you are actually driving something that can kill you... planes are much, much safer,” Chakravarthy remarks. Furthermore, by engineering the smallest aircraft footprint in its class, ePlane ensures its flying vehicles can land on existing hospital helipads and urban rooftops, including Metro station plazas. With commercialisation targeted for 2028, ePlane represents a critical test case for the maturing Indian deeptech ecosystem. While government grants have provided crucial runway, private venture capital continues to struggle with long development cycles. “Patient capital still is more or less an oxymoron,” Chakravarthy reflects. Yet by pairing aerospace innovation with disciplined business strategy, India’s deeptech sector is proving that moonshot technologies can land firmly on commercial ground.

title: 5 Lessons to learn from Nexus by Yuval Noah Harari
content: Information has always shaped human civilisation. From ancient stories and religious texts to newspapers, television and social media, the way people share information influences what they believe, how they make decisions and whom they trust. In Nexus, historian and author Yuval Noah Harari examines how information networks have shaped human history and how they may influence our future. Published in 2024, the book explores the relationship between information, power, truth and the development of artificial intelligence. Harari challenges the assumption that having more information automatically makes societies wiser or better informed. What matters is how information is organised, who controls it and whether the systems that distribute it help people correct their mistakes. Here are five important lessons to learn from Nexus and how they apply to the world we live in today. 5 Lessons to learn from Nexus by Yuval Noah Harari 1. More information does not always mean more truth One of the most important lessons from Nexus is that the availability of information does not automatically make people better informed. We often assume that access to more facts, news and opinions will help us understand the world more accurately. However, information can also be misleading, incomplete or deliberately manipulated. Throughout history, information networks have helped societies organise themselves, preserve knowledge and cooperate on a large scale. Yet the same networks have also spread myths, propaganda and misinformation. Harari explores this tension through historical examples ranging from religious institutions to modern political systems. The same challenge exists today. Social media allows us to access information within seconds, but it can also expose us to misleading headlines, unverified claims and content designed to provoke emotional reactions. The lesson is to become more thoughtful about the information we consume. Instead of believing something simply because it appears frequently online, examine the source, look for supporting evidence and consider alternative explanations. What to remember: Being informed is not just about knowing more. It is about learning to distinguish reliable information from misleading narratives. 2. The stories we believe shape society Human beings depend on shared stories to build communities, establish institutions and coordinate their actions. These stories can include national identities, cultural traditions, political ideologies and ideas about how society should function. In Nexus, Harari examines how information networks help these shared narratives spread across generations and large populations. Such stories can bring people together around common goals, but they can also reinforce divisions when people accept different or conflicting versions of reality. Consider how a single event can be interpreted differently by different communities. The facts may overlap, yet people's beliefs, experiences and sources of information can lead them to completely different conclusions. Understanding this helps explain why disagreements are not always resolved by presenting more facts. Sometimes, people are also defending a larger story about their identity, values or place in the world. What to remember: Question the narratives that influence your thinking . Understanding why you believe something is an important step towards forming independent opinions. Also Read 6 Books that teach lessons from ordinary everyday life 3. Information is closely connected to power Information has always been an important source of power. Those who control how information is collected, recorded and distributed can influence public opinion, shape decisions and determine which perspectives receive attention. Harari traces this relationship through historical examples, examining how empires, religious institutions and political regimes have used information networks to maintain authority or influence society. He also considers how modern information systems affect the distribution of power. Today, this relationship extends to digital platforms, search engines and algorithmic systems that determine what people see online. The information presented to us can influence what we consider important, which issues we discuss and how we understand current events. This does not mean every information system is deliberately manipulative. Rather, it highlights the importance of asking who controls a system, what incentives shape it and whose interests it serves. What to remember: Whenever information influences an important decision, consider who created it, who distributes it and who benefits from the way it is presented. 4. Artificial Intelligence makes information networks more complicated Artificial intelligence is one of the most significant themes in Nexus. Harari explores how AI differs from earlier information technologies and why systems capable of generating content and making decisions could change the way information networks operate. Unlike traditional tools that primarily store or transmit information, AI systems can generate persuasive text, images and other content at enormous scale. They can also perform tasks that previously required human judgement, raising questions about accountability and control. These developments create opportunities in areas such as education, research and healthcare. At the same time, they raise concerns about fabricated information, automated manipulation and the difficulty of identifying who is responsible when AI systems cause harm. The lesson is not to reject technology outright. It is to recognise that technological progress needs to be accompanied by critical thinking, appropriate safeguards and clear accountability. What to remember: AI can help us process information, but we should not automatically treat its outputs as accurate or allow automated systems to make consequential decisions without appropriate oversight. 5. Human responsibility matters more than technological progress alone A central concern in Nexus is that technological advancement does not guarantee that societies will make wise decisions. Humans have developed increasingly powerful tools and information networks, but the consequences depend on how these systems are designed, governed and used. Harari argues that the future of information networks is not predetermined. The choices made by individuals, institutions and governments can influence whether new technologies strengthen society or create additional risks. This is particularly relevant as AI becomes more integrated into everyday life. Decisions about privacy , misinformation, automated systems and the concentration of technological power will affect how people interact with information in the years ahead. Responsibility therefore cannot rest entirely with technology companies or governments. Readers, citizens and technology users also have a role to play by checking claims, recognising uncertainty and thinking carefully about what they share. What to remember: Progress is not simply about developing more powerful technology. It is about making responsible choices about how that technology affects human lives. Final thoughts Nexus: A Brief History of Information Networks from the Stone Age to AI explores how information has shaped human civilisation, from shared beliefs to artificial intelligence. The book argues that more information does not always mean more truth or wisdom. For readers navigating social media, digital news and AI-generated content, it highlights the need to question claims, examine evidence and think critically about how information shapes decisions.

title: As chip prices surge, EV maker Ultraviolette is working on ways to absorb costs
content: The global shortage of memory chips has driven up costs, placing a huge strain on electric vehicle makers in the country. Bengaluru-based Ultraviolette—which produces high-performance electric motorcycles—says it will not pass on the high input costs to customers and is exploring other ways to tide over the situation. Memory chips are a critical component of an electric vehicle, used to store data, run control software, and manage real-time operations across critical systems. According to Ultraviolette’s Founder and CTO, Niraj Rajmohan, RAM (random access memory) alone adds Rs 20,000 to the cost of a vehicle. With global companies building very large data centres, there has been a surge in memory chip consumption, he added. AI data centres are projected to consume 70% of global memory chip production in 2026. The data centre boom has led to a supply crunch, subsequently shoring up costs of chips. But it would not be fair to pass on the costs to customers, said Rajmohan, adding that a threefold jump in memory prices in recent times cannot translate into a threefold jump in the price of an electric bike, and customers cannot be asked to suddenly pay far more. The company is working on alternatives to absorb costs. For now, Ultraviolette is scouting for alternative parts, including software, components and technologies, and alternative manufacturers to partner with. The company is also relying on partners who hold a stake in the company, including TVS, TDK Ventures, and Intel, for their knowhow and expertise, said Rajmohan. He, however, did not elaborate on the alternatives. Rajmohan was speaking at the launch of X-47 Venom, Ultraviolette’s first bike built on its new platform ‘VX-100’, What is VX-100? VX-100 is a 100V electric powertrain architecture that seeks to improve performance and efficiency in electric two-wheelers. An electric powertrain architecture is the integrated system of energy storage, electronics, and mechanical components that converts stored electrical energy into mechanical motion to propel the vehicle. Rather than upgrading the parts one at a time, Ultraviolette has redesigned the battery, motor, and control electronics together, as one system. The X-47 Venom is the first bike built on this new architecture. The company claims it offers better battery cooling, lighter components, and stronger power delivery, along with support for DC fast charging at up to 12 kW. Most electric two-wheelers run on 48V, said Rajmohan, adding that the telecom industry and Southeast Asian manufacturers built their systems around it. At 100V, X-47 Venom’s system draws lower current, and hence produces less heat. The objective is to provide high speed and better performance without the heat, energy loss, and extra weight that usually come with electric vehicles. Currently, Qualcomm supplies the chips that power the bike's new dashboard, while TDK provides the RF (radio frequency) components and capacitors. The X-47 Venom is priced at Rs 2,65,000 for the first 5,000 buyers. Bookings opened on October 22, and deliveries are set to start in November. The European launch will happen on November 3 at EICMA, an international motorcycle expo in Milan. The bike has undergone extensive test rides covering 150 to 200 km a day for several months, said Rajmohan. Ultraviolette’s product portfolio includes the F77 sports bike that is targeted at sports enthusiasts, while the X-47 Crossover is intended to appeal to a broader set of customers, including sports, adventure and street riders. The Crossover makes up about 90% of the company’s sales. The new VX-100 platform will go into all of Ultraviolette’s forthcoming products. Four launches are expected next year, including the Tesseract (a scooter) and Shockwave (an Enduro motorcycle), and an upgraded F77 bike. Roughly 90% of sales come from India and 10% from abroad, including the European market, where the company has been expanding. There are more than 7,000 Ultraviolette bikes on the roads worldwide today. Ultraviolette was founded in 2016 by Narayan Subramaniam and Niraj Rajmohan. Its backers include Lingotto, TDK Ventures, Qualcomm Ventures, Zoho Corporation, TVS Motors, Yali Capital, and Speciale Invest. Edited by Swetha Kannan

title: Autonomy and control are not opposites, they go together: EY GDS at DevSparks Chennai
content: Ask a room of developers about agents today and you will get plenty of answers. Almost everyone has built one, and most have a demo they are proud of. The harder question is what happens after that, when the agent has to hold up against real customers, real data, and real consequences. At DevSparks Chennai 2026 , Arvind Purushothaman, Global Cloud Consulting, Microsoft Practice and Alliances Leader at EY GDS , opened with a version of it. He asked how many people in the room had built an AI agent, and plenty of hands went up. Then he asked how many had built one that made it to production for a business-critical system. "I think that's where the numbers dramatically drop," he said. "Not because of anybody's fault, but that's how it is." That gap is the whole problem, and it is not a model problem. Cloud, low code tools, and open model APIs have pushed the entry barrier close to zero. What has not changed is the difficulty of industrializing what you build. "Access to intelligence is not the bottleneck, but the ability to industrialize is going to be the bottleneck," said Arvind Purushothaman. From the nets to the match Drawing on a cricket analogy, he said that hackathon builds are like net practice, where a few lines of Python and an API key let you rehearse your reverse scoop all afternoon. The match is different. You need 12 runs off six deliveries under pressure, and the strokes only matter alongside the ability to read the situation. For agents, that pressure arrives when the demo meets regulated data, compliance requirements, integration points, and business-critical workflows. Skip the rigor and the exposure is concrete: a bad transaction, financial loss, reputational damage, security and privacy failures. The question itself changes, Purushothaman said, from does it work in a demo to "can we trust it repeatedly under real operating conditions." More autonomy means more engineering Traditional software ran on deterministic rules and stage gates that everything had to clear before production. Agents behave differently. They interpret context, reason about a goal, and decide for themselves which tools to use to reach an outcome. The instinct is to read it as less work for engineers. Purushothaman argued the opposite. More freedom for the agent means more engineering responsibility for the people around it, because the system has to constrain, restrict, and verify what the agent does. "Autonomy and controls … they are not the opposite of each other in this world," he said. He offered three maturity levels to locate yourself against. Task-based agents automate specific steps and return an output. Goal-oriented agents are handed an objective, such as how much credit limit a customer should get, and assemble their own data and policies to reach a recommendation. The third horizon is humans and agents as one team, with judgment reserved for critical calls. Ontologies, controls, and platform Three foundations make production deployment possible, and they only work together. Domain context and ontologies codify business knowledge, taxonomy, and decision logic, and mature vendors now ship them by industry. Controls evaluate outcomes for quality, bias, and risk, and produce traceability. The platform makes execution repeatable and scalable. Ontologies without controls create chaos, controls without a platform are not repeatable, and a platform without domain context is generic. The same logic scales up. The model is only one part of the system, so the engineering has to cover data context, cloud and compute, integration APIs, security and identity, responsible AI, and FinOps discipline around cost. "The outcome is only as strong as the weakest link in your chain," Purushothaman said. Every agent needs a passport Take a customer asking a bank to raise their credit limit. The agent has to establish identity, retrieve the applicable risk policy before anything else so it knows which boundary it is operating under, pull the relevant data, and interpret context. The recommendation has to stay inside policy guidelines, and if the risk is high, it should transfer to a human. Every step has to be auditable. Without that preserved history, he said, it is not a production-ready system. Hence the agent passport. Every agent gets an identity, a named business owner and technical owner, defined permissions covering where it can operate, and escalation points. Organizations already carry deprecated software they cannot account for, and agents will multiply that problem faster. Production systems also need circuit breakers: anomaly detection, the ability to halt execution, roll back, and escalate to humans. What value actually looks like Asked how to measure return, Purushothaman pushed back on counting agents deployed and tokens consumed. The number that matters is cost per governed business outcome, counting cloud and agent running costs, the human effort still in the loop, and the risk profile. "You don't want to over-engineer a simple ask, and you don't want to under-engineer a complex ask. It should be right for the outcome." Testing, he added, has to shift from fixed test cases toward simulating production like runtime conditions. Asked whether robustness holds as attackers keep evolving, he conceded that the how will change while the fundamentals will not. "We talked about the why. We talked about the what. The how will evolve." He closed on the sharpest line of the session. "Intelligence is abundant, but trust, accountability, and repeatability, we must still engineer."

title: Startup news and updates: Daily roundup (October 23, 2026)
content: YourStory brings you today’s headlines with the latest developments across sectors. Funding news GVFL leads Rs 3.7 Cr seed funding round in SpectraGaze Systems GVFL has led a Rs 3.7 crore seed round in Ahmedabad-based SpectraGaze Systems, with participation from angel investors. Founded in 2023 by former ISRO scientist Arup Banerjee, the startup develops indigenous optical imaging sensors and electro-optical payloads for space, defence and scientific applications. SpectraGaze's customers include ISRO, Physical Research Laboratory, and Kaynes Technology. It has delivered an infrared detector and test system to ISRO and secured an image sensor development contract for its HRSAT programme. The funding will support product development, engineering expansion, testing infrastructure and existing customer projects. The company is also developing a hyperspectral imaging camera for a 3U satellite. haf.vc invests Rs 3 Cr in conversational AI startup Hunar.AI Hyderabad-based venture capital fund haf.vc has invested Rs 3 crore in Hunar.AI, a conversational artificial intelligence startup focused on frontline workforce management. The investment will support AI infrastructure, product development, sales and market expansion as the company targets businesses managing large, multilingual workforces across locations. Founded in 2022 by Krishna Khandelwal and Shantanu Bhattacharyya, Hunar.AI develops conversational AI agents that help enterprises hire, onboard, train and engage frontline workers through voice and WhatsApp. Kalyan Sivalenka, Managing Partner at haf.vc, said the company’s understanding of workforce challenges and its technology-driven approach made it an attractive investment. Hunar.AI co-founder and CEO Krishna Khandelwal said the funding would strengthen its presence in Hyderabad and Telangana’s logistics, retail and services sectors. Other news India’s GCCs are projected to grow to about 3.7M employees by 2031 India’s global capability centres (GCCs) are projected to grow from 2.3 million employees to 3.3-3.7 million by 2031, adding 1-1.4 million net jobs and generating 150-170 million sq ft of additional office demand, according to an Embark report. Based on a survey of 100 GCC leaders, the report found that 92% have moved beyond selective AI adoption, but realised productivity gains remain below 15%. Around 80% of workforce additions are expected from existing centres, while demand shifts towards specialised AI, data and cybersecurity roles. Bengaluru and Hyderabad account for 67% of Tier I GCC leasing, while BFSI and technology, media and telecom are expected to drive 54% of incremental office demand. Read more Honasa Consumer elevates Vipul Maheshwari to CPTO Honasa Consumer has elevated Vipul Maheshwari to chief product and technology officer, overseeing product, technology, engineering and analytics. He will lead the company's AI-led transformation and development of agentic AI systems. Maheshwari has spent six years at Honasa, building its data and product capabilities. His new role will focus on developing AI-powered workflows to automate processes, improve decision-making and increase operational efficiency. Before joining Honasa, he held roles at Delhivery and Global Analytics India. He holds a master's degree in mathematics and computer science from IIT Delhi. Microsoft, MeitY Startup Hub, 1M1B launch CoE in Hyderabad Microsoft, MeitY Startup Hub and 1M1B Foundation have launched a Green Skills and Applied AI Centre of Excellence at SAS iTower, Hyderabad, with a dedicated AI and Green Pharma training track. The centre will provide practical training in applied AI, pharmaceutical manufacturing, solar energy, electric vehicles and wind energy, alongside industry mentoring, internships and employment pathways. At the launch, 1M1B Jobs Express reported 100 job offers on its first day. The Hyderabad facility is part of a planned network of five centres aiming to train 100,000 young people in AI and green skills by 2030. Purple Finance posts 101% AUM growth Purple Finance's standalone assets under management rose 101% year-on-year to Rs 329.21 crore in H1 FY27. The NBFC's board has approved exploring entry into affordable housing finance through an acquisition, investment or subsidiary, subject to regulatory approvals. The company has introduced two MSME lending products, PURPLE SARAL, offering loans of Rs 75,000 to Rs 2 lakh, and SAKSHAM LAP, providing mortgage loans of Rs 2 lakh to Rs 4 lakh. It has also launched institutional lending to NBFCs serving MSMEs. Gross non-performing assets remained below 2.5%. Following its acquisition of Saksham Gram Credit, combined AUM reached Rs 853 crore across 205 branches. Lenskart opens its first concept flagship store in India Lenskart has opened its first concept flagship store in India, Lenskart evolv, at Worli, Mumbai. The store combines eyewear retail with design, technology and fashion, featuring chrome-finished interiors and interactive installations Lenskart evolv's services include AI-assisted eye testing, remote optometrist consultations, and a digital shopping assistant. The store also uses Tango Eye technology to support the shopping experience. Lenskart CEO Peyush Bansal said the concept store aims to expand how customers discover and experience eyewear. The company plans to explore a limited number of similar stores in the future. Delhivery, Peak XV Partners launch Demo Day Delhivery and Peak XV Partners have launched Demo Day, powered by Amazon Web Services, to support startups developing technology for supply chains and logistics. The initiative will focus on artificial intelligence applications in logistics, robotics and industrial automation. Selected startups will present their solutions to Delhivery and Peak XV leaders and may access mentorship, cloud infrastructure support, potential investment and opportunities to test technologies in live logistics environments through Delhivery’s network. The programme is open to startups developing solutions for the Indian market, with an emphasis on technologies that can be deployed in real-world operations. Unicorn India Ventures launches US operations to support Indian deeptech startups Deeptech venture capital firm Unicorn India Ventures has launched operations in the US, appointing former Google executive Kishore Kanakamedala as Venture Partner. He will lead the expansion, build a team of mid-to-senior professionals and develop relationships with investors and technology ecosystems in the US to help Indian portfolio companies expand internationally. The move follows the firm’s closure of its third fund of Rs 1,200 crore earlier this year. The fund said it had observed significant interest among US investors in Indian deeptech startups during its fundraising process. Kanakamedala will also help build the US investor base and track global technology developments. Unicorn India Ventures invests in early-stage Indian deeptech companies across sectors including semiconductors, space, defence, healthcare, robotics and agritech. The firm manages approximately $350 million across its funds and has backed 54 companies. ZFunds launches US stocks and ETFs, opens 5,000 accounts on day one Wealth management platform ZFunds has launched US stocks and exchange-traded funds (ETFs), enabling Indian investors to access securities listed in the US market. The platform opened around 5,000 new accounts on the first day of the launch. Investors can access US-listed companies, including Apple, NVIDIA, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and Berkshire Hathaway, along with ETFs. The offering brings international investing into ZFunds’ wealth manager-led model, allowing customers to manage global investments through the financial professionals handling their other wealth requirements. Manish Kothari, CEO and Co-founder of ZFunds, said global diversification could improve risk-adjusted returns and provide exposure to investment themes such as artificial intelligence and semiconductors. The company cited Reserve Bank of India data showing that overseas equity and debt investments under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme rose 56% to approximately $2.65 billion in FY26. Cortex DC plans 2 GW data centre capacity across India Cortex DC, the AI-focused subsidiary of The Chatterjee Group (TCG), has entered the data centre sector with plans to develop 2 GW of capacity across India. The company aims to serve hyperscalers, cloud service providers and advanced artificial intelligence workloads amid growing demand for computing infrastructure. Cortex DC is targeting operational readiness for its first data centre within 18 months of construction commencing. It also plans to source 51% of its energy from green sources, incorporating renewable power into its infrastructure strategy. Rahul Sharma, CEO of Cortex DC, said the company aims to deliver scalable, resilient and AI-ready infrastructure for domestic and international customers. The company has assembled a leadership team with experience in engineering, construction and digital infrastructure. Its investments are also expected to generate direct and indirect employment across construction, engineering, supply chains and facility operations. (This article will be updated with the latest news throughout the day.)

title: Building a New Foundation for Education: Anshu Kumar’s Neev Ki Eent Foundation for Children of Bihar’s Brick Kiln Workers
content: Every year, thousands of families in Bihar move from one place to another in search of employment. A significant number of these families work at brick kilns. For them, migration is not simply about changing locations. It means changing homes and workplaces. In the process, children’s education often takes a back seat. When a family leaves its village for a few months to work at a brick kiln, its children usually move with it. Schools may be located far away, and a lack of essential documents can make it difficult to access government services. Limited awareness of welfare schemes adds to the challenges. The impact is felt not only in children’s education but also in the entire family’s access to social security. Anshu Kumar Jaiswal from Bihar had not encountered this challenge for the first time through a report or a set of statistics. He had witnessed it on the ground. Between 2019 and 2021, while working with the Piramal Foundation as a Gandhi Fellow, he arrived in Sheikhpura. It was here that he came face to face with the lives of families living and working at brick kilns. This experience changed the direction of his work. He eventually went on to establish the Neev Ki Eent Foundation (NKEF). Today, the NGO works to improve access to education for children of brick kiln workers, help families obtain essential documents, connect them with government welfare schemes, and strengthen local leadership. A change that began in Sheikhpura Anshu’s early education and career gradually led him towards development and public institutions. He studied mass communication and later earned a master’s degree in social work, specialising in youth and community development. He also had opportunities to represent India at international youth programmes. These included the ASEAN-India Youth Summit and a youth exchange programme in China under the Government of India’s Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports. His subsequent work brought him into contact with various government and development institutions. He worked with the Aspirational Districts Programme, Parliament, the Ministry of Labour and Employment, and the Ministry of Panchayati Raj. These experiences helped him understand how government schemes are designed and how they are implemented on the ground. However, his experience in Sheikhpura was different. Here, he had the opportunity to understand policies and ground-level needs more closely. While working among families employed at brick kilns, he identified several opportunities to improve children’s education and help them connect with schools. He realised that if education could be made more accessible to these families and adapted to their circumstances, children would have a better chance of continuing their studies. Also Read ShuruKar: Your next business could start in your hometown Speaking to YourStory, Anshu Kumar Jaiswal explains, “After meeting families working at brick kilns, I realised that children’s education is not just a school-related issue. Wherever a family works, the child often stays there too. If the family keeps moving from one place to another, the child’s education is likely to suffer. Therefore, simply trying to send a child to school is not enough. Family documents, access to government schemes, and community participation are equally important.” This realisation motivated him to work towards educating the children of brick kiln workers. The initiative is being implemented under Project Swabhimaan, led by Sheikhpura Collector and District Magistrate Shekhar Anand, an IAS officer from the 2018 batch. Launched in February 2026, the initiative has been implemented across the district. While working under this project, Anshu observed that many families lacked essential documents such as birth certificates, Aadhaar cards, ration cards, and bank accounts. The consequences of missing documents extended beyond administrative procedures. They directly affected access to education, ration supplies, healthcare, and social security services. Another question also emerged: if a child must stay with their family at a brick kiln for a certain period, why should education not be made accessible there? Taking Education Where the Children Are After 2022, Anshu began spending time with migrant workers and families employed at brick kilns. Gradually, his focus shifted towards developing a model that could address educational needs alongside other challenges faced by these families. In 2023, he established the Neev Ki Eent Foundation. The NGO works to reduce the social and economic challenges faced by migrant workers and families employed at brick kilns. Its primary programme is Project Swabhimaan. The initiative focuses on education, documentation, access to government schemes, community mobilisation, and preparing young people to take on leadership roles. An important component of this initiative is the Akshar Learning Centre. Through these centres, the organisation attempts to bring education closer to children at the locations where their families work. Children receive foundational instruction in reading, writing, and mathematics. They are also prepared to transition into the formal education system. The distinctive feature of this model is that it takes children’s actual circumstances into account. When families move elsewhere for work, efforts are made to ensure that education remains accessible to their children. Anshu says, “For us, education does not simply mean that a child’s name is entered into a school register. The real question is whether the child continues to learn. The biggest challenge for children of migrant workers is that their lives keep changing. Therefore, we need a system that understands their circumstances and keeps them connected to education. Our effort is to create that continuity.” Under Project Swabhimaan, the foundation also works with children’s families. The NGO assists them in obtaining essential documents, including birth certificates, Aadhaar cards, caste certificates, ration cards, bank accounts, and Ayushman cards. This work goes beyond helping families obtain paperwork. Essential identity documents enable families to establish their presence within the government system. They also open up opportunities to access public services and welfare schemes. That is why the Neev Ki Eent Foundation’s model does not treat education and civic identity as separate issues. Bridging the Gap Between Communities and the Administration One of the challenges faced by grassroots organisations is that their impact can remain limited to a small geographical area. From the beginning, Anshu emphasised working alongside government institutions. Sheikhpura is an example of this approach. The district where he first encountered brick kiln communities as a Gandhi Fellow has now become a place where the Neev Ki Eent Foundation is working with the district administration on a larger scale. Currently, around 55 brick kilns in Sheikhpura have been brought within the initiative’s scope. Efforts are underway to reach thousands of migrant workers and children. Alongside education, the programme focuses on documentation, access to government welfare schemes, community participation, and connecting children with formal schools and Anganwadi services. According to Anshu, more than 15,000 documentation-related needs have been identified or addressed with assistance across different categories. These include birth certificates, Aadhaar cards, caste certificates, ration cards, Ayushman cards, and bank accounts. Another aspect of this work is protection from extreme heat. People working at brick kilns often have to work for long hours in intense heat. Children also live in the same environment. In response, the Neev Ki Eent Foundation has worked with public institutions towards developing heat-resilient spaces. These spaces aim to bring together cooling facilities, children’s education, care, and community-related activities. Anshu explains, “Our objective is not to create a parallel system separate from the government. Government institutions have both the resources and the responsibility. Our role is to reduce the distance between communities and the system. When a family’s needs reach the right department and a department’s scheme reaches the right person, its impact becomes visible. We believe that if communities, civil society organisations, and the administration work together, the model can be scaled up.” This approach is also connected to Anshu’s earlier experience with public administration. He has seen first-hand that having a scheme on paper and ensuring that its benefits reach a family are two different things. Empowering Young People to Lead Change Anshu’s work is not limited to providing external assistance. He also wants to develop people within communities who understand local challenges and can play an active role in addressing them. With this objective, the Swabhimaan Fellowship was launched. Through the fellowship, local young people are trained to support children’s education, inform families about government schemes, and work closely with their communities. The goal is to enable these young people to become voices for their communities and play an important role in bringing about change. Trust plays a crucial role when working with brick kiln workers. Someone from outside the community may understand a family’s problems, but a young person from within the same community is more familiar with its language, relationships, and everyday difficulties. Also Read Taruwar Agro: Three Bihar Friends Built a Rs 2.5 Crore Business from Banana Waste Anshu believes that local leadership is essential to making social change sustainable over the long term. He says, “If change within a community depends entirely on people coming from outside, it will have its limitations. We want young people from the community to step forward themselves. They can support children’s education, inform families about government services, and communicate with the administration when necessary. This ensures that the community is not merely receiving assistance but becomes an active participant in its own transformation.” This is where the energy of Bihar’s youth can be connected to the need for social change. From Sheikhpura to the Rest of Bihar As its work in Sheikhpura expands, Anshu is also looking towards other brick kiln communities across Bihar. The Neev Ki Eent Foundation is working on a model that can be replicated in different parts of the state. Seasonal migration is not new to Bihar. For decades, families have moved from one place to another in search of employment, making migration a longstanding feature of the rural economy. Therefore, the solution to this challenge cannot be limited to a single project or district. For Anshu, the larger question is whether it is possible to create a system in which children can continue their education even when their families must migrate for work. Essential family documents should remain accessible, access to government schemes should continue, and workers should be recognised not merely as labourers but as citizens with rights. Anshu says, “Our efforts are not limited to changing the situation at a single brick kiln. The bigger question is whether children can continue their education despite seasonal migration. Can families retain their identity documents and access to government services wherever they go? If we can find practical answers to these questions, the model could also be used for other migrant communities across Bihar.” A New Approach, A New Bihar The story of Anshu and the Neev Ki Eent Foundation did not begin in a large office or with a major project. It started with his work in Sheikhpura as a fellow. There, he encountered families whose lives are often reduced to a number in government statistics. A few years later, he returned to the same place in a different role. This time, he had his own organisation, the experience he had gained over the years, and a model that brought communities, young people, and the administration together. This shift represents an important aspect of Bihar’s evolving development story. The state’s development is no longer defined solely by infrastructure, roads, or employment statistics. Access to education, digital and civic identity, government welfare schemes, local leadership, and community participation are also becoming increasingly important. Young people like Anshu Kumar are playing a significant role in this transformation. They are not simply identifying problems but also exploring new ways for communities, public policies, and administrative institutions to work together. The Neev Ki Eent Foundation’s work is ongoing, as are its efforts to expand beyond Sheikhpura into other parts of Bihar. However, the significance of this journey lies in more than its current reach. It represents a larger possibility. When government policies and welfare schemes are combined with local knowledge and the participation of young people and grassroots organisations, social change can become more effective and sustainable. Such efforts matter because development does not happen only from the top down. It becomes stronger when policies reach the ground and the voices of communities reach policymakers. Anshu’s journey, which began among the brick kilns of Sheikhpura, is an example of this dialogue. A young man witnessed a problem, understood its underlying causes, and began working towards a solution. Today, Bihar increasingly needs young people, local organisations, and administrative initiatives that connect development with people’s everyday lives. When education, identity, social security, and employment are addressed collectively, the impact can extend beyond a single family. Gradually, it can change the direction of an entire community. Perhaps this is one of the most important aspects of Bihar’s changing development story: the foundation of progress is not built solely through large projects. It is also built through small but consistent efforts that give people access to opportunities, dignity, and a path towards a better future. title: 5 Lessons from Prithvi Raj Banerjee’s Mindful Thinking
content: Anxiety, distraction and overthinking can make everyday life feel overwhelming. In Mindful Thinking: Simple Ways to Let Go of Your Anxiety, Boost Your Productivity and Rewire Your Thoughts , technologist and mindfulness coach Prithvi Raj Banerjee explores how people can understand and gradually change unhelpful thinking patterns. As the founder of the MindGym Initiative, Banerjee approaches mindfulness as a practical skill rather than an abstract spiritual concept. Drawing on mindfulness, cognitive science and everyday exercises, he explains how people can improve their focus, manage anxious thoughts and respond more consciously to life's challenges. 5 Lessons from Prithvi Raj Banerjee’s mindful thinking 1. Train your attention like a muscle Attention can be strengthened through regular practice. Instead of becoming frustrated whenever your mind wanders, recognise the distraction and gently return to the task at hand. Like physical exercise, consistent practice can help you develop better focus over time. The lesson: Focus is a skill you can build through small, consistent efforts. 2. Learn to observe your thoughts without believing them Not every thought reflects reality. Anxiety can make ordinary situations seem threatening, encouraging you to believe worst-case scenarios without questioning them. Banerjee's approach encourages you to observe thoughts without immediately accepting or reacting to them. The lesson: Recognising that thoughts are not always facts can help you respond more thoughtfully. 3. Practise mindfulness through small exercises Mindfulness does not always require long meditation sessions. Techniques discussed in the book, such as Belly Breathing, Bumblebee Humming and the Sensation Scan, offer practical ways to bring attention back to the present moment. You can experiment with these exercises and find what works for your routine. The lesson: Small mindfulness practices can make awareness part of everyday life. Also Read 7 insightful books on anxiety, identity, and online chaos 4. Protect your attention in a digital world Notifications, social media and constant screen-switching can make sustained concentration difficult. Banerjee also highlights the importance of using artificial intelligence thoughtfully rather than accepting its outputs without questioning them. Setting boundaries around technology can help preserve focus and independent thinking. The lesson: Use technology intentionally instead of allowing it to dictate your attention. 5. Pause before reacting to stress Stress can trigger impulsive responses and unnecessary worry. Taking a few deliberate breaths and identifying your emotions before reacting can create space to consider your options. Mindfulness does not eliminate difficult feelings; it encourages you to respond to them more consciously. The lesson: A brief pause can help you make more thoughtful decisions. Final thoughts Prithvi Raj Banerjee's Mindful Thinking presents mindfulness as a practical way to understand thoughts, manage distractions and strengthen attention. Its central message is that you do not need to eliminate every negative thought to think more clearly. By practising awareness, questioning assumptions and making deliberate choices, you can gradually develop a healthier relationship with your mind.

title: [Weekly funding roundup Oct 17-23] VC funding falls below $100M amid lack of big deals
content: Venture capital funding for Indian startups saw a steep decline in the third week of October, primarily due to a lower number of deals and the absence of any large-value transactions. Venture capital funding during the week stood at just $96 million across 15 deals. In contrast, startups raised a total of $180 million in the previous week. This sharp drop in venture capital funding highlights the challenges the Indian startup ecosystem continues to face in raising a steady flow of capital. This is also the eighth time so far this year that weekly venture capital funding has fallen below the $100 million mark. The only large deal during the week was Even Healthcare’s $50 million raise. The other deals were worth $11 million or less. While transactions during the week saw investors place their bets across segments such as healthcare, consumer and AI, there were no other significant deals. The biggest challenge for the Indian startup ecosystem so far this year has been the low number of large-value deals. In fact, there have been just 16 deals worth $100 million or more. This does not bode well for the ecosystem as 2026 draws to a close. However, there is hope for a revival in 2027. Key transactions Even Healthcare raised $50 million from Khosla Ventures and Alpha Wave. The Pant Project , a premium menswear label, raised Rs 109 crore ($11.4 million approx.) from Mirae Asset Venture Investments, Sorin Investments, Alteria Capital, and family offices. Rural healthcare platform CureBay raised Rs 100 crore ($10.4 million approx.) from IvyCap Ventures, Trifecta Capital, Alteria Capital and VentureSoul Partners. Chapter Home , a home and kitchen consumer brand, raised Rs 63 crore ($6.6 million approx.) from Bessemer Venture Partners, Stride Ventures, influencer Tanmay Bhat, and select family offices. Traveltech startup TravClan raised $5 million from Flipkart, August One, and Trifecta Capital. AI startup Hunar AI raised Rs 40 crore ($4.2 million) from Blume Ventures, Hyderabad Angels Fund, Together Fund, Seedstars, AVNM Ventures and startup founders.

title: Tonbo Imaging shares make stellar market debut; jump 66%
content: Shares of Tonbo Imaging India, a defence electronics maker, on Friday listed with a premium of 66% against the issue price of Rs 700. The stock made its debut at Rs 1,162 apiece, registering a premium of 66% from the issue price on the BSE. Later, it traded at Rs 1,059.05, down 8.86% from its listing price, still maintaining a premium of 51.28% over its issue price. On the NSE, the shares opened at Rs 1,160 apiece, a jump of 65.71% over the issue price. It was later trading at Rs 1,058.30, down by 3.64% from the opening level, but 51.18% higher than the issue price. Following the listing, the company's market capitalisation stood at Rs 6,191.91 crore on the BSE and Rs 6,060.45 crore on the NSE. The broader equity market was trading in the red, with the BSE Sensex falling 409.06 points, or 0.56%, to 72,840.33, while the NSE Nifty dropped 173.65 points, or 0.77%, to 22,514. The Rs 852.18-crore initial public offering (IPO) was subscribed nearly 136 times on the final day of bidding on Monday. The public issue was fully subscribed on the first day of bidding on Thursday last week. The issue comprises an offer-for-sale (OFS) of 1.22 crore equity shares by promoters and existing shareholders, with no fresh issue component. Since the IPO is entirely an OFS, the company will not receive any proceeds from the issue. The price band for the IPO has been fixed at Rs 665-700 per share. The Bengaluru-based Tonbo Imaging designs and manufactures sensing, processing, communication and guidance systems used in surveillance, reconnaissance, targeting and control applications. Its product portfolio includes thermal imaging cores, weapon sights, targeting systems, missile seekers, fire control systems and missile guidance systems. As of June 30, 2026, the company has deployed over 28,000 tactical systems and served customers across 24 countries. According to the F&S Report, Tonbo Imaging competes with the likes of Epirus and Teledyne FLIR (US), Hensoldt (Germany), Theon International, and Controp (Israel), which represent established players in electro-optical/ infrared, thermal imaging, and advanced defence electronics in the global market.

title: Swiggy’s Q2: Net loss drops nearly 16%, revenue rises 36%; What sells? The celebrity or the product?
content: Dear Reader, Shiprocket expands into the food commerce market. The company’s AI-native commerce platform fastrr has partnered with Vegorama Group, which operates Punjabi Angithi, and Bikkgane Biryani, to help the restaurant brands manage direct orders, customer engagement, and hyperlocal deliveries. The round comprises Rs 69 crore in equity from IvyCap Ventures and existing investors, and more than Rs 30 crore in debt from Trifecta Capital, Alteria Capital, and VentureSoul Partners. CureBay will use the funds to expand its operations across India, strengthen its healthcare delivery network, and develop its technology and AI capabilities.
